Here is the full locality guide produced by the research agent:

---

# Locality Guide: Berkshire County, Massachusetts (1820–1850)

## An important correction to the survey's premise

The request assumes no civil records exist before Massachusetts's unified registration act of 1841. **This is not accurate.** The [FamilySearch Wiki's Massachusetts Vital Records page](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records) states that vital recording was ordered by law as early as 1639. The 1841 act created a *statewide unified* layer on top of an already-existing town-clerk system. For 1820–1840, town clerk records are the primary civil source. For 1841–1850, both the town series and the state series exist. FamilySearch confirms this with a digitized browse-only volume (DGS 004500891) covering Berkshire County vital and town records 1761–1850 and an indexed statewide collection (ID 2061550). Church registers and cemetery inscriptions remain vital supplements — especially where town compliance was uneven — but they do not substitute for a void that does not exist.

---

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** 1761 from Hampshire County
- **County seat:** Pittsfield
- **State borders:** New York (west), Vermont (north)
- **Economy:** Agriculture, iron manufacturing, paper mills; Hudson River trade corridor shapes migration
- **Religion:** Predominantly Congregational; also Methodist, Baptist, Episcopal; Roman Catholic arriving by the 1840s
- **Key historical events:** War of 1812 (pension records extend well into the target window); Mexican-American War 1846–1848; accelerating Irish immigration by the 1840s

---

## Available record types

### 1. Vital records (town clerk level)

- **Coverage:** Town clerks were required to record births, marriages, and deaths under Massachusetts law from 1639. For 1820–1840, town records are the only civil series. For 1841–1850, the state series duplicates or supplements them.
- **Digitized at FamilySearch:**
  - DGS 004500891 — "Berkshire County Town Clerk Vital and Town Records, 1761–1850," 512 images, **browse-only** (not indexed, not full-text searchable; must be paged through image by image)
  - Collection ID 2061550 — "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890," 3.4 million records, **indexed with images** — this likely corresponds to the published *Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850* series produced for 200+ Massachusetts towns
- **Strategy:** Search the indexed collection first; browse DGS 004500891 for entries the index may have missed; then contact the individual town clerk's office for undigitized originals.
- **Marriage intentions note:** Per the Massachusetts Vital Records wiki, intentions were commonly recorded in the bride's home town and may also appear in the groom's home town and their current residence. Search all three locations.

### 2. Church records

- **Denominations confirmed by this survey:** Congregational (Pittsfield, confirmed by DGS 004500892, 274 images, 1791–1850, **browse-only**). Methodist, Baptist, Episcopal, and Catholic congregations are known to have been present but no additional Berkshire County church volumes were returned in this survey.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations. Catholic registers from the 1840s onward are typically in Latin.
- **Indexed at FamilySearch:** Collection ID 1921657 — "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920," ~988,000 records, **indexed with images**.
- **Physical holdings:** Individual church archives; Berkshire Athenaeum (Pittsfield); Congregational Library and Archives (Boston) for Congregational records; New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS, Boston).

### 3. Cemetery records

- **Online:** [Find A Grave](https://www.findagrave.com/) — transcribed inscriptions and photographs, volunteer-sourced; coverage is uneven. Absence of a memorial does not mean the person is not buried there.
- **Physical:** Sexton records and burial registers, where they survive, are held by town clerks, cemetery associations, or the Berkshire Athenaeum.
- **Value:** Death dates and ages on stones can establish birth years and family groupings for years when vital records compliance was thin.

### 4. Census records

- **Federal censuses:** 1820, 1830, 1840 (head of household only; all other members tallied by age bracket and sex). **1850** (the first to name every household member individually by name, age, sex, birthplace, and occupation) — the most important single census for the target window.
- **Mortality schedules:** Begin in 1850. The 1850 mortality schedule names individuals who died in the year before enumeration (June 1849–May 1850), with age, sex, birthplace, occupation, and cause of death — a proxy death record for that narrow window.
- **Access:** Free at FamilySearch; subscription at Ancestry.

### 5. Probate records

- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, letters of administration (intestate), guardianship bonds, dower releases.
- **Value:** Probate files name heirs, ages, and sometimes relationships — especially useful for reconstructing families in years where vital records are thin.
- **Date range:** From county formation 1761 through and beyond the target window.
- **Digitized at FamilySearch:** Collection ID 1678901 — "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991," ~568,000 records, **indexed with images**.
- **Physical holdings:** Berkshire County Probate Court, Pittsfield.

### 6. Land records (deeds)

- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds.
- **Coverage:** County-level deed recording from formation in 1761; unbroken through the target window.
- **Content:** Deeds name grantor, grantee, neighbors, witnesses, and sometimes relationships. They can establish residence dates and kin networks where vital records are silent.
- **Status:** No indexed FamilySearch collection for Berkshire County deed records was returned by this survey. Physical or microfilm access only at the **Berkshire County Registry of Deeds, Pittsfield**.

### 7. Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** War of 1812 (pension files extending into the 1820s–1840s are prime sources for men born 1760–1800; affidavits often name wife, marriage date, and children); Mexican-American War 1846–1848.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants.
- **Online:** [Fold3](https://www.fold3.com/) (subscription) — War of 1812 pension files, Mexican-American War service records. NARA ([archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/)) is the original holder.

### 8. Naturalization records

- **Note:** Naturalizations before 1906 were filed in any court of record — Berkshire County courts as well as state and federal courts.
- **Digitized at FamilySearch:** Collection ID 1459213 — "Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906," ~346,000 records, **indexed with images**.

### 9. Passenger lists

- **Context:** Berkshire County is inland; family members arriving from abroad likely came through Boston or via Albany/Hudson (New York) ports.
- **Digitized at FamilySearch:** Collection ID 1784312 — "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891," ~1.2 million records, **indexed with images**. For arrivals via New York ports, search NARA's separate New York arrival collections.

### 10. Tax records

- **Types:** Town-level property tax and poll tax lists; run continuously through the target window.
- **Value:** Tax lists can establish residence in intercensal years (1821–1829, 1831–1839, etc.) when neither a census year nor a vital event pins the person in place.
- **Physical holdings:** Individual town clerk offices; Massachusetts State Archives (Boston). No digitized FamilySearch collection was returned for these.

### 11. Other records

- **Town meeting records:** Name residents not found in any vital or church series. Held at individual town clerk offices.
- **County court minute books (Sessions, Common Pleas):** Road assignments, poor relief, guardianships, civil/criminal proceedings — name people found nowhere else. Held at the Massachusetts State Archives and the county courthouse.
- **Newspapers:** Death notices, marriage announcements, estate notices, probate postings. [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/) (subscription) covers many 19th-century Massachusetts titles. The Berkshire Athenaeum holds local microfilm.
- **Town and county histories:** Published 19th- and early-20th-century histories frequently reprint original records (family lists, early vital records, church rolls) and sometimes are the only surviving transcription of records since lost.

---

## Repository guide

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Collections 2061550, 1921657, 1678901, 1459213, 1784312; browse volumes DGS 004500891, 004500892 | Free |
| Ancestry | Federal censuses 1820–1850; additional Massachusetts records | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery transcriptions and photos | Free |
| Fold3 | Military service and pension records | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Massachusetts newspapers | Subscription |
| NARA, Washington DC | Pension files, military service records, passenger lists | Free (online via partners) |
| Berkshire County town clerk offices (each town) | Original town clerk vital records; tax lists; town meeting records | In person or written request |
| Berkshire County Probate Court, Pittsfield | Original probate dockets from 1761 | In person |
| Berkshire County Registry of Deeds, Pittsfield | Deed books and grantor/grantee indexes from 1761 | In person; some microfilm |
| Massachusetts State Archives, Boston | Colony and commonwealth records; court records; additional vital series | In person |
| Berkshire Athenaeum, Pittsfield | Local history, newspaper microfilm, town histories, cemetery transcriptions | In person |
| New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS), Boston | Largest genealogical library in the region; manuscript collections; published *Vital Records to 1850* series | In person + AmericanAncestors.org (subscription) |

---

## Records NOT online

- Berkshire County deed books (land records), 1820–1850 — physical/microfilm only at the Registry of Deeds
- Town clerk original vital records (pre-1841 period) — the browse-only DGS 004500891 covers some, but most originals remain with individual town clerks
- Town meeting records and town tax lists — physical access at each town clerk office
- Berkshire County court minute books — physical access at the Massachusetts State Archives or county courthouse
- Most individual church registers outside Pittsfield Congregational — only one church volume (DGS 004500892) was returned; other Berkshire County congregational archives may be undigitized
- New York and Vermont cross-border records — entirely separate systems not covered here

---

## Research tips

1. **Town clerk records first.** Search the indexed "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890" (ID 2061550) for every birth, marriage, and death event in this window before concluding a record doesn't exist in civil form. Then browse DGS 004500891 for entries the index may have missed.

2. **Marriage intentions in multiple places.** Per the Massachusetts Vital Records wiki, intentions were commonly recorded in the bride's home town and may also appear in the groom's town and their current residence. Search all three when the intention is a research target.

3. **1841 is a threshold, not an origin.** For 1820–1840, only town clerk records and church registers provide civil coverage. For 1841–1850, both the town series and the state series exist; discrepancies between them can flag transcription errors or delayed registration.

4. **Search across the New York and Vermont lines.** This is a border county; members of a family near the state lines may have been baptized, married, or buried on the other side. New York vital registration did not begin statewide until 1880 (before that: church registers, cemetery transcriptions, county deed and probate files). Vermont began statewide registration in 1857 (before that: town records required from 1779, plus church registers). Identify the specific bordering New York and Vermont counties by mapping the target town's location, then search those county records separately.

5. **Use the 1850 mortality schedule as a death-record proxy.** It names individuals who died in the year before enumeration (June 1849–May 1850) with age, birthplace, occupation, and cause of death. It is the earliest federal enumeration to do so and is indexed on both Ancestry and FamilySearch.

6. **Consult NEHGS and the *Vital Records to 1850* published series.** The Massachusetts Genealogy wiki notes the series was published for more than 200 towns. NEHGS (AmericanAncestors.org) holds these volumes along with manuscript collections not digitized elsewhere. For a border county, also check town histories from the adjacent New York and Vermont sides.

7. **Treat tax lists and deed books as residence anchors.** For the intercensal years 1821–1829 and 1831–1839, when no census year lands, tax lists and deeds can pin a person to a specific Berkshire County town and establish kin networks through named neighbors and witnesses.

---

*Note on FamilySearch Wiki coverage:* The place-specific FamilySearch Wiki pages for Berkshire County (home, getting started, online records, research tips) and several Massachusetts topic pages (Church Records, Census, Land and Property) returned only generic boilerplate during this survey, on both initial and retry calls. Only the Massachusetts Vital Records page and the Massachusetts Genealogy article returned substantive guidance. These topic pages likely exist and may contain additional relevant detail; re-run this survey to retrieve them before treating their absence as confirmed.

- **Where held (originals):** Individual church archives, the Berkshire Athenaeum (local history library in Pittsfield), and denominational archives (e.g., the Congregational Library and Archives in Boston for Congregational records). - **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Per the Massachusetts Genealogy wiki article, land deeds were recorded at the county level from the 1630s ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial)). The specific Massachusetts Land and Property wiki page could not be loaded during this survey.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, grantor/grantee indexes. Town proprietor records may exist for earlier settlement but are mostly pre-period for Berkshire County.
- **Date range:** County-level deed recording from formation in 1761 through and beyond the target window.
- **Where held:** Berkshire County Registry of Deeds, Pittsfield. No indexed FamilySearch collection for Berkshire County land records was returned in this survey's results. Land records for this period appear to be physical or microfilm only.
- **Value:** Deeds name grantor, grantee, neighbors (by name), witnesses, and sometimes relationships. They can establish residence dates and kin networks where vital records are silent.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** War of 1812 (ended 1815, but pension files extend decades into the target period and are a prime source for men born 1760–1800); Mexican-American War 1846–1848 (falls squarely in the window).
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files (War of 1812 and earlier), bounty land warrants, draft registrations. Pension files often include affidavits naming wife, marriage date, and children — a substantial supplement to vital records.
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA). Fold3 ([https://www.fold3.com/](https://www.fold3.com/)) is a curated external link returned for Massachusetts in this survey and provides digitized military records with subscription access.
- **Digitization:** NARA pension files are indexed on Fold3 and Ancestry; images vary by collection.

### Cemetery records

- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave ([https://www.findagrave.com/](https://www.findagrave.com/)) is a curated external link for this place and provides transcribed inscriptions and photographs with free access. Coverage for Berkshire County is volunteer-sourced and therefore uneven; absence of a memorial does not mean the person is not buried there.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers, where they survive, are held by individual town clerks, cemetery associations, or the Berkshire Athenaeum.
- **Value for 1820–1850:** Death dates and ages on stones can establish birth years and family groupings for years before even town clerk records are complete.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** Specific Berkshire County newspaper titles and their date ranges are not returned in any tool result this survey retrieved.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com ([https://www.newspapers.com/](https://www.newspapers.com/)) is a curated external link for Massachusetts and covers many 19th-century titles with subscription access. The Berkshire Athenaeum holds local microfilm.
- **Content value:** Death notices, marriage announcements, estate notices, and legal notices (including probate postings) routinely appear in Berkshire County papers of this period and provide dates and kin names not always entered in registers.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Context:** The target window (1820–1850) covers the beginning of substantial transatlantic immigration. Berkshire County is inland and far from a port, but family members may have arrived via Albany (Hudson River) or Boston.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests at ports (Boston, New York/Albany area), declarations of intention and naturalization petitions filed in Berkshire County courts, and alien registrations.
- **Naturalization:** Naturalizations before 1906 were filed in any court of record — Berkshire County courts as well as state and federal courts. Collection "Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790-1906" (ID 1459213, 345,678 records) at [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1459213](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1459213) — **indexed + images**.
- **Passenger lists:** "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820-1891" (ID 1784312, 1,234,567 records) at [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1784312](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1784312) — **indexed + images**. For arrivals via New York ports, search NARA's passenger list collections separately. Examine the full manifest for all family members — children including infants travel with parents and are listed by name.
- **New York cross-border note:** Families near the New York line may have used Albany or Hudson as their port city. New York arrival manifests are held at NARA and indexed on Ancestry.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Town-level property tax and poll tax lists. Massachusetts used town-level taxation throughout this period.
- **Date range:** Town tax lists generally run from the colonial period onward, through the entire target window.
- **Where held:** Individual town clerk offices and the Massachusetts State Archives (Boston). The Massachusetts Archives is noted in the Massachusetts Genealogy wiki article as the repository for colony records ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial)).
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists for 1820, 1825, 1835 (intercensal years) can establish a person's residence and approximate wealth bracket when census years don't pin them. Men who appear in tax lists but not in church or vital records are still locatable.

### Other record types

- **Town meeting records:** Massachusetts towns maintained meeting records recording votes, appointments, and local assessments. These name residents not found in any vital or church series. Held at individual town clerk offices.
- **Court records:** Berkshire County court minutes (Sessions, Common Pleas) record road-maintenance assignments, poor relief, guardianships, and civil/criminal proceedings — naming people found nowhere else. Held at the Massachusetts Archives and the county courthouse.
- **Town and county histories:** 19th- and early-20th-century published histories of Berkshire County towns frequently reprint original records (family lists, early vital records, church membership rolls) and sometimes are the only surviving transcription of records since lost. NEHGS and the Berkshire Athenaeum hold these.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890 (ID 2061550); Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920 (ID 1921657); Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991 (ID 1678901); Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790-1906 (ID 1459213); Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820-1891 (ID 1784312); browse-only volumes DGS 004500891 and 004500892 | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (all years 1820–1850); additional Massachusetts records | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery transcriptions and photographs ([https://www.findagrave.com/](https://www.findagrave.com/)) | Free |
| Fold3 | Military records including War of 1812 pension files and Mexican-American War service records ([https://www.fold3.com/](https://www.fold3.com/)) | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Massachusetts newspapers ([https://www.newspapers.com/](https://www.newspapers.com/)) | Subscription |
| NARA | Passenger lists, military service and pension records, naturalization records ([https://www.archives.gov/](https://www.archives.gov/)) | Free (online via partners) |

**Coverage of this survey:** The `volume_search` returned a complete set of 2 digitized volumes for Berkshire County, 1820–1850. Both are browse-only. The 5 state-level indexed collections above cover Massachusetts broadly and include Berkshire County records.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Berkshire County town clerk offices (each town) | Original town clerk vital records 1820–1850; tax lists; town meeting records | In person or written request to each town |
| Berkshire County Probate Court, Pittsfield | Original probate dockets from 1761 onward | In person; county courthouse |
| Berkshire County Registry of Deeds, Pittsfield | Deed books and grantor/grantee indexes from 1761 | In person; some microfilm |
| Massachusetts State Archives, Boston | Colony and commonwealth records; court records; additional vital record series | In person; [https://www.archives.gov/](https://www.archives.gov/) for federal holdings |
| Berkshire Athenaeum, Pittsfield | Local history collection, newspaper microfilm, town histories, cemetery transcriptions | In person; contact for access |
| New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS), Boston | Largest genealogical library in the region (Massachusetts Genealogy wiki, [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Military](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Military)); manuscript collections, published vital records series | In person and online (AmericanAncestors.org, subscription) |

---

## Records NOT online

- **Berkshire County deed books (land records), 1820–1850:** No indexed FamilySearch collection for county deed records was returned in this survey. Physical or microfilm access only at the Berkshire County Registry of Deeds.
- **Town clerk original vital records, 1820–1850 (pre-1841 period):** The browse-only volume DGS 004500891 covers some of this but is not name-indexed. Original registers remain with individual town clerks.
- **Town meeting records and town tax lists:** No digitized collection was returned for these. Physical access at each town clerk office.
- **Berkshire County court minute books:** Not returned as a digitized FamilySearch collection. Physical access at the Massachusetts State Archives or county courthouse.
- **Most individual church registers outside Pittsfield Congregational:** Only one church volume (DGS 004500892) was returned; other Berkshire County congregational archives are not represented in the volume_search results and may be undigitized.
- **New York and Vermont cross-border records:** Records generated in adjacent New York counties (west border) or Vermont (north border) are entirely separate systems not covered here.

---

## Known record losses

No tool result in this survey states that a specific Berkshire County record set for 1820–1850 was destroyed or lost. Absence from the online search results is a coverage gap, not confirmed destruction. When a series is missing online, contact the holding repository named above before concluding the records do not exist.

---

## Research tips

1. **Town clerk records are a primary source, not a substitute.** The delegation's framing that only church and cemetery records cover 1820–1850 contradicts the Massachusetts Vital Records wiki page ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records)). Search the indexed "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890" collection (ID 2061550) first for every birth, marriage, and death event in this window; then check the browse-only DGS 004500891 for entries the index may have missed.

2. **Marriage intentions are recorded separately and in two places.** The Massachusetts Vital Records wiki states that marriage intentions were "commonly recorded in the bride's home town and additional recordings may be found in the groom's home town and their current residence." Search all three locations when the marriage intention itself is a research target.

3. **Treat 1841 as a threshold, not an origin.** For events 1820–1840, only town clerk records and church registers provide civil or quasi-civil coverage. For 1841–1850, both the town series and the state series exist; discrepancies between them can flag transcription errors or delayed registration.

4. **Search across the New York and Vermont lines.** The family's town near both state lines means members may have been baptized, married, or buried on the other side. New York vital registration did not begin statewide until 1880 (towns varied), so the primary cross-border sources for 1820–1850 in New York are church registers, cemetery transcriptions, and county deed and probate files. Vermont began statewide registration in 1857; before that, town records (required from 1779) and church registers are the primary Vermont sources. The specific neighboring county names on the New York and Vermont sides were not returned in any tool result this survey retrieved (the FamilySearch Wiki Berkshire County home page, which would carry the Neighboring Counties table, returned only generic content); identify the bordering counties by mapping the target town's location before searching cross-border records.

5. **Use the 1850 mortality schedule as a death-record proxy.** The 1850 mortality schedule (names individuals who died in the year before the census enumeration, June 1849–May 1850) is the earliest federal enumeration to do so. It is indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch and can supply death dates unavailable elsewhere.

6. **Consult NEHGS and the "Vital Records to 1850" published series.** The Massachusetts Genealogy wiki article ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial)) notes that the "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" series was published for more than 200 Massachusetts towns. NEHGS (AmericanAncestors.org) holds these volumes and many manuscript collections not digitized elsewhere. For a family near the county's borders, town histories from both sides of the state line can carry transcribed records since lost.

---

**FamilySearch Wiki coverage note:** All four `wiki_place_page` sections (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) returned only generic boilerplate for Berkshire County and Massachusetts on both the initial call and a full retry. The `wiki_read` calls for Massachusetts_Church_Records, Massachusetts_Census, Massachusetts_Land_and_Property, and Berkshire_County,_Massachusetts_Genealogy likewise returned only generic content. Only the Massachusetts_Vital_Records page and the Massachusetts_Genealogy wiki_search result returned substantive, place-specific information. These wiki pages may exist and contain relevant guidance; re-run this locality survey to retrieve them before treating their absence as confirmed.

---

Berkshire County, Massachusetts sits in the state's westernmost strip, its towns lying within a short distance of both New York and Vermont. Old records for this area survive in multiple layers: town clerks recorded births, marriages, and deaths going back to colonial law, church registers tracked congregational life, and county courts produced an unbroken run of probate and deed files from 1761 forward. The most important thing to know is that none of these layers is redundant with the others — a family may appear in church registers but not in the town clerk's book, in the clerk's book but not in census, in the deeds but nowhere else — so all of them need to be searched. Because the family's town sits near two state lines, New York and Vermont records must be pulled alongside Massachusetts sources for a complete picture, and the rules governing what records exist and where they are held differ in each state for this period.

This guide covers the full record landscape; a research plan built around specific family names and research questions is the logical next step.

output.text_response:
## Locality Guide: Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Ireland (1780–1870)

> **Important caveat:** The genealogy tools used to build this guide returned no Ireland-specific data — every wiki page, place/collection/volume query came back empty or redirected to a generic US-focused fallback. The guide below is therefore honest about what the tools confirmed (essentially nothing) versus what is known from the structure of Irish records. Consult PRONI and the FamilySearch Wiki directly in a browser; the guidance on what records *exist* is reliable, but no collection IDs or digitization levels are confirmed by a tool result.

---

### Jurisdiction overview

- **Billy civil parish** is in the barony of Cary, County Antrim, Province of Ulster. Bushmills town lies within it.
- County Antrim was part of the Kingdom of Ireland until 1801, then the United Kingdom.
- The religious landscape was mixed: Church of Ireland, **Presbyterian** (dominant among Protestants in north Antrim), and Roman Catholic — each denomination kept its own registers, and those systems do *not* map onto the civil parish boundary.

---

### Key fact for a Presbyterian family

Billy is a *Church of Ireland civil parish*. A Presbyterian family there was **not recorded in the Church of Ireland register**. You need to identify the specific Presbyterian meeting-house (congregation) that served the Bushmills area independently of the civil-parish system. ### Probate & Court Records

- **Before 1858:** Probate was in the Church of Ireland diocesan courts (Diocese of Connor for Billy parish) and the Prerogative Court of Armagh for larger estates. Almost all pre-1858 original Irish wills were destroyed in 1922; will abstracts, indexes, and surviving copies are at PRONI and the **National Archives of Ireland (NAI)**

### Land Records

- **Registry of Deeds, Dublin (from 1708):** Memorials of deeds, wills, and instruments affecting land, voluntarily registered; covers all of Ireland

Belfast Newsletter (1738+) is searchable at [britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk](https://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk) (subscription). Irish newspaper archives: [irishnewsarchive.com](https://www.irishnewsarchive.com).

## Research Tips for a Presbyterian Family in Billy Parish

1. **Start at PRONI's church records catalog.** Search for Presbyterian and Covenanter congregations in Bushmills, Dervock, and the Dunluce area. The register microfilm number format for County Antrim Presbyterian records at PRONI is typically MIC 1P/[number].

2. **Griffith's Valuation (1858–60) is your mid-period anchor.** It places a family in a specific townland and identifies their landlord and neighbors — enough to narrow a church search geographically.

3. **Tithe Applotment Books bridge back to c. 1823.** Together with Griffith's, they give you two census-substitute snapshots roughly 30 years apart in the core period.

4. **Presbyterian marriages 1845–1870 appear in both civil and church registers.** The civil marriage entry (at irishgenealogy.ie) may supply the father's name even if the church register is sparse.

5. **The 1901 census works backward.** Anyone born in the 1820s–1840s who was still alive in 1901 or 1911 will appear with stated age, County Antrim birthplace, and religion — confirm denomination and townland before searching church registers.

6. **Covenanters are a separate series.** If the denomination is uncertain, check Reformed Presbyterian registers independently — they did not share registers with the Presbyterian Church in Ireland.

7. **Famine emigration gap (c. 1846–1852).** Records thin out sharply. If a family trail goes cold in the late 1840s, check Famine-era passenger manifests arriving at Quebec, New York, Philadelphia, and Baltimore.

The wiki-query-api is in an outage state — all four `wiki_place_page` sections and all `wiki_read` calls for Ireland-specific pages returned the same generic "Genealogy Records" placeholder, not the actual Ireland pages. ---

# Locality Guide: Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Ireland (1780–1870)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Civil parish:** Billy, County Antrim, Province of Ulster, Ireland
- **Baronies:** Partly in the Barony of Cary, chiefly in the Barony of Lower Dunluce. Source: FamilySearch wiki search result for Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Northern Ireland Genealogy (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy).
- **Poor law union:** Coleraine
- **Post town:** Bushmills; also contains a portion of Dunserverick
- **Ecclesiastical context:** Billy was formerly the head of an ecclesiastical union that comprised also the parishes of Armoy, Ballyclug, Donegore, and Kilbride. This is a civil, not diocesan, structure — church of Ireland and Roman Catholic jurisdictions ran separately.
- **Roman Catholic:** The parish is part of the RC district of Coleraine.
- **Denominations confirmed in parish:** Presbyterian meeting house, Covenanter meeting house, Wesleyan Methodist meeting house. All three are confirmed from the FamilySearch wiki_search result cited above.
- **Economy during period:** This area of north Antrim was agricultural (small tenant farms) with linen weaving as a cottage industry earlier in the period, and fishing at Bushmills.
- **Population data:** The place_search tool resolved no standardPlace for County Antrim or Ireland, so place_population could not be queried. No population figures were returned by any tool.
- **Key historical event:** The Great Famine (1845–1852) caused severe emigration from County Antrim throughout the mid-period of this survey, which directly reduces record density for the late 1840s.

## Boundary changes

- Billy civil parish boundaries appear stable across the 1780–1870 period within County Antrim.
- The Act of Union (1800, effective 1801) brought Ireland formally into the United Kingdom. This affected administrative structure but did not alter the civil parish boundary or the repositories that held local records.
- Civil registration in Ireland began on 1 April 1845 for non-Catholic marriages, and on 1 January 1864 for all births, deaths, and Catholic marriages — a split that matters for the target period: a Presbyterian marriage in Billy before 1845 appears in church registers only. Note: the registration dates given here are taken from standard Irish genealogy knowledge, not from a tool result. The FamilySearch Wiki Ireland Vital Records page could not be read during this survey due to the wiki-query-api outage (see below); verify these dates at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Vital_Records before treating them as confirmed.

## FamilySearch Wiki outage — important limitation

The wiki-query-api was unreachable during this survey. Every call to `wiki_place_page` (all four sections: home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) and every `wiki_read` call for Ireland-specific pages (Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Ireland Genealogy, Ireland Vital Records, Ireland Church Records, Northern Ireland Genealogy) returned the same generic placeholder page, not the actual article. The specific content of those pages is therefore not available in this guide. **Re-run this locality guide before relying on any absence noted below** — the pages exist and likely contain congregation-level detail and collection links not captured here.

The only Ireland-specific content returned by any tool was two chunks from the `wiki_search` index, both from the Billy Civil Parish page at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy. That is the primary sourced reference for this guide.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Birth and death registration:** Civil registration of all births and deaths in Ireland began at the state (General Register Office) level on 1 January 1864 — covering only the final six years of this survey's window. Births, marriages, and deaths registered after that date are held by the General Register Office (GRO) for Ireland; original registers and indexes are searchable at www.irishgenealogy.ie (free) and in copy at PRONI Belfast for births/deaths up to 1922 in the present Northern Ireland counties.
- **Marriage registration:** Non-Catholic (including Presbyterian) marriages were civilly registered from 1 April 1845 onward, so Presbyterian marriages in Billy from 1845 to 1870 should appear in both civil registers and church registers. Before 1845, only church registers document Presbyterian marriages.
- **Gaps:** The entire period 1780–1864 (births, deaths) and 1780–1845 (Presbyterian marriages) is not covered by civil registration. Church registers are the primary source for these years.
- **Caveat:** These registration dates are not from a tool result returned during this survey. The FamilySearch Wiki Ireland Vital Records page was unreachable. Confirm dates at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Vital_Records.

### Church records

The FamilySearch wiki_search result for Billy Civil Parish confirmed that the parish had the following meeting places; the wiki page's Church Records section contained only headers with no transcribed detail. What is confirmed:

**Presbyterian**

The wiki page confirms a Presbyterian meeting house was present in Billy parish. No register dates or specific congregation name were returned by any tool for Billy parish itself. As a cross-reference, the wiki_search result for Ballylinny Civil Parish (also in County Antrim) showed that Presbyterian records in County Antrim are typically held with the local congregation in original form, with microfilm copies at the Public Record Office of Northern Ireland (PRONI). For Ballylinny, PRONI microfilm number MIC 1P/327 and FamilySearch Library film 973220 were cited. No equivalent numbers were returned for Billy parish in any tool result.

The Presbyterian congregation most likely to have served Bushmills and the Billy parish area is the Bushmills Presbyterian congregation (First Bushmills), but no tool result confirmed this or its register dates. PRONI holds microfilm of the great majority of surviving Presbyterian registers for County Antrim; search their online catalog at https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/proni under church records, filtered to County Antrim and the denomination "Presbyterian Church in Ireland."

The Reformed Presbyterian Church (Covenanters) also had a meeting house in Billy parish, confirmed by the wiki_search result. Covenanter congregations' registers are typically also held at PRONI.

**Church of Ireland**

Billy was formerly the head of an ecclesiastical union comprising Armoy, Ballyclug, Donegore, and Kilbride. No Church of Ireland register dates for Billy parish were returned by any tool during this survey. Church of Ireland registers for County Antrim parishes are held in part at PRONI and in part at the Representative Church Body Library (RCBL) in Dublin. Many were destroyed in the 1922 Public Record Office of Ireland fire in Dublin, which destroyed the original pre-1870 registers that had been deposited there. Registers retained locally or of which copies existed before 1922 sometimes survived. The status of Billy's Church of Ireland registers is not confirmed by any tool result in this survey.

**Roman Catholic**

Billy parish is part of the RC district of Coleraine (confirmed by the wiki_search result). RC registers for Coleraine district are the relevant series to search. The FamilySearch wiki page for Billy Civil Parish contains a Catholic church records section header but no content was returned. RC registers for County Antrim are searchable at www.irishgenealogy.ie. For the Coleraine district, search there first.

**Wesleyan Methodist**

A Wesleyan Methodist meeting house was confirmed in Billy parish by the wiki_search result. No register dates were returned by any tool. Methodist registers for County Antrim are generally held at PRONI or at the Methodist Church in Ireland archives in Belfast.

### Census records

- **1901 and 1911 censuses:** These survive in full and are free online at www.census.nationalarchives.ie. Both are outside or at the edge of the 1780–1870 target period, but the 1901 census names everyone in a household including older persons born in the 1830s–1840s, making it useful for confirming ages, relationships, and birthplaces of persons who were children or young adults in the target period.
- **1851 census:** The 1851 census for County Antrim was destroyed (along with 1821, 1831, 1841 returns) in the 1922 Dublin fire. No census microfilm or indexed collection for County Antrim 1780–1870 was returned by `volume_search` or `collections_search` in this survey — these tools returned zero results because place resolution failed (see note below under Repository guide).
- **Census substitutes:** Griffith's Primary Valuation (conducted in County Antrim 1858–1860) is the closest near-census source for the mid-period; it records the occupier of every land parcel and building. The Tithe Applotment Books (c. 1823–1837) record landholders liable for tithes, covering much of the rural population of Billy parish. Both are free at www.askaboutireland.ie and partially indexed on various genealogy sites.

### Probate and court records

- **Probate before 1858:** Probate jurisdiction was held by the Church of Ireland diocesan and prerogative courts. For Billy parish (Diocese of Connor), wills and administrations before 1858 were proved in the Consistorial Court of Connor (and in the Prerogative Court of Armagh for larger estates). The great majority of original pre-1858 Irish wills were destroyed in 1922; will abstracts, indexes, and surviving copies at PRONI and the National Archives of Ireland (NAI) are the main substitutes.
- **Probate from 1858:** Civil probate began in 1858 under the Principal Registry and district registries. The district registry for County Antrim was in Belfast. Original wills from 1858 onward are held at PRONI.
- **Note:** These repository and jurisdiction assignments are not from a tool result in this survey (the wiki-query-api outage prevented reading the relevant pages). Confirm at PRONI's online catalog.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Ireland used metes-and-bounds and townland descriptions, not rectangular survey. The townland is the smallest land unit.
- **Tithe Applotment Books (c. 1823–1837):** Cover landholders in Billy parish who were liable for tithes. Free online at www.askaboutireland.ie.
- **Griffith's Primary Valuation (1858–1860 for County Antrim):** Lists every occupier of land and buildings. Free at www.askaboutireland.ie. This is the most important land-based census substitute for the mid-period.
- **Registry of Deeds, Dublin (from 1708):** Memorials of deeds, wills, and other instruments affecting land, registered voluntarily. Covers the entire island. Access at the Registry of Deeds in Dublin or via PRONI extracts for some.
- **Estate papers:** Much of north Antrim was held in large estates; estate records (rentals, maps, correspondence) may name tenant families. These survive in various archives — NAI, PRONI, and private deposits.
- **No land collection hits** were returned by any tool for Billy parish in this survey because place resolution failed.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts in period:** United Irish Rebellion 1798, Napoleonic Wars (service in British Army and militia), and various militia and yeomanry establishments throughout the period.
- **British Army service records:** Held at The National Archives, Kew (UK). Pension records for soldiers discharged before 1913 are partly available via Ancestry and Findmypast.
- **Muster rolls and militia:** The 1798 period generated some surviving records; yeomanry and militia muster rolls for County Antrim are at PRONI.
- **No military volume or collection** for Billy parish was returned by any tool in this survey.

### Cemetery records

- The FamilySearch wiki_search result noted two graveyards in Ballylinny (one Presbyterian, one unstated denomination) — this is a neighboring parish, not Billy itself. No cemetery data specific to Billy parish was returned by any tool.
- Bushmills area churchyard records: search www.findagrave.com and www.billiongraves.com. The Ulster Historical Foundation has indexed some County Antrim burial grounds.
- Church of Ireland parish churchyards in the former ecclesiastical union (Armoy, Billy) may contain graves of all denominations, including Presbyterian families who could not be buried in their own meetinghouse yard.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The Coleraine Chronicle (from 1844) and the Ballymena Observer (from 1855) covered north Antrim including the Bushmills area. The Belfast Newsletter (from 1737) is the major early newspaper for all of Ulster and regularly carried notices, deaths, and legal announcements from County Antrim.
- **Online access:** The Belfast Newsletter from 1738 is searchable at www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk (subscription) and partially digitized elsewhere. The Irish Newspaper Archives (www.irishnewsarchive.com) covers some Ulster titles.
- **Content:** Death notices, farm sales, legal notices, and letters of administration published in local papers are important substitutes when registers are sparse.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Emigration context:** North Antrim saw significant emigration throughout 1780–1870, including an earlier wave to America (pre-Revolutionary and post-Revolutionary) and the Famine-era mass emigration of the late 1840s. Presbyterian families from this area emigrated heavily to Pennsylvania, the Carolinas, and later to Canada.
- **Passenger lists:** Outbound lists from Belfast and Londonderry (Derry) are the main departure points. Some survive and are held at PRONI and the NAI. The Famine-era manifests arriving at American ports are at NARA and are indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch. Passenger lists record all persons aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents — examine the full manifest for all family members when researching emigrating families.
- **No emigration or passenger collection** for Billy parish was returned by any tool in this survey because place resolution failed.

### Tax records

- **Hearth money rolls (1660s):** A pre-period source listing householders; surviving fragments for County Antrim are published and indexed.
- **Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837):** Covered above under Land records.
- **Griffith's Valuation (1858–1860):** Covered above under Land records.
- Both function as census substitutes for the years between the destroyed Irish censuses. No tax record volume or collection was returned by tool for Billy parish in this survey.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Relevant collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| www.irishgenealogy.ie | Civil registration births/deaths (from 1864), marriages (non-Catholic from 1845); RC and Church of Ireland registers for some parishes | Free |
| www.askaboutireland.ie | Griffith's Valuation; Tithe Applotment Books | Free |
| www.census.nationalarchives.ie | 1901 and 1911 census of Ireland | Free |
| www.proni.gov.uk | Church registers (microfilm catalog), estate papers, wills post-1858, militia/yeomanry, indexes to many record types | Catalog free; access varies |
| www.irishnewsarchive.com | Ulster and national newspapers | Subscription |
| www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk | Belfast Newsletter and other Ulster titles | Subscription |

**Coverage note:** `collections_search`, `volume_search`, and `external_links_search` all returned zero Ireland-specific results in this survey. The place_search tool resolved no standardPlace for County Antrim or Ireland, which caused these downstream tools to fail. The online repositories listed above are drawn from the wiki_search result's context (PRONI reference cited for Ballylinny, same county) and from the existence of the Billy Civil Parish FamilySearch wiki page. No FamilySearch collection IDs, record counts, or volume identifiers were returned; this is a tool coverage gap, not evidence those collections are absent at FamilySearch.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Relevant holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Public Record Office of Northern Ireland (PRONI), Belfast | Church registers (microfilm), estate papers, valuation records, wills post-1858, militia/yeomanry muster rolls | In-person; catalog at www.nidirect.gov.uk/proni; some records online at www.nidirect.gov.uk/PRONI |
| National Archives of Ireland (NAI), Dublin | Pre-1922 probate abstracts, Tithe Applotment originals, some estate papers | In-person; www.nationalarchives.ie |
| General Register Office (GRO), Dublin | Original civil registration registers from 1864 | Searchable via www.irishgenealogy.ie |
| Representative Church Body Library (RCBL), Dublin | Church of Ireland diocesan registers not held at PRONI | In-person; www.ireland.anglican.org/rcbl |
| Presbyterian Historical Society, Belfast | Presbyterian congregational histories and some register copies | In-person; phs-ni.org |
| The National Archives (UK), Kew | British Army service and pension records | In-person or via Ancestry/Findmypast |

## Records NOT online

- Pre-1864 Protestant non-marriage vital events (baptisms, deaths/burials) that survive in physical Presbyterian, Covenanter, Methodist, or Church of Ireland registers not yet digitized — these must be accessed at PRONI or the local congregation.
- Estate rentals and tenancy records for Billy parish's landholding families.
- Pre-1858 probate records surviving as abstracts or copies at NAI and PRONI.
- Militia and yeomanry muster rolls.
- Many Church of Ireland burial registers, to the extent the original was not destroyed in 1922 and a surviving copy has not been digitized.

## Known record losses

The 1922 fire at the Public Record Office of Ireland, Dublin, destroyed the centrally deposited collection of Church of Ireland parish registers (pre-1870), nearly all pre-1858 original wills, the original 1821, 1831, 1841, and 1851 census returns for all of Ireland including County Antrim, and many estate papers. This is an Ireland-wide loss, not specific to Billy parish, and the extent of surviving Billy-specific registers is not confirmed by any tool result in this survey. The status of Billy's Church of Ireland registers — whether originals were deposited in Dublin and lost, retained locally and surviving, or of which typescript or microfilm copies exist at PRONI — should be verified directly at PRONI's online catalog before concluding that pre-1870 registers are absent.

## Research tips

- **Presbyterian families: search PRONI first.** The majority of surviving Presbyterian registers for County Antrim are held at PRONI on microfilm, deposited by individual congregations. The correct congregation for a Billy parish Presbyterian family is most likely a Bushmills-area congregation, but no tool result during this survey confirmed the congregation name or its register dates. Search PRONI's church records catalog filtered to "County Antrim" and "Presbyterian Church in Ireland" and look for Bushmills, Dervock (nearby), or the Dunluce area. Source from this survey: wiki_search result, Ballylinny Civil Parish page noting PRONI MIC 1P/327 format for County Antrim Presbyterian records (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ballylinny_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy#Church_records).
- **Covenanters are a separate register series.** Billy parish had a Covenanter (Reformed Presbyterian) meeting house, confirmed by the wiki_search result. If your ancestor's denomination is uncertain, check Covenanter registers separately — they did not share registers with the Presbyterian Church in Ireland.
- **Griffith's Valuation (1858–60) is your mid-period anchor.** For any family present in Billy parish around 1860, Griffith's gives the townland, the landowner/lessor, and the annual valuation — enough to place a family geographically and identify neighbors. Available free at www.askaboutireland.ie.
- **Tithe Applotment Books bridge back to c. 1823.** They name the occupying tenant of each tithe-able parcel. For families present in Billy parish in the 1820s–1830s, the Tithe books predate Griffith's by roughly 30 years.
- **Civil registration of Presbyterian marriages starts in 1845, not 1864.** A Presbyterian marriage in Billy parish from 1 April 1845 through 1870 should appear in both the civil register (searchable at www.irishgenealogy.ie) and the congregation's own register. Use both — the civil register may supply the father's name on the entry if the church register is sparse.
- **The 1901 census works backward.** Anyone born in the 1820s–1840s and still living at census time (1901 or 1911) will appear with stated age, birthplace county, and religion. This can confirm the townland and denomination for a family you found in Griffith's or the Tithes.
- **Famine emigration gap.** The years roughly 1846–1852 produce thin records in Billy parish: emigration, mortality, and administrative disruption all reduced registration. If a family's trail goes cold in the late 1840s, consider whether emigration to North America (particularly Canada via the Londonderry/Belfast route) accounts for it.

**FamilySearch Wiki unreachable during this survey (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips for Ireland, plus Billy Civil Parish full text, Ireland Vital Records, Ireland Church Records, Northern Ireland Genealogy); these pages exist and very likely contain Presbyterian congregation register dates and FamilySearch collection links not captured here — re-run locality-guide before relying on their absence.**

---

This guide covers Billy civil parish, County Antrim, in what was then part of Ireland (after 1801, the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland), from about 1780 to 1870. The core problem for this period is that civil registration only catches the last decade or two of your window — before 1864 (births, deaths) and before 1845 (Presbyterian marriages), church registers are the only routine vital records, and many of those were lost in the 1922 Dublin fire. What survives for a Presbyterian family is primarily the congregation's own register microfilmed at PRONI in Belfast, supplemented by Griffith's Valuation and the Tithe Applotment Books as near-census land sources, and the 1901/1911 censuses for anyone born in the target period who survived. The FamilySearch Wiki and several collection-search tools were unreachable during this survey, so the guide was built from a partial wiki index result; re-running it after the outage clears will likely add specific congregation names and register dates.

The recommended first step is to search PRONI's online church records catalog for Presbyterian and Reformed Presbyterian (Covenanter) congregations in the Bushmills and Dunluce area of County Antrim, then check www.irishgenealogy.ie for any civil marriage entries from 1845 onward and civil births/deaths from 1864 onward.

dimensions.rationale: The guide is substantially accurate but contains a critical unresolved conflict regarding Presbyterian registers. # Locality Guide: Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Ireland (1780–1870)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Civil parish:** Billy, barony of Lower Dunluce (chiefly) and barony of Carey (eastern fringe); Poor Law Union of Coleraine; County Antrim; Province of Ulster
- **Post town / centre:** Bushmills
- **Ecclesiastical history:** Billy was formerly head of a union with Armoy, Ballyclug, Donegore, and Kilbride
- **Denominations confirmed in parish:** Presbyterian (meeting house), Covenanter/Reformed Presbyterian (meeting house), Wesleyan Methodist (meeting house), Church of Ireland, Roman Catholic (RC district: **Coleraine**)
- **Key loss event:** The 1922 Public Record Office of Ireland fire destroyed most pre-1858 original Church of Ireland diocesan wills and administration bonds for the Diocese of Connor (which covers County Antrim). County Antrim church registers held at PRONI in Belfast were not affected.

---

## Record Types Available

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **Non-Catholic marriages:** registered from **1845**
- **Births, all deaths, all marriages:** from **1864** only
- For the bulk of 1780–1870, **church registers are the only source of vital events**
- **Where held:** General Register Office, Belfast; copies at PRONI; some indexes at [irishgenealogy.ie](https://www.irishgenealogy.ie)

---

### Church Records *(primary source for a Presbyterian family)*

**Presbyterian**
- Billy parish had at least one mainstream Presbyterian congregation and a separate **Covenanter (Reformed Presbyterian)** congregation — these are different registers catalogued separately at PRONI
- Registers are held at PRONI under the **MIC 1P series** (this is confirmed from the adjacent County Antrim parish; apply as a pointer and verify at PRONI's catalog for Billy specifically)
- Some registers also available on FamilySearch
- **Action item:** Visit the [Billy Civil Parish FamilySearch Wiki page](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy#Church_records) for specific opening dates and PRONI microfilm numbers — these could not be confirmed in this survey

**Church of Ireland**
- Registers for County Antrim held at PRONI and (some) at the Representative Church Body Library, Dublin
- Many pre-1870 Antrim registers survived since they were not deposited in Dublin

**Roman Catholic**
- **The RC district for Billy is Coleraine** — search the Coleraine RC register, not a local Billy register, for Catholic events in this parish

**Wesleyan Methodist**
- Registers kept at the circuit level; check PRONI's catalog for the relevant Bushmills-area circuit

---

### Census Records
- **1901 and 1911:** Fully survive; free at [census.nationalarchives.ie](https://www.census.nationalarchives.ie) — valuable for identifying survivors born in the 1780–1870 window
- **1821–1891:** Largely destroyed (1922 fire + government destruction of 1861–1891 series). Fragments of the **1831** census survive for some County Antrim areas — check for Billy parish townlands
- **Substitute censuses (essential):**
  - **Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837):** List male heads of household paying tithe, by townland. Free at [askaboutireland.ie](https://www.askaboutireland.ie) and FamilySearch (*Ireland, Tithe Applotment Books* collection)
  - **Griffith's Primary Valuation (1850s):** Household-level snapshot of all landholders and occupiers. Free at [askaboutireland.ie](https://www.askaboutireland.ie) and [irishgenealogy.ie](https://www.irishgenealogy.ie); also on Ancestry
  - **Flax Growers List (1796):** Government survey of linen flax growers in Ulster by townland. Available on IrishGenealogy.ie and at PRONI — covers the start of the target period

---

### Land and Estate Records
- **Registry of Deeds (from 1708):** Leases and conveyances enrolled in Dublin; memorial index at the National Archives of Ireland and on FindMyPast
- **Estate papers at PRONI:** Much of Lower Dunluce barony was held under large landlord estates (Ulster Plantation system). Tenant leases, rent rolls, and estate correspondence can document families back well before 1780. Identify the estate holding the specific townland and search its PRONI papers.
- **Hearth Money Rolls (1660s):** Published for County Antrim; can document earlier generations in townlands

---

### Probate Records
- **Pre-1858:** Diocesan courts (Diocese of Connor for Billy); original wills largely destroyed in 1922 — will abstracts, administration bonds, and testamentary indexes survive at PRONI and in published volumes
- **Post-1858:** Belfast District Probate Registry; largely survive; held at PRONI. Some indexes at [irishgenealogy.ie](https://www.irishgenealogy.ie)

---

### Military Records
- **County Antrim Militia:** Muster rolls and description books at PRONI name men with physical descriptions, ages, and townlands (1798–1815 period especially relevant)
- **British Army service records:** At The National Archives (Kew), WO series; searchable via FindMyPast
- **Pension records:** Royal Chelsea Hospital; at TNA Kew

---

### Newspaper Records
- ***Belfast Newsletter*** (from 1737): Oldest continuously published Irish newspaper; marriage and death notices; digitized and searchable at British Newspaper Archive and newspapers.com
- ***Coleraine Chronicle*** (from 1844): Covered the Bushmills area
- **Access:** British Newspaper Archive (subscription); PRONI holds some physical runs

---

### Immigration / Emigration Records
- Heavy Ulster-Scots emigration to North America during this period; a Presbyterian family from Billy may have relatives who emigrated via **Belfast or Londonderry/Derry**
- Passenger lists free on FamilySearch for major departure ports
- Irish Emigration Database at PRONI covers many Ulster emigrants

---

### School Records
- National school registers from **1831** onward
- Admission registers at PRONI (County Antrim schools); inspector's reports at the National Archives of Ireland

---

## Repository Quick Reference

| Repository | Key Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **PRONI, Belfast** (proni.gov.uk) | Presbyterian, CoI, Methodist registers (MIC 1P and other series); estate papers; militia records; post-1858 probate; Tithe originals | In-person; some online |
| **IrishGenealogy.ie** | Church records (CoI, RC, Presbyterian) for Antrim; civil registration indexes | Free |
| **AskAboutIreland.ie** | Griffith's Valuation; Tithe Applotment Books | Free |
| **FamilySearch** | Tithe Applotment Books collection; civil registration; wiki page for Billy parish | Free |
| **AncestryIreland.com (Ulster Historical Foundation)** | Indexed Antrim church registers; cemetery inscriptions | Subscription |
| **National Archives of Ireland / Census.NationalArchives.ie** | 1901/1911 census; 1821/1831 fragments; will indexes | Free |
| **British Newspaper Archive** | *Belfast Newsletter*, *Coleraine Chronicle*, etc. | Subscription |
| **TNA Kew** | British Army service/pension records | In-person; FindMyPast/Ancestry |
| **Representative Church Body Library, Dublin** | CoI Diocese of Connor records | In-person (appointment) |

---

## Key Research Tips for a Presbyterian Family in Billy Parish

1. **Start at the [Billy Civil Parish FamilySearch Wiki page](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy)** for specific register opening dates and PRONI film numbers — these are the essential orientation before searching.

2. **Distinguish the two Presbyterian congregations.** The main Presbyterian meeting house and the Covenanter (Reformed Presbyterian) meeting house kept separate registers, catalogued separately at PRONI. If the family is not found in one, search the other.

3. **Use the three-source substitute-census bracket:** Tithe Applotment Books (1820s–30s) → Griffith's Valuation (1850s) → 1901/1911 census. Because pre-1901 censuses are mostly destroyed, this sequence is the standard method for placing an Irish family in a townland across time.

4. **Check estate papers at PRONI** for the townland where the family lived. Landlord leases and rent rolls can carry a family back to the 1700s — well before church registers begin.

5. **For any Catholic events, search the Coleraine RC register**, not a local Billy register.

6. **The 1796 Flax Growers List** is a useful early snapshot at the very start of the target window — worth checking for the surname before the Tithe books begin.

---

> **Survey note:** The FamilySearch Wiki and place-resolution tools experienced a service outage during this survey, so specific register opening dates, PRONI film numbers, and FamilySearch collection counts for County Antrim could not be confirmed from tool output. The guide above draws on confirmed content from the Billy Civil Parish and adjacent Ballylinny wiki pages plus established knowledge of Irish records. Re-run the locality guide when tools are restored to fill in those gaps.

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Civil parish:** Billy, partly in the barony of Carey, chiefly in the barony of Lower Dunluce; Poor Law Union of Coleraine; County Antrim; Province of Ulster
- **Post town / administrative centre:** Bushmills; the parish also includes a portion of Dunserverick
- **Parent jurisdiction:** County Antrim, under the jurisdiction of the Crown of Ireland / United Kingdom (Ireland Act of Union 1800)
- **Population during period:** Population figures were not returned by the tools in this survey; Griffith's Valuation (1850s) and the 1831 and 1841 census fragments are the best period-level sources for this
- **Economy:** The Bushmills area combined small-scale agriculture (tenant farming under the Ulster Plantation landlord system), fishing along the north Antrim coast, and linen production, all of which shape the land, estate, and tenant records that survive
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly Ulster-Scots Presbyterian settlers in the townlands around Bushmills; smaller Church of Ireland gentry and farming population; a Roman Catholic minority

## Boundary changes

- **Ecclesiastical:** Billy was formerly the head of an ecclesiastical union comprising the parishes of Armoy, Ballyclug, Donegore, and Kilbride. This union affected where Church of Ireland registers and vestry records were maintained. By the 1780–1870 period the ecclesiastical boundary had already evolved from that earlier union structure.
- **Civil/administrative:** No boundary change specific to Billy civil parish was returned in this survey. The parish boundary is in the barony of Lower Dunluce for the greater portion, with the Carey barony covering the eastern fringe; both baronies sat within County Antrim throughout the target period.
- **Roman Catholic:** The RC district for Billy is Coleraine — Catholic vital events before civil registration will appear in Coleraine RC registers, not in a local Billy-based register.

These post-date the target window (1780–1870) but are valuable for identifying surviving members of the generation born in that window.
- **Pre-1901 censuses:** The 1821, 1831, 1841, 1851, 1861, 1871, 1881, and 1891 census records for Ireland were largely destroyed (1922 fire and earlier destruction of the 1861–1891 series by government order). Both are searchable free at [https://www.askaboutireland.ie](https://www.askaboutireland.ie) and [https://www.irishgenealogy.ie](https://www.irishgenealogy.ie).
- **Access:** No indexed FamilySearch collections for County Antrim were returned in this survey due to place resolution failure; re-run after the tool outage resolves.

### Probate and court records
- **Pre-1858:** Probate was handled by the Church of Ireland diocesan courts. Billy parish fell under the diocese of Connor (Church of Ireland). Pre-1858 wills proved in that court and deposited in Dublin were destroyed in 1922. Will abstracts, administration bonds, and testamentary indexes survive at PRONI and in published will abstract volumes.
- **Post-1858:** The Principal Registry (later District Probate Registries) took over. County Antrim fell under the Belfast District Probate Registry. Post-1858 wills were not deposited in Dublin and largely survive; they are held at PRONI.
- **Types to search:** Will books, administration bonds, testamentary inventories, guardianship records. Ulster Historical Foundation and PRONI have published indexes.
- **Access:** PRONI in-person or via their online catalog; some will indexes are on IrishGenealogy.ie

### Land records
- **Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837):** Cover Billy civil parish; list titheable landholders by townland. Available free at askaboutireland.ie and familysearch.org (Ireland, Tithe Applotment Books collection).
- **Griffith's Primary Valuation (1850s):** Household-level survey of all landholders and occupiers. The definitive substitute census for the pre-civil-registration period. Free at askaboutireland.ie and irishgenealogy.ie; also on Ancestry.
- **Estate papers:** Much of the land in Lower Dunluce barony was held under large landlord estates. Estate papers (leases, rent rolls, tenant lists) survive at PRONI for many County Antrim estates and can document families back well before 1780. Check PRONI's online catalog by estate name or townland.
- **Registry of Deeds:** Deeds of lease and conveyance were enrolled in Dublin from 1708. The Registry of Deeds, Dublin holds the originals; a memorial index is available at the National Archives of Ireland website and on FindMyPast.
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds, with the townland as the standard land division

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** The 1798 rebellion (United Irishmen) affected County Antrim; the Peninsular War and Napoleonic Wars drew men from Ulster regiments; the period also covers the Indian campaigns.
- **Record types:** British Army service records (held at The National Archives, Kew, WO series); pension records (Royal Chelsea Hospital); muster rolls; militia records for the Antrim Militia held at PRONI
- **Ulster militia:** County Antrim had an active militia during the 1798–1815 period; muster rolls and descriptions books at PRONI name men with physical descriptions, ages, and townlands
- **Access:** The National Archives (Kew) online catalog; FindMyPast (British Army records); PRONI for Antrim Militia

### Cemetery records
- **Coverage:** The Billy Civil Parish wiki page does not list specific cemeteries in the content returned by this survey. The Church of Ireland parish churchyard at Bushmills/Billy and graveyard records associated with the Presbyterian congregations are the primary sources.
- **Online:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) may have volunteer-contributed transcriptions; the Ulster Historical Foundation has carried out County Antrim cemetery surveys. PRONI holds some Church of Ireland vestry burial records.
- **Gravestone inscriptions:** The Association for Scottish and Irish Studies (and earlier the IGRS Gravestone Inscription project) have published survey volumes for County Antrim graveyards.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The *Coleraine Chronicle* (from 1844), *Northern Constitution* (Coleraine area), and *Belfast Newsletter* (from 1737 — the oldest continuously published newspaper in Ireland) covered County Antrim and carried marriage notices, death notices, and estate sale announcements.
- **Where held:** British Newspaper Archive (britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk, subscription) holds digitized runs of many Ulster papers; the *Belfast Newsletter* 1738–1900 is freely searchable at newspapers.com and the British Newspaper Archive; PRONI holds some physical holdings.
- **Content value:** Death and marriage notices in Belfast and Coleraine papers are common for farming and merchant families; estate and tenancy auction notices name occupiers.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevance:** The 1780–1870 period in County Antrim covers heavy Ulster-Scots emigration to North America, particularly to Pennsylvania, Ohio, and Ontario. A Presbyterian family in Billy parish in this era may have relatives who emigrated.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (held at NARA for US arrivals; free on FamilySearch for major departure ports); naturalization records filed in US courts; Canadian immigration records at Library and Archives Canada
- **Port of departure:** Most North Antrim emigrants left via Belfast or Londonderry/Derry, or via Liverpool; some via Newry. Search Londonderry/Derry emigrant records particularly.
- **Ulster emigrant databases:** The Linen Hall Library and Public Record Office of Northern Ireland have emigrant databases; the Irish Emigration Database (from PRONI) covers many Ulster emigrants.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) name all persons aboard including infants traveling with parents; examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Hearth Money Rolls:** 1660s hearth tax lists can document earlier generations of families in County Antrim townlands; published for Antrim by the Irish Manuscripts Commission.
- **Tithe Applotment Books:** See Land records above — this is both a land record and a tax substitute census for 1823–1837.
- **Substitute census value:** Because most pre-1901 census records are destroyed, the Tithe books and Griffith's Valuation are the main population snapshots for the 1780–1870 window. Use them in sequence to bracket a family's presence in a townland across time.

- **Flax growers list (1796):** A government survey of linen flax growers in Ulster, including County Antrim, lists household heads by townland. Available on IrishGenealogy.ie and in PRONI. Covers the beginning of the target period.
- **Ulster Historical Foundation publications:** The UHF has published indexed transcriptions of many County Antrim record types (gravestone inscriptions, census fragments, church registers). Their catalog at ancestryireland.com is searchable by surname and parish.
- **School records:** National school registers from 1831 onward; the National Archives of Ireland holds national school inspector's reports and some admission registers. PRONI holds registers for County Antrim national schools.
- **Estate papers:** Addressed under Land records; re-emphasize here that landlord accounts, rent rolls, and tenant correspondence at PRONI can extend family documentation back decades before civil registration.
