# Locality Guide: Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Ireland (1780–1870)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Civil parish:** Billy
- **Baronies:** Partly Carey, chiefly Lower Dunluce
- **Poor Law Union:** Coleraine
- **Principal settlement:** Bushmills
- **Ecclesiastical (Church of Ireland):** Billy formerly headed a union that also comprised Armoy, Ballyclug, Donegore, and Kilbride. For Roman Catholics, the district is part of the Coleraine RC district.
- **Denominations documented in parish:** Presbyterian, Covenanters (Reformed Presbyterian), Wesleyan Methodist, Church of Ireland, and Roman Catholic.

---

## Boundary Notes

- Billy civil parish straddled two baronies throughout the period but remained wholly in County Antrim.
- The Poor Law Union of Coleraine was formed in 1838; post-1838 poor law, valuation, and registration records are filed under Coleraine Union.
- After 1864, civil registration for the area was filed under the **Coleraine district registrar**.
- Bushmills sits close to the County Londonderry boundary — families in western Billy townlands may have had connections to Londonderry-side congregations.

---

## Record Types Available

### Church Records (Most Important for a Presbyterian Family)

No civil registration existed before 1845 (non-Catholic marriages) or 1864 (all events), so church registers are **the primary source for 1780–1864**.

**Presbyterian congregations and their registers:**
- The two most likely congregations serving Billy parish are **Bushmills Presbyterian** and the **Covenanting (Reformed Presbyterian)** meeting house.
- Presbyterian registers typically record: baptisms (child's name, father's name, often mother's maiden name, date, townland) and marriages (parties' names, witnesses, date). Burial entries are less common.
- **Important:** The Covenanters (Reformed Presbyterian) maintained *separate* registers from the mainstream Presbyterian Church in Ireland. If a family attended the Covenanting meeting house, their baptisms and marriages will be in the Reformed Presbyterian register — a different PRONI microfilm.

**Where held:**
- Microfilm copies at **PRONI (MIC 1P series)** — the standard repository for County Antrim Presbyterian and Reformed Presbyterian registers. Specific film numbers for Bushmills/Billy were not returned by tools in this survey; look them up via the PRONI church records finding aid or contact PRONI directly.
- The **Presbyterian Historical Society (Belfast)** can help identify which congregation served a specific townland.
- Presbyterian registers were **not** included in the NLI digitization project and are **not** accessible through IrishGenealogy.ie — PRONI microfilm or in-person congregation access is the route.

**Church of Ireland:** Registers deposited at PRONI or the **Representative Church Body Library (RCBL)**, Dublin.

**Roman Catholic:** Part of the Coleraine RC parish; registers digitized through the NLI project, viewable free at **IrishGenealogy.ie** (registers.nli.ie).

---

### Civil Registration

| Category | Start date | Registrar district |
|---|---|---|
| Non-Catholic marriages | 1845 | Coleraine |
| All births, deaths, and Catholic marriages | 1864 | Coleraine |

**Free online access:** IrishGenealogy.ie — births 1864–1922, non-Catholic marriages 1845–1943, deaths 1878–1969. The master civil registers are held by **GRONI (General Register Office for Northern Ireland)**, Belfast.

---

### Census Records

- **1841 and 1851:** Survive only as fragments; household returns sometimes kept as proof of age for Old Age Pensions (some deposited at the NAI).
- **1861, 1871, 1881, 1891:** Destroyed (pulped during WWI; 1922 Four Courts fire). No County Antrim household returns survive for these years.
- **1901 and 1911:** Survive in full; free at IrishGenealogy.ie and the NAI website.

**Census substitutes for the 1780–1870 gap:**
- **Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837):** Lists tithe-paying landholders by townland. Free at Askaboutireland.ie and IrishGenealogy.ie.
- **Griffith's Primary Valuation (c.1856–1864):** Lists every property occupier and their immediate lessor. Free at Askaboutireland.ie; searchable with household context at Griffithsvaluation.com (Ulster Historical Foundation, subscription).

---

### Land Records

| Record | Date range | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Tithe Applotment Books | 1823–1837 | Free at Askaboutireland.ie / IrishGenealogy.ie |
| Griffith's Primary Valuation | c.1856–1864 | Free at Askaboutireland.ie; UHF subscription |
| Registry of Deeds | From 1708 | In-person Dublin; some indexed on Ancestry |
| Estate papers (Bush Estate, etc.) | Varies | PRONI (estate-specific references) |

---

### Probate Records

- **Pre-1858:** Ecclesiastical jurisdiction, Diocese of Connor and Down.
- **Post-1858:** Belfast District Probate Registry.
- **Major loss:** The 1922 Four Courts fire destroyed the centralized repository of Irish wills before 1904. Use surviving indexes, abstracts, and PRONI-held Belfast District Registry copies.

---

### Other Record Types

- **School registers (from 1831):** National School roll books, naming pupils and sometimes parents/guardians; at PRONI for County Antrim schools.
- **Poor Law records (Coleraine Union):** Board of Guardians minutes, workhouse admission/discharge registers — at PRONI under the BG series. Useful for Famine-era families.
- **Presbyterian Session minutes:** Where surviving, deposited at PRONI or held by congregations. Can document membership, moral censures, and family situations.
- **Ordnance Survey Memoirs (1830s):** Detailed topographical memoirs for each County Antrim parish, naming churches, clergy, population, occupations, and social life by townland. The Billy/Bushmills memoir directly answers which congregations were active in the 1830s. Published in print by Queen's University Belfast (Institute of Irish Studies).
- **Military records:** British Army service records and pension files at the National Archives (Kew); some on Ancestry and Findmypast. County Antrim Militia records may be at PRONI.
- **Newspapers:** *Coleraine Chronicle* (from 1844), *Belfast Newsletter* (from 1737), *Northern Whig* (from 1824). Obituaries, marriage notices, and legal notices. Available on the British Newspaper Archive (subscription) and at the Linen Hall Library (Belfast).
- **Immigration/emigration:** North Antrim had heavy emigration to North America, especially in the Famine period. Post-1820 US passenger lists are on Ancestry; PRONI holds some emigrant lists.

---

## Repository Summary

| Repository | Key holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **PRONI, Belfast** | Presbyterian registers (MIC 1P series); Church of Ireland registers; Poor Law; estate papers; will calendars; school registers; newspapers on microfilm | In-person; catalogue free online at nidirect.gov.uk/proni |
| **IrishGenealogy.ie** | Civil births/marriages/deaths; NLI-digitized Catholic and Church of Ireland registers; 1901/1911 census; Tithe Applotment; Griffith's | Free |
| **Askaboutireland.ie** | Tithe Applotment; Griffith's; 1901/1911 census | Free |
| **GRONI, Belfast** | Civil registers from 1864/1845 for Northern Ireland | In-person / GRO search service |
| **NAI, Dublin** | Testamentary indexes/abstracts; surviving 1841/1851 census fragments | In-person |
| **RCBL, Dublin** | Church of Ireland diocesan and parish records | In-person |
| **Presbyterian Historical Society, Belfast** | Congregational histories; some register microfilm | In-person |
| **Ulster Historical Foundation / ancestryireland.com** | Indexed Presbyterian and other church records; gravestone inscriptions; Griffith's | Subscription |
| **British Newspaper Archive** | Coleraine Chronicle, Belfast Newsletter, Northern Whig | Subscription |
| **FamilySearch Catalog** | County Antrim microfilm holdings; check directly at familysearch.org/catalog | Free |

---

## Practical Next Steps for a Presbyterian Family born c.1825

1. **Identify the townland** from Griffith's Valuation (free at Askaboutireland.ie) — this tells you exactly where the family lived within Billy parish.
2. **Contact PRONI** (nidirect.gov.uk/proni) for the MIC 1P film number covering the Bushmills Presbyterian congregation, and separately the Reformed Presbyterian (Covenanting) congregation, for that townland.
3. **Read the Ordnance Survey Memoir for Billy parish** to confirm which congregation(s) were active in the Bushmills area in the 1830s and which townlands each served.
4. **Search Tithe Applotment Books** (1823–1837) to find the father's name and landholding in the same townland, confirming the family's presence before the ancestor's birth ca. 1825.
5. For post-1864 vital events, go to IrishGenealogy.ie; for pre-1845, church registers via PRONI microfilm are the only option.

- **All births, deaths, and Catholic marriages:** Civil registration began in 1864 for all three categories (all births, all deaths, all marriages regardless of denomination). The registrar district is Coleraine.
- **Where held:** The General Register Office (GRO) of Ireland, now based in Roscommon, holds the master civil registers from 1864. The IrishGenealogy.ie website provides free online access to birth registrations 1864–1922, marriage registrations 1845–1943, and death registrations 1878–1969.

This is the primary record class for Presbyterian families in Billy parish across the entire 1780–1870 period.

See: [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy#Church_records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy#Church_records)

The two most likely Presbyterian congregations serving Billy parish in this period are Bushmills Presbyterian and the Covenanting (Reformed Presbyterian) congregation. For County Antrim Presbyterian records generally, PRONI holds microfilm copies of congregational registers in its MIC 1P series (the Ballylinny Civil Parish's Presbyterian records appear in PRONI MIC 1P/327 as one example of this numbering scheme). The specific MIC 1P film numbers for Bushmills/Billy were not returned by any tool in this survey — look them up at:

**Church of Ireland:** Billy had a Church of Ireland presence; the parish formerly headed the union of Armoy, Ballyclug, Donegore, and Kilbride. - **1841 and 1851 censuses:** Survive only in fragments. Household returns for 1841 and 1851 were kept by families as proof of age for Old Age Pensions after 1908; some have been deposited with the National Archives of Ireland (NAI) in Dublin.
- **1861, 1871, 1881, 1891 censuses:** Destroyed, partly by deliberate government order and partly by the 1922 Four Courts fire. No household returns survive for these years for County Antrim.
- **1901 and 1911 censuses:** Survive in full; freely searchable at IrishGenealogy.ie and at the NAI website. These postdate your target period but are the first full surviving enumeration; use them to work backward to your 1825-born ancestor's family.
- **Alternative enumerations (substitute for lost census years):** The Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837) list landholders in each townland; Griffith's Primary Valuation (1847–1864, County Antrim coverage varies by district) lists all property occupiers with landlord names. Both are essential census substitutes for 1780–1870 research. Both are available free online at IrishGenealogy.ie and Askaboutireland.ie.

### Probate and court records

- **Probate jurisdiction:** Wills and administrations for County Antrim were proved at the Diocese of Connor and Down (Ecclesiastical) or, after the reorganization of 1858, at the District Probate Registry in Belfast.
- **Catastrophic loss:** The Public Record Office of Ireland (Dublin) was destroyed in the Four Courts fire of 1922. This destroyed the centralized repository of Irish wills and administration bonds from before 1904. For County Antrim wills, the main surviving substitutes are:
  - Will abstracts and indexes that survived outside the main PRO building (some survive at the NAI)
  - PRONI-held testamentary records (Belfast District Registry copies)
  - The Index to Irish Wills (various published volumes) for names and approximate dates
- **For 1780–1870:** Expect to work from surviving indexes and abstracts rather than original wills in most cases. PRONI holds surviving Belfast District Registry records post-1858.
- **Court of Chancery and Exchequer:** Equity proceedings sometimes document family relationships and property; records at the NAI.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Ireland used a townland-based system; land was not distributed through public domain survey but through landlord holdings and tenancies.
- **Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837):** The most useful pre-Famine land record. Lists tithe-paying landholders (Protestant and Catholic, tenant farmers) by townland in each civil parish. Billy parish's Tithe Applotment books list occupiers in each townland. Available free at Askaboutireland.ie and IrishGenealogy.ie.
- **Griffith's Primary Valuation (c.1856–1864 for County Antrim):** Lists every property occupier and their immediate lessor/landlord, with lot descriptions and valuation figures. This is effectively a census substitute for the mid-1850s. Free online at Askaboutireland.ie and at Griffithsvaluation.com (Ulster Historical Foundation, subscription).
- **Registry of Deeds (Dublin, from 1708):** Memorial copies of deeds, mortgages, and leases. Covers the whole target period 1780–1870. Useful for landowners and larger tenant farmers. Online at the Registry of Deeds, Dublin (some indexed through Ancestry.com).
- **Estate papers:** Many north Antrim townlands were held under large Protestant estates. Estate records (rentals, maps, correspondence) may survive at PRONI under estate-specific references. The Bush Estate and other local landholdings in the Bushmills area may have records at PRONI.
- **Land-grant jurisdiction:** The land-distribution authority for Ulster Plantation grants was the crown, acting through the Plantation scheme from the early 1600s. PRONI is the main repository for Ulster land records.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** United Irish Rebellion (1798), Napoleonic Wars (1793–1815), Crimean War (1853–1856)
- **British Army records:** Service records and pension files are at the National Archives (Kew, UK). Attestation papers for soldiers who took the King's/Queen's shilling are there. Many have been digitized and are on Ancestry.com and Findmypast.com.
- **Muster rolls and description books:** Identify County Antrim men in named regiments; at Kew.
- **Militia records:** County Antrim Militia records may be at PRONI.
- **1798 Rebellion:** Some lists of rebels, persons charged, and those who submitted exist in various collections at NAI and PRONI.

### Cemetery records

- **Church of Ireland graveyards:** The main Church of Ireland graveyard for Billy parish is at Bushmills. Sexton's burial registers, where they survive, are at PRONI or the RCBL.
- **Presbyterian graveyards:** Presbyterian congregations maintained their own burial grounds. Memorial inscriptions surveys have been conducted by the Ulster Historical Foundation and local groups.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave ([findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com)) has partial coverage for County Antrim graveyards; coverage for rural north Antrim in this period is sparse. The North of Ireland Family History Society (NIFHS) and the Presbyterian Historical Society have published gravestone inscription surveys.
- **Dissenters:** Covenanting and Methodist communities may have used the Church of Ireland graveyard or maintained separate burial grounds.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers serving the Bushmills/north Antrim area:**
  - *Coleraine Chronicle* (from 1844): covers north Antrim including Bushmills area; obituaries, marriage notices, legal announcements
  - *Belfast Newsletter* (from 1737): Ulster-wide; occasional notices from County Antrim parishes
  - *Northern Whig* (from 1824): Belfast-based; Ulster coverage
- **Where held:** British Newspaper Archive ([britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk](https://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk)) has the Coleraine Chronicle and other Ulster titles, subscription. The Linen Hall Library (Belfast) holds physical runs. PRONI has microfilm of some Ulster papers.
- **Value:** Obituaries in 19th-century Ulster papers often name the deceased's townland, age, relatives, and sometimes birthplace.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Context:** North Antrim had significant emigration, especially to North America, throughout 1780–1870. The Famine period (1845–1852) accelerated this. Presbyterian families from this area were among the core of the Ulster-Scots (Scots-Irish) emigrant stream.
- **Passenger lists (pre-1820):** Early passenger lists for Ireland are sparse; some survive in newspaper notices and isolated collections. PRONI holds some emigrant lists.
- **Post-1820 US arrival records:** Customs passenger lists 1820–1891 at NARA, digitized on Ancestry.com. Castle Garden (New York, 1830s–1890) and Ellis Island (1892–) records.
- **Naturalization records:** Pre-1906 naturalizations filed in any US court of record. Declarations of intention ("first papers") and petitions are worth searching for immigrant family members.
- **Ulster emigration:** The Roulston/PRONI emigration indexes and the Famine Irish records at the NAI supplement passenger lists.

### Tax records

- **Hearth Money Rolls (1660s):** Very early but useful as an ancestor-finding list; covers some north Antrim townlands.
- **Penal era tax records:** Limited survival for the 18th century.
- **Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837):** Already listed under land records — these function as a tax-and-property census substitute and are the main pre-Griffith's survey document for identifying family landholdings in Billy parish.
- **Griffith's Valuation (c.1856–1864):** Also already listed; functions as a mid-century property record.
- **Value as census substitute:** Both Tithe Applotment and Griffith's are the standard substitutes for the destroyed census returns for County Antrim in the 1830s–1860s.

### Other record types

- **School records:** National Schools were established from 1831. National School registers (roll books) naming pupils and sometimes parents/guardians are at the Public Record Office of Northern Ireland for many County Antrim schools. The Billy area schools' registers, if surviving, would be at PRONI.
- **Poor law records:** Coleraine Union Board of Guardians minutes, indoor relief registers (workhouse admission/discharge), and outdoor relief lists are at PRONI under the BG (Board of Guardians) reference series. Useful for Famine-era families.
- **Freeholders' and voters' lists:** County Antrim freeholders and voters' lists survive for some periods; at PRONI.
- **Presbyterian Session minutes:** Some Presbyterian congregations kept session (disciplinary) minutes that name members, record moral censures, and document family situations. Where surviving, deposited at PRONI.
- **Ordnance Survey memoirs (1830s):** The OSI topographical memoirs for County Antrim parishes (including Billy) describe local families, occupations, churches, and community life in remarkable detail. Published by the Institute of Irish Studies (Queen's University Belfast); the memoir for the Billy/Bushmills area is a valuable contextual source.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Relevant content for Billy parish 1780–1870 | Access |
|---|---|---|
| IrishGenealogy.ie | Civil births 1864–1922, non-Catholic marriages 1845–1943, deaths 1878–1969; Catholic and Church of Ireland registers (NLI digitization) | Free |
| Askaboutireland.ie | Tithe Applotment Books; Griffith's Valuation; 1901 and 1911 census | Free |
| PRONI Online (nidirect.gov.uk/proni) | PRONI catalogue; microfilm references for Presbyterian, Church of Ireland registers; Poor Law; estate papers; will calendar | Free catalogue; some docs free, others in-person |
| Ancestry.com | British Army records; some Ireland civil registration; Griffith's Valuation; UK/US passenger lists | Subscription |
| Findmypast.com | Irish records including Tithe Applotment, Griffith's, church records; British Army records | Subscription |
| Ulster Historical Foundation / ancestryireland.com | Indexed Presbyterian and other church records; gravestone inscriptions; Griffith's (Griffithsvaluation.com) | Subscription (some free) |
| National Archives of Ireland (NAI) / census.nationalarchives.ie | 1901 and 1911 census; surviving 1841/1851 fragments; testamentary records post-1858 | Free for census; some in-person |
| British Newspaper Archive | Coleraine Chronicle, Belfast Newsletter, Northern Whig | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** The place_search tool returned no results for any Irish place name, so collections_search and volume_search were unable to resolve a standard place for Ireland. As a result, no FamilySearch digitization counts, collection lists, or volume breakdowns could be generated by the tools — these figures are absent from this guide, not because they don't exist, but because the tool infrastructure could not resolve them. Consult the FamilySearch Catalog directly at [https://www.familysearch.org/catalog](https://www.familysearch.org/catalog) for County Antrim microfilm holdings.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Public Record Office of Northern Ireland (PRONI), Belfast | Presbyterian, Church of Ireland, Methodist registers (MIC 1P series); Poor Law records; estate papers; will calendars; school registers; voters' lists; newspapers on microfilm | In-person; some online via PRONI catalogue |
| Representative Church Body Library (RCBL), Dublin | Church of Ireland diocesan and parish records | In-person; appointment recommended |
| National Archives of Ireland (NAI), Dublin | Pre-1922 probate records (indexes/abstracts); surviving census fragments; Tithe Applotment originals | In-person |
| General Register Office for Northern Ireland (GRONI), Belfast | Civil birth, marriage, death registers from 1864/1845 for Northern Ireland | In-person; GRO search service |
| Linen Hall Library, Belfast | Historical Ulster newspapers; local history; some genealogical reference collections | In-person |
| North of Ireland Family History Society (NIFHS) | Gravestone inscription surveys; local indexes | Contact society |
| Presbyterian Historical Society, Belfast | Presbyterian congregational histories and some register microfilm | In-person |

## Records NOT online

- **Pre-1864 vital records for Billy parish:** No civil registration existed. The only surviving vital record equivalents are church registers, most of which are either held physically at PRONI (on MIC 1P microfilm for Presbyterian congregations) or at the local church. The specific Billy parish Presbyterian and Covenanting registers were not identified by any tool in this survey — their PRONI film numbers must be looked up in PRONI's church records finding aid.
- **1861, 1871, 1881, 1891 census returns for County Antrim:** Destroyed; no substitutes exist for these specific enumerations.
- **Estate papers (Bush Estate and other Bushmills-area landlords):** Held physically at PRONI under estate-specific references; not comprehensively digitized.
- **Poor law records (Coleraine Union):** Largely physical at PRONI.
- **Presbyterian Session minutes:** Where surviving, physical at PRONI or congregation custody.
- **Ordnance Survey memoirs for Billy parish:** Published in print by Queen's University Belfast; not freely available online.

## Known record losses

- **Four Courts fire, Dublin, 1922:** Destroyed the master repository of Irish wills, administration bonds, and many other pre-1904 civil records. This is the central archival loss for Irish genealogy. For County Antrim wills before 1904, researchers must work from surviving will indexes, abstracts, and PRONI-held Belfast District Registry copies. No tool result in this survey confirmed a specific loss within Billy parish records themselves — the fire is a country-level loss to the NAI holdings.
- **Irish census destruction:** Returns for 1861–1891 were deliberately pulped during World War I; 1922 fire destroyed remaining census material. Only 1901/1911 survive intact. Only fragments of 1841/1851 survive.

## Research tips

- **Start with Tithe Applotment and Griffith's Valuation before church registers.** These two land surveys (1823–1837 and c.1856–1864) will place your family in a specific townland within Billy parish. Once you have a townland, you can narrow which Presbyterian congregation served that community — congregations in north Antrim typically covered a cluster of townlands — and request the right PRONI MIC 1P film.
- **Presbyterian register access route:** Contact PRONI directly ([https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/proni](https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/proni)) and ask for the church records guide for Billy civil parish. The MIC 1P series covers most County Antrim Presbyterian congregations. The Presbyterian Historical Society (Belfast) can also assist in identifying which congregation served a specific townland.
- **The Covenanting/Reformed Presbyterian registers are distinct.** The Covenanters maintained separate registers from the mainstream Presbyterian Church in Ireland (which joined the General Assembly in 1840). If a family attended the Covenanting meeting house specifically, their baptisms and marriages will be in the Reformed Presbyterian register, not the mainstream Presbyterian one — these are different PRONI microfilm references.
- **Search the Ordnance Survey Memoir for Billy parish.** The OSI memoirs for County Antrim parishes (compiled 1830s) describe churches, clergy, population, occupations, and social life by townland. The Billy memoir will name the actual congregations and ministers active in Bushmills in the 1830s — this directly answers which church your family attended.
- **For cross-border research:** Bushmills sits close to the boundary between County Antrim and County Londonderry/Derry. Families in the western townlands of Billy parish may have had connections to Londonderry-side congregations and their registers. Check whether the ancestor's specific townland is near the county boundary.
- **IrishGenealogy.ie is the first stop for post-1864 civil records and NLI church register images.** The NLI project digitized the surviving registers it holds; Presbyterian registers were not in the NLI deposit and must be accessed via PRONI.

---

This guide covers Billy civil parish (partly Carey barony, chiefly Lower Dunluce, Coleraine Poor Law Union, County Antrim) for 1780–1870. The parish contains the town of Bushmills and had active Presbyterian, Covenanting (Reformed Presbyterian), Methodist, Church of Ireland, and Roman Catholic communities. Because Ireland had no civil registration before 1845 for non-Catholic marriages or 1864 for all events, church registers — especially the Presbyterian and Covenanting registers accessible through PRONI's MIC 1P microfilm series — are the main source for a family in this parish across most of the target period. The 1861–1891 census returns for County Antrim were destroyed, so the Tithe Applotment Books and Griffith's Primary Valuation are the essential census substitutes. The place-resolution and URL-based wiki tools could not retrieve Irish data during this survey; FamilySearch collection counts and digitization percentages are therefore absent, and you should consult the PRONI catalogue and the FamilySearch Catalog directly.

The practical next step is to identify your ancestor's townland from Griffith's Valuation (free at Askaboutireland.ie), then contact PRONI to get the MIC 1P film reference for the Presbyterian congregation serving that townland in Bushmills.

output.text_response:
# Locality Guide: County Cork, Ireland (1830s–1840s)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **County Cork** is part of the province of Munster, under the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland during this period.
- **Cork City** is a distinct sub-jurisdiction within the county with separate civic administration — if your ancestor lived in the city, search both city and county record series.
- **Key historical event:** The Great Famine (1845 onward) directly shaped emigration from Cork's port at Cobh (then called Queenstown) in the late 1840s.

---

## Record Types Available

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
**Critical gap:** Civil registration had not yet begun for most events in this period:
- **Births and deaths:** State registration began **1 January 1864** — entirely after your target window.
- **Non-Catholic (Church of Ireland) marriages:** Registered from **1845 onward** only.
- **Catholic marriages:** State registration began **1 January 1864**.

**Consequence:** For the 1830s–1840s, **church registers are the mandatory substitute** for births, deaths, and marriages.

---

### Church Records *(primary vital record source for this period)*

| Denomination | Record Types | Where Held | Online? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Roman Catholic | Baptisms, marriages (burials rare) | National Library of Ireland (NLI) — microfilm/digital images to 1880 | **Free** at https://registers.nli.ie |
| Church of Ireland (Anglican) | Baptisms, marriages, burials | Representative Church Body Library (RCBL), Dublin | Partly online; partly physical |

- Many Cork Catholic parishes have registers beginning in the **1810s–1830s**, making them directly relevant to your period.
- Survival varies by parish — some Cork parishes' registers begin later and may leave gaps in the 1830s.

---

### Census Records

Ireland held censuses in **1821, 1831, 1841, and 1851**, but the **1922 Four Courts fire in Dublin destroyed most pre-1901 census returns**, including the 1841 and 1851 Cork returns. The primary substitutes are:

| Record | Date Range | Coverage | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Tithe Applotment Books** | 1823–1837 | Occupiers of tithe-liable (agricultural) land | Does NOT cover landless laborers or urban dwellers |
| **Griffith's Valuation** | Early 1850s (Cork) | Every householder, landlord, property description by townland | Just after target window; standard substitute for destroyed 1841/1851 censuses |

Both are held at the **National Archives of Ireland**, with significant online indexing on third-party services.

---

### Land Records

- **Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837):** Lists agricultural land occupiers — both a land record and census substitute for the 1830s.
- **Griffith's Valuation (early 1850s for Cork):** Townland-by-townland survey naming every occupier, their landlord, and property details. The standard starting point for identifying Cork families in the absence of census returns.

---

### Probate & Court Records

- The **1922 Four Courts fire** destroyed most wills and probate records held in Dublin before 1922. A missing will is likely a fire loss, not evidence no will existed.
- **What may survive:** Copies, abstracts, and indexes made before 1922 — including the **Betham Abstracts** and the **Index to Irish Wills** — sometimes held at the National Archives of Ireland, RCBL, and NLI.
- Probate in this period fell under ecclesiastical prerogative courts; the Probate Act 1857 transferred jurisdiction to civil courts from 1858.

---

### Military Records

- British Army recruited heavily in Ireland during the 1830s–1840s.
- **Service and pension records** for Irish soldiers are held at **The National Archives UK, Kew**; some are online via Ancestry/Findmypast.

---

### Cemetery Records

- Catholic parishes **rarely recorded burials** during this period.
- **Church of Ireland** churches more commonly maintained burial registers — held at the RCBL and by individual parishes.
- Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has some coverage.

---

### Newspaper Records

- Cork papers published during this period include the **Cork Examiner (founded 1841)** and the **Cork Constitution**.
- Content value: obituaries, marriage notices, estate/probate notices, emigration advertisements.
- Some coverage on **Newspapers.com** (subscription).

---

### Immigration/Emigration Records *(especially relevant for 1845–1849)*

- **Cork port at Cobh (Queenstown)** was a major Famine-era departure point.
- **Famine-era passenger manifests** list complete family groups, including infants traveling with parents — search the full manifest row, not just the head of household.
- **US arrival manifests** indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry; original records at NARA (https://www.archives.gov/).

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | Key Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| National Library of Ireland (NLI) | Catholic parish register images to 1880 | Free — https://registers.nli.ie |
| National Archives of Ireland, Dublin | Tithe Applotment Books, Griffith's Valuation, surviving probate indexes/abstracts | In-person; some digitized |
| Representative Church Body Library (RCBL), Dublin | Church of Ireland registers | In-person; research requests |
| Cork County Archives | Local Cork records | In-person |
| National Archives UK, Kew | British Army service and pension records | In-person; some online |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free — https://www.findagrave.com/ |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Subscription — https://www.newspapers.com/ |
| NARA (US) | US arrival passenger manifests | Physical; indexed on Ancestry/FamilySearch |

---

## Known Record Losses

The **1922 Four Courts fire destroyed**:
- Most pre-1901 Irish census returns (1841 and 1851 Cork censuses are almost certainly gone)
- Many wills, probate files, and government records held in Dublin

Catholic and Church of Ireland parish registers held *outside* Dublin were not affected by the fire and largely survive.

---

## Recommended Research Strategy

1. **Identify the specific townland** your ancestor came from — through any family letter, American record, or naturalization paper naming a parish or village in Cork. This is the essential starting point.

2. **Begin with the NLI Catholic parish images** at https://registers.nli.ie for the specific Cork parish — many Cork parishes have registers going back to the 1820s–1830s.

3. **Search the Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837)** to establish where the family was living and confirm the townland — this is the closest census equivalent for the 1830s.

4. **Search Griffith's Valuation** for the same townland (early 1850s Cork) as a cross-check and household survey.

5. **If they emigrated in the late 1840s**, search US arrival passenger manifests via FamilySearch or Ancestry — examine the full manifest row for all family members, not just the head of household.

6. **For probate:** Check surviving indexes and Betham Abstracts at the National Archives of Ireland; treat any absence as a potential fire loss.

---

The two defining facts of Cork genealogy in the 1830s–1840s are: **civil registration had not yet begun** (making church registers the only primary vital record source), and **the 1922 fire destroyed the census returns** that would otherwise cover this period exactly. The NLI's free online Catholic parish images, the Tithe Applotment Books, and Griffith's Valuation are the three records that matter most for this window.

# Locality Guide: County Cork, Ireland (1830s–1840s)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **County:** Cork (standardPlace: Cork, Munster, Ireland), formed in 1606; county type confirmed by place_search_all.
- **Cork City** (standardPlace: Cork, Cork, Munster, Ireland) is a distinct city within the county, recorded from 1185; it had separate civic administration and may have generated separate record series.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Munster, Ireland, under the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland during this period.
- **Population during period:** The place_population tool returned no data for Cork, Munster, Ireland; no population figures from tool results.
- **Economy:** Not returned by tools for this period.
- **Ethnic/Religious composition:** From the wiki page at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy, the population was predominantly Roman Catholic; Church of Ireland (Anglican) families formed a minority. This directly determines which record series applies to your ancestor.
- **Key historical events:** The Great Famine began in 1845 and directly affected the emigration records produced at Cork's port (Cobh/Queenstown) in the late 1840s, per the wiki page above.

## Boundary changes

Cork County has been a county under the province of Munster since 1606. The target period 1830s–1840s falls squarely within that stable boundary. Cork City functions as a separate sub-jurisdiction; if your ancestor lived in Cork City rather than the rural county, search under "Cork City" records as well as county records.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start dates (from https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy):**
  - Births and deaths: state registration began 1 January 1864 — entirely after the 1830s–1840s target period.
  - Non-Catholic (mostly Church of Ireland) marriages: registered from 1845 — only the very end of the target period.
  - Roman Catholic marriages: state registration began 1 January 1864.
- **Consequence:** There are no civil birth, marriage, or death certificates for the 1830s–1840s, with the sole exception of non-Catholic marriages from 1845 onward. Church registers are the mandatory substitute for this entire window.
- **Where held:** The General Register Office (GRO) holds post-1864 civil records; these do not apply to your period.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Roman Catholic and Church of Ireland parish registers (see Church Records below).

### Church records

- **Denominations present and record types (from https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy):**
  - **Roman Catholic:** Parish registers recording baptisms and marriages (burials rarely registered). The wiki page states survival varies by parish; many Cork parishes' registers begin in the 1810s–1830s, making them directly relevant to your period.
  - **Church of Ireland (Anglican):** Baptism, marriage, and burial registers.
- **Where held:**
  - Roman Catholic registers: The National Library of Ireland (NLI) holds microfilm and digital images of Catholic registers up to 1880, available free online. This is the starting point for Catholic families.
  - Church of Ireland registers: Held by the Representative Church Body Library (RCBL) and in some cases local custody.
- **Language:** English for the period of these registers.
- **Digitization level:** NLI Catholic images are available online (free); indexing varies by parish. Church of Ireland registers are partly online and partly physical-only.
- **Critical gap:** The wiki page states survival varies widely by parish. If a Cork parish's register does not begin until after the 1830s, there may be no extant record of events in that decade. Check the NLI catalog for the specific parish.

### Census records

- **National census:** Ireland conducted censuses in 1821, 1831, 1841, and 1851 — all within or just before the target period. However, the wiki page at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy states that most pre-1901 census returns were destroyed in the 1922 Four Courts fire. The 1841 and 1851 returns for Cork are almost certainly destroyed.
- **Census substitutes (from the same wiki page):**
  - **Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837):** Lists occupiers of tithe-liable land — the primary census substitute for the 1830s. Covers County Cork during the target period.
  - **Griffith's Valuation (Cork, early 1850s):** Lists every householder; the major substitute for the destroyed 1841 and 1851 censuses. Published for Cork in the early 1850s, just after the target window, but records households who survived the Famine period.
- **Digitization/access:** The wiki page does not state the digitization level of the Tithe Applotment Books or Griffith's Valuation for Cork specifically. These are widely indexed by third-party services; the external_links_search tool did not resolve County Cork to any curated specific links (the tool returned only generic results with an empty resolved place).

### Probate and court records

- **Consequence of 1922 fire (from https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy):** The Four Courts fire destroyed many pre-1922 wills and probate records held in Dublin. Wills proved in Irish ecclesiastical and civil courts before 1858, and many afterward, were heavily affected.
- **What may survive:** Copies, abstracts, and indexes made before 1922 — including the Index to Irish Wills and the Betham Abstracts — sometimes survive in the National Archives of Ireland, the Public Record Office of Northern Ireland (PRONI), the RCBL, and the National Library of Ireland. The wiki page does not give Cork-specific survival data.
- **Date range:** Probate in this period fell under ecclesiastical prerogative courts; the Probate Act 1857 transferred jurisdiction to civil courts from 1858.
- **Digitization level:** No collections_search or volume_search results were obtained for Cork probate records; access details cannot be confirmed from tool results alone.

### Land records

- **Key sources for the period (from https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy):**
  - **Tithe Applotment Books 1823–1837:** A land-based taxation survey of occupiers of tithe-liable land (primarily agricultural land). Cork entries cover this period directly.
  - **Griffith's Valuation (Cork, early 1850s):** A townland-by-townland valuation listing every occupier, landlord, and property description. The government survey that generated it is the main land record for identifying Cork families in the decade after the target window.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The wiki pages specific to Ireland Land and Property redirected to the generic Ireland Genealogy page and provided no additional detail on Cork land grants or the survey system.
- **Where held:** These records are held at the National Archives of Ireland and various repositories; online access exists but specific collection details were not returned by tools in this survey.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts in the period:** The British Army recruited in Ireland throughout the 1830s–1840s. No Cork-specific military record data was returned by tools in this survey.
- **Record types that may apply:** British Army service records for Irish soldiers; muster rolls; pension records (held at the National Archives UK, Kew).
- **Where held:** The National Archives UK, Kew holds service and pension records. The generic external link returned by external_links_search points to Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/), but no Ireland-specific Fold3 collection was identified by the tool for this place and period.

### Cemetery records

- **What exists:** Burial registers were rarely maintained in Catholic parishes for this period (the wiki page notes Catholic registers rarely recorded burials). Church of Ireland churches more commonly maintained burial registers.
- **Online coverage:** The generic external_links_search result includes Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/), but no Cork-specific cemetery collection was identified by the tool.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and vestry burial registers, where they survive, are held by individual parishes and the RCBL for Church of Ireland.

### Newspaper records

- **Cork papers published in this period included the Cork Examiner (founded 1841) and the Cork Constitution, though the wiki pages specific to Ireland newspapers redirected to the generic page and no digitization details were returned.**
- **Online coverage:** The generic external_links_search result includes Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/), but no Cork-specific digitized newspaper collection was confirmed by the tool for this period.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, estate and probate notices, and emigration advertisements.

### Immigration/emigration records

- **Relevant ports (from https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy):** Cork port — historically Cobh, known as Queenstown during the British period — was a major departure point. Famine-era passenger manifests list complete family groups, including infants traveling with parents.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests at American, Canadian, and Australian ports; British and Irish departure records where they survive.
- **Where held:** US arrival manifests are held at NARA and indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch. The generic external link to NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) was returned by tools; no Cork-specific passenger list collection URL was identified by the tool.
- **Content note:** The wiki page states that passenger manifests list "complete family groups including young children traveling with parents" — when researching the emigrating family, examine the full manifest for all members, not only the head of household.

### Tax records

- **Tithe Applotment Books 1823–1837** (covered above under Land Records) function as both a land record and a tax/census substitute. They are the most direct tax-equivalent source for the 1830s.
- **Other tax records:** Hearth Money Rolls and other earlier levies predate the target period. No additional Cork tax record data was returned by tools.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Relevant to Cork 1830s–1840s | Access |

| National Library of Ireland (NLI) | Catholic parish register images to 1880 (free online) | Free — https://registers.nli.ie |

| Fold3 | Military records | Subscription — https://www.fold3.com/ |
| NARA (US) | US arrival passenger manifests | Physical; indexed on Ancestry/FamilySearch — https://www.archives.gov/ |

**Coverage note:** The external_links_search tool did not resolve County Cork to curated Ireland-specific external collection URLs. The links in the generic result above are not Cork-confirmed by the tool; the NLI, RCBL, and NAI URLs above come from the FamilySearch wiki page at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy, not from external_links_search. No collections_search, volume_search, or catalog_search was successfully resolved to Cork-specific results in this survey; those gaps should be checked directly at FamilySearch.org by searching for County Cork.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives of Ireland, Dublin | Tithe Applotment Books, Griffith's Valuation, surviving probate indexes and abstracts | In-person; some online |
| National Library of Ireland, Dublin | Catholic parish register microfilm/digital images to 1880 | Free online; in-person |
| Representative Church Body Library, Dublin | Church of Ireland registers | In-person; research requests |
| Cork County Archives | Local Cork records | In-person |
| National Archives UK, Kew | British Army service and pension records for Irish soldiers | In-person; some online |

---

## Records NOT online

The following are confirmed from the wiki page or tool results as existing but not fully accessible online:

- **Church of Ireland parish registers:** Partly held physically at the RCBL; not fully digitized.
- **Probate abstracts and indexes** surviving from before the 1922 fire: Held at the National Archives of Ireland; access varies by collection.
- **Cork newspaper archives** for the 1830s–1840s: Digitization details not confirmed by tools.
- **British Army service records for Irish soldiers:** Held at The National Archives, Kew; some are online via Ancestry/Findmypast but Cork coverage not confirmed by tools in this survey.

---

## Known record losses

The FamilySearch wiki page at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy states explicitly that the **1922 Four Courts fire destroyed most pre-1901 census returns and many wills and government records**. This applies directly to the 1841 and 1851 censuses, which would have been the principal census sources for County Cork in the target period. The Tithe Applotment Books and Griffith's Valuation are the surviving substitutes, as the wiki page states.

No tool result reports the destruction of Catholic parish registers or Church of Ireland registers for Cork specifically; those collections held outside Dublin survived the fire.

---

## Research tips

- **Church records before civil registration (from https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy):** Because civil registration did not begin for births, deaths, and Catholic marriages until 1864, Roman Catholic parish registers are the only primary vital record source for the 1830s–1840s. Begin with the NLI's free online images at https://registers.nli.ie before looking elsewhere.
- **Identify the specific parish first:** Cork is a large county with many parishes. The Tithe Applotment Books or Griffith's Valuation can establish the townland your ancestor occupied, which in turn identifies the civil and Catholic parish — both are needed to locate the right register.
- **Use Griffith's Valuation as a household inventory:** Published in the early 1850s for Cork, it names every householder and their landlord, provides property descriptions, and gives townland locations. Even though it falls just after the 1840s, it reflects families who survived the Famine period and is the standard starting point in the absence of 1841/1851 census returns.
- **Tithe Applotment Books for the 1830s specifically:** These 1823–1837 books list occupiers of tithe-liable land and are the closest available census-equivalent for the target decade. They do not list all residents — only those occupying agricultural land — so landless laborers and urban dwellers may be absent.
- **Search emigration records from Cork port (Cobh/Queenstown):** The wiki page notes that Famine-era passenger manifests from Cork ports list complete family groups including infants. If your ancestor emigrated in the late 1840s, search US arrival manifests; the full manifest row (not just the head-of-household) may name children, spouses, and siblings.
- **Account for the 1922 fire when probate records are absent:** A missing will or probate file for the 1830s–1840s is likely a fire loss, not evidence that no will existed. Check surviving indexes, abstracts (Betham Abstracts), and copies held at the National Archives of Ireland, the RCBL, and the NLI.

County Cork in the 1830s and 1840s is a research environment defined above all by two facts: civil registration had not yet begun (births, deaths, and Catholic marriages would not be recorded by the government until 1864), and the 1922 fire in Dublin destroyed most of the census returns and probate records that might otherwise have documented this period. The surviving records that matter most are Roman Catholic parish registers — many Cork parishes have registers beginning in the 1820s and 1830s, now freely viewable at the National Library of Ireland's website — along with the Tithe Applotment Books of 1823–1837 and Griffith's Valuation from the early 1850s, which together act as census substitutes naming the households who lived on the land. If your ancestor emigrated during or after the Famine (1845 onward), passenger manifests from Cork's port at Cobh are another key source and can name the whole family group, not just the head of household.

The recommended next step is to identify the specific townland your ancestor came from — through any family document, letter, or American record that names a parish or village — and then search the NLI's Catholic parish images for that parish alongside the Tithe Applotment and Griffith's records for the same townland.

**Where to find an 1812 marriage in Javorje nad Škofjo Loko**

**Administrative context first.** In 1812 Javorje was not in Slovenia as a modern state — it sat inside the **French Illyrian Provinces** (1809–1813). Napoleon had introduced civil registration there under French law. That means two separate record series could document a marriage in 1812: the Catholic parish register (which continued to be kept) and a French civil registration record (*acte de mariage*) produced alongside it. After Austria reclaimed the territory in 1813 the French civil system ended, but records created under it did not disappear.

---

**Primary record: Catholic parish marriage register**

The main source is the marriage register of whatever Catholic parish served Javorje, which falls within the **Archdiocese of Ljubljana** (the historical territory of Carniola/Krain).

Your two concrete paths to the parish register:

1. **Matricula Online** — https://data.matricula-online.eu/en/slovenia/
   This is the primary online source for Slovenian Catholic parish registers. Registers are browse-only images. Browse to the Škofja Loka area, identify which parish served Javorje, and open its marriage book covering 1812. Entries are typically in Latin and German, giving the groom's and bride's names, fathers' names, witnesses, and date.

2. **Archdiocesan Archive in Ljubljana** — Original registers from before the 1880s are held in archdiocesan archives, not at the local parish:
   > Nadškofijski arhiv, Krekov trg 1, 1000 Ljubljana — arhiv.lj@rkc.si

   Contact them to confirm which parish covered Javorje in 1812 and whether the register survives.

---

**Secondary record: French civil registration**

Under Napoleonic rule the Illyrian Provinces kept civil marriage registers at the commune level, written in French. When French rule ended, these passed to Austrian and eventually Slovenian archives. Survivors are held at the **Archive of Slovenia** (Arhiv Republike Slovenije, Zvezdarska 1, Ljubljana — https://www.arhiv.gov.si/). Their online catalogue is worth checking for Illyrian Provinces civil records for the Škofja Loka commune.

---

**What FamilySearch has for this area**

FamilySearch has no digitized or indexed collections for Javorje or Škofja Loka for the 1790–1830 period — this is a digitization gap, not evidence the records don't exist. The FamilySearch Catalog (https://www.familysearch.org/catalog/search) does show 36 items filed under Škofja Loka; browsing the full list may turn up film or DGS numbers for the relevant parish marriage series.

---

**Practical search sequence**

1. Go to **Matricula Online**, navigate to the Škofja Loka area, open the marriage register covering 1812, and browse by date.
2. If no Javorje-area register appears there, email the **Archdiocesan Archive in Ljubljana** to identify the parish and inquire about access.
3. Check the **Archive of Slovenia** for Illyrian Provinces civil marriage records for the Škofja Loka commune, 1812.
4. Browse all 36 FamilySearch Catalog entries for Škofja Loka for any parish register entries.

---

**Language note.** The Catholic parish register will be in Latin and German. A French civil registration entry will be in French. Neither record type uses Slovenian in this period.

Javorje is a small settlement just outside Škofja Loka town. Its 1812 marriage record almost certainly lives in the Catholic marriage register of the parish that covered that village — most accessible today through **Matricula Online** or directly from the **Archdiocesan Archive in Ljubljana**. Because 1812 falls squarely in the Illyrian Provinces period, there is also a chance a civil marriage record was created alongside the church one — that would be at the **Archive of Slovenia**.

# Locality Guide: Berkshire County, Massachusetts (1820–1850)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Formed:** 1761; boundaries were stable throughout the target period
- **County seat:** Pittsfield
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Massachusetts, United States
- **Religious denominations:** Congregational (dominant), Methodist, Episcopal, Baptist
- **Economy:** Agricultural with early industrialization — iron furnaces, paper mills, textiles

---

## Vital Records (Births, Marriages, Deaths)

**The most important thing to understand:** Massachusetts had *town-level* vital recording, not county-level. Each town kept its own records. A statewide system didn't start until **1841** — so for 1820–1841, the town clerk is the *only* civil authority that made these records.

- **Marriage intentions** were commonly recorded in the bride's home town, with possible additional entries in the groom's town — search both if one comes up empty.
- **Published series:** *Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850* covers over 200 Massachusetts towns. Many Berkshire County towns are included. The New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS) or the Berkshire Athenaeum can confirm which towns have published volumes — this is the fastest starting point.

**FamilySearch indexed collection:**
- [Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550) — indexed + images, searchable by name

**Browse-only (unindexed) FamilySearch volume:**
- **imageGroupNumber 004500891** — Berkshire County Town Clerk Vital and Town Records, 1761–1850, 512 images, 0% name-indexed. Must be browsed image by image.

---

## Church Records

For 1820–1841 especially, church records are often the **only** source for vital events before the statewide system began — not just a fallback.

**FamilySearch indexed collection:**
- [Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657) — covers Berkshire County within the statewide collection

**Browse-only FamilySearch volume:**
- **imageGroupNumber 004500892** — Pittsfield Congregational Church Records, 1791–1850, 274 images, 0% name-indexed. Pittsfield only; other congregations' records may exist physically or in the indexed collection above.

---

## Census Records

| Year | Coverage | Names |
|------|----------|-------|
| 1820 | ✓ | Head of household only |
| 1830 | ✓ | Head of household only |
| 1840 | ✓ | Head of household only |
| 1850 | ✓ | **Every individual** — includes ages, birthplaces, occupations |

The **1850 mortality schedule** lists deaths in the year preceding the census — valuable for death information before death registration was well established.

**Tip:** Work backward from the 1850 census (which names everyone) to establish the full household, then trace vital events through town and church records.

---

## Probate Records

Filed at the county level at the **Berkshire County Probate Court, Pittsfield**.
- Wills (testate), administrations (intestate), guardianships, inventories — all filed here from 1761 onward.

**FamilySearch:**
- [Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901)

---

## Land Records

- **System:** Metes and bounds (not federal land state)
- **Filed at:** Berkshire County Registry of Deeds, Pittsfield (deed books from 1761 onward in a remarkably complete run)
- No digitized FamilySearch volume for county deed books was found; check the Registry directly for online index availability.

---

## Military Records

Relevant conflicts within the period:
- **War of 1812** (service 1812–1815; pensions filed for decades after)
- **Mexican-American War** (1846–1848)

**Access:**
- [Fold3](https://www.fold3.com) — service records, pension files
- NARA (originals) — pension case files, bounty land warrants
- Massachusetts Archives, Boston — state adjutant general records

---

## Cemetery Records

- [Find A Grave](https://www.findagrave.com/) covers many Berkshire County cemeteries
- Sexton and burial registers held by individual cemeteries and churches
- Berkshire Athenaeum (Pittsfield) holds local cemetery transcription materials

---

## Newspaper Records

- [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/) — includes historical Berkshire County papers (the *Pittsfield Sun* published from 1800)
- Berkshire Athenaeum holds local newspaper microfilm
- Value: obituaries, marriage and death notices, legal notices (estate administration, land sales)

---

## Repository Guide

### Online
| Repository | Key Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Town Vital Records 1620–1890; Church Records 1630–1920; Probate 1635–1991; two browse-only volumes | Free |
| Ancestry | Federal censuses 1820–1850 | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records (War of 1812, Mexican-American War) | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Berkshire County newspapers | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free |

### Physical
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| Berkshire County town clerks (each town) | Original birth, marriage, death records; town meeting records |
| Berkshire County Probate Court, Pittsfield | Wills, administrations, guardianships from 1761 |
| Berkshire County Registry of Deeds, Pittsfield | Deeds and land records from 1761 |
| Massachusetts Archives, Boston | Court records; state records; some military |
| NEHGS, Boston | Largest regional genealogical library; published vital records series |
| Berkshire Athenaeum, Pittsfield | Local histories, newspaper microfilm, Berkshire County records |

---

## Critical Tips for Your Border Location

**Check both sides of the state line.** A family near the New York and Vermont borders frequently generated records in adjacent jurisdictions too — church memberships, land purchases, and vital registrations could appear in neighboring counties. Consider searching:
- **New York:** Columbia, Rensselaer, or Washington Counties
- **Vermont:** Bennington County

**Don't assume the state system covers 1820–1841.** Massachusetts's statewide vital registration only began in 1841. For events before that date, the town clerk's records and church registers are your only civil/religious options.

**Both FamilySearch digitized volumes are browse-only.** If you can narrow down a specific town and approximate date, browsing becomes manageable. Otherwise, start with the indexed statewide collection ([collection 2061550](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550)) before attempting a manual browse.
