# Locality Guide: Alabama Region, Pre-Statehood (ca. 1780–1820)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Alabama achieved statehood 14 December 1819. The territory that became Alabama was organized as part of the **Mississippi Territory** from 1798 to 1817, then briefly as the **Alabama Territory** (1817–1819). Before 1798, most of interior Alabama was under Georgia's charter claim, while the Mobile area was under French (1702–1763), British (1763–1780), and Spanish (1780–1813) administration.
- **Administrative center (territorial era):** Washington, Mississippi Territory (later Natchez) for the broader territory; Huntsville and St. Stephens for the Alabama portion.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Mississippi Territory (United States) for the period 1798–1817.
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the place_population tool for this jurisdiction and period.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, early cotton cultivation in the Tennessee Valley (post-1810 migration surge), fur trade, and river commerce at Mobile.
- **Ethnic composition:** Creek and Cherokee nations across the interior; Anglo-American settlers migrating primarily from Georgia, the Carolinas, Virginia, and Tennessee after the Creek War (1813–1814); French Creole and Spanish Creole communities at Mobile; enslaved African Americans throughout.
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist circuit riders, Baptist frontier congregations, Catholic parishes in the Mobile area (continuing from French/Spanish colonial era), and Presbyterian missions.
- **Key historical events:** Creek War 1813–1814 (opened interior Alabama to settlement; records may reference militia service and refugee movement); U.S. seizure of Mobile 1813 (shifted Mobile's record-keeping jurisdiction from Spain to the U.S.); land rush following the Indian land cessions, 1814–1819.

## Boundary changes
- **Before 1798:** The region was claimed by Georgia (via its colonial charter) but controlled in practice by Spain in the south and Native nations in the interior. Georgia ceded its western land claims to the U.S. in 1802, retroactively clarifying federal jurisdiction.
- **1798:** Mississippi Territory organized from the ceded Georgia lands plus territory acquired from Spain at the 31st parallel; it encompassed what is now both Alabama and Mississippi.
- **1804 and 1812:** The Territory expanded northward and eastward.
- **1817:** Western half of Mississippi Territory became the state of Mississippi; eastern half organized as the **Alabama Territory**.
- **1819:** Alabama admitted as a state.
- **Mobile area:** Remained under Spanish control until 1813 (U.S. occupation during the War of 1812). Records for Mobile before 1813 must be sought in Spanish colonial archives; county-level records begin only from U.S. administration.
- **Earliest counties in Alabama portion of Mississippi Territory:** Washington County (1800), Baldwin County (1809), Madison County (1808). Most interior counties were formed after 1814. Any event before those formation dates falls under the parent territorial jurisdiction.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No statewide civil registration existed during this period. The FamilySearch Wiki Alabama Vital Records page did not return specific content during this survey; consult it directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Vital_Records for confirmed start dates by registration level.
- **What exists:** County marriage registers beginning at county formation dates — the earliest is Washington County (formed 1800). FamilySearch has indexed the collection "Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950" (collection 1598408; 612,345 records, 1,224,690 persons). Birth and death registration was not systematically required in this era.
- **Where held:** County probate courts (original registers); ADAH (microfilm and some originals); FamilySearch collection 1598408 (indexed, with images).
- **Gaps:** No marriage records predate county formation. No civil birth or death registers for this period.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism/burial registers; estate inventories naming heirs; territorial censuses.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic parishes (Mobile and surrounding area, continuous from French/Spanish colonial era); Methodist and Baptist congregations (frontier circuits, beginning ca. 1808–1815 in interior Alabama).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials (Catholic Mobile); membership lists and minutes (Protestant frontier churches).
- **Where held:** Catholic records for the Mobile Diocese held at the Archdiocese of Mobile Archives; Protestant records scattered at denominational archives and local churches. FamilySearch collection "Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950" (coll. 1986396; 156,789 records) covers some of this. FamilySearch also has browse-only images for Washington County records 1803–1820 (DGS 004512890, 96 images). The Alabama_Church_Records wiki page did not return Alabama-specific content during this survey.
- **Language:** Catholic colonial-era records from the Mobile area are in French and Spanish; Protestant records are in English.

### Census records
- **Territorial censuses:** The Mississippi Territory conducted enumerations in **1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810** covering present-day Alabama. These are held at the **Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH)** in Montgomery, per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records.
- **Federal census:** The **1810 federal census** is the earliest decennial census that includes the Alabama region. FamilySearch collection "Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890" (coll. 2016756; 287,634 records) covers this. The companion Mississippi Territory collection (coll. 1927171) covers 1792–1890.
- **Access:** The 1810 federal census index is searchable by name on FamilySearch; the territorial censuses at ADAH require in-person or mail access.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, letters of administration, guardianships; territorial court minutes; deed records.
- **Date range:** From county formation dates (Washington County 1800 is earliest). FamilySearch collection "Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985" (coll. 1537764; 438,210 records). FamilySearch also has two browse-only digitized volumes: DGS 004512889 (214 images, 1808–1819, territorial court and land records for Alabama) and DGS 004512890 (96 images, 1803–1820, Washington County deed and probate records).
- **Where held:** County probate courts (originals); ADAH; FamilySearch (indexed collection + browse-only volumes). The Mississippi Territory volume (DGS 004498712, 143 images, 1799–1817) covers territorial-level land and court records.
- **Digitization level:** The FamilySearch indexed collection (1537764) is searchable by name with images. The three individual volumes (DGS 004512889, 004512890, 004498712) are browse-only — 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable; each must be examined image by image.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Federal rectangular survey (township and range), adopted at statehood. Pre-statehood grants used metes and bounds and Spanish/British survey conventions.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Federal land state — the U.S. General Land Office (GLO) issued patents after statehood. Pre-statehood: Spain issued grants in the Mobile area; the U.S. government issued grants in the Mississippi Territory from 1798 onward.
- **Types:** Federal land patents (GLO records portal, https://glorecords.blm.gov/); Spanish colonial land grants; territorial deed books at county courthouses.
- **Where held:** BLM GLO portal for federal patents; ADAH for territorial and early state deeds; Library of Congress for copies of Spanish colonial grants; Archivo General de Indias (Seville, Spain) for original Spanish records. FamilySearch collection "Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907" (coll. 1919694; 312,450 records) covers territorial-era land grants.
- **Date range:** Colonial grants from pre-1798; U.S. territorial grants from 1798 onward.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Creek War 1813–1814 (Alabama militia and U.S. Army service); War of 1812 (Mobile garrison); earlier Territorial-era militia musters.
- **Record types:** Service records and pension files at NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); militia rolls in ADAH; bounty land warrants.
- **Where held:** NARA for federal records; ADAH for territorial and state militia records; Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) for digitized military records.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Church cemeteries (Catholic in Mobile area; Protestant frontier cemeteries inland); a small number of formally platted cemeteries after 1815.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) for some cemeteries; coverage for the 1800–1820 period is sparse.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records rare for this period; gravestone inscriptions are often the primary source.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Mobile area had early newspapers (the Mobile Centinel, founded 1811 is among the earliest). Interior Alabama had no newspapers in this period.
- **Where held:** ADAH holds microfilm of early Alabama newspapers; Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) has some Alabama holdings, but coverage for pre-1820 papers is limited.
- **Content value:** Legal notices, land sales, estate announcements.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Mobile (Gulf Coast port; primary point of entry for the region). New Orleans was an important secondary port for people moving up the rivers.
- **Record types:** Passenger manifests at NARA; naturalization records at territorial and county courts (pre-1906, any court of record could naturalize); Spanish colonial passport and permission records for the Mobile District.
- **Where held:** NARA for U.S.-era manifests; Archivo General de Indias and Library of Congress for Spanish colonial records.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Territorial tax lists; county personal property and real property assessments.
- **Date range:** Mississippi Territory tax lists from ca. 1800 onward.
- **Where held:** ADAH; county tax assessors' offices (originals).
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists for 1801, 1805, 1808 substitute for the missing census years and name heads of household.

### Other record types
- **Territorial legislative and executive records:** Acts, petitions, and governor's correspondence at ADAH and in published territorial papers (Clarence Carter, ed., *Territorial Papers of the United States*, vols. 5–6 cover Mississippi Territory).
- **Creek and Cherokee nation records:** Removal-era records (post-1830) are outside this period, but earlier treaty records and agent correspondence name Native individuals and mixed-heritage families; held at NARA (Record Group 75, Bureau of Indian Affairs).

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950 (coll. 1598408); Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985 (coll. 1537764); Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890 (coll. 2016756); Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950 (coll. 1986396); Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907 (coll. 1919694); Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920 (coll. 1855293); plus 3 browse-only digitized volumes (DGS 004512889, 004512890, 004498712) | Free |
| BLM General Land Office | Federal land patents for Alabama (post-statehood 1819) | Free — https://glorecords.blm.gov/ |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Military service, pension, naturalization records | Free finding aids; some records fee-based — https://www.archives.gov/ |
| Fold3 | Digitized military records (War of 1812, Creek War era) | Subscription — https://www.fold3.com/ |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census (1810 and later) | Subscription — https://www.ancestry.com/ |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free — https://www.findagrave.com/ |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 2 volumes for Alabama (1780–1820) and 1 volume for Mississippi Territory — all 3 were examined and are the complete result set for those searches. These are all browse-only.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Alabama Dept. of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery, AL | Territorial censuses 1801, 1805, 1808; militia rolls; county deed books; newspaper microfilm; colonial records copies | In-person; some online finding aids at adah.alabama.gov |
| County probate courts (each county) | Marriage registers, wills, deeds, court minutes | In-person or mail |
| Archdiocese of Mobile Archives | Catholic parish registers from the colonial era onward | Contact the archives directly |
| National Archives (NARA), Southeast Region, Atlanta, GA | Federal territorial records, court records | In-person or written request |
| Library of Congress, Washington, DC | Copies of Spanish colonial records for the Mobile District | In-person; some digitized holdings online |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Original Spanish colonial records (census, land grants, church registers) for the Mobile area pre-1813 | In-person or through Portal de Archivos Españoles (PARES) online |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial records for Mobile (1702–1763) | In-person or written request |
| Mobile Municipal Archives, Mobile, AL | Microfilm of French colonial records for Mobile | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- Territorial censuses for 1801, 1805, and 1808 (ADAH; not digitized online).
- Most county tax lists and territorial tax assessments pre-1810.
- Spanish colonial church registers for Mobile (originals in Seville; partial microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives — not on a major genealogy platform).
- French colonial records for Mobile (originals in Aix-en-Provence; partial microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives).
- County court minute books for the territorial period.

## Known record losses
No tool result returned during this survey specifically identified destroyed or lost record sets for this place and period. The absence of records in a database is a coverage or digitization gap, not necessarily a loss. For confirmed losses (e.g., courthouse fires), consult the ADAH and local historical societies directly.

## Research tips
- **Search under Mississippi Territory, not Alabama**, for any event before 1817. FamilySearch collections and catalog entries filed under 'Alabama' may not surface territorial-era records; explicitly search the Mississippi Territory collections as well (e.g., coll. 1919694 for land records). Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records
- **The Mobile area is a separate research trail.** Records for Mobile before 1813 are in French and Spanish archives (Archivo General de Indias, Seville; Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence; copies at the Library of Congress and Mobile Municipal Archives). Do not confuse this colonial-era record series with the territorial Alabama records filed after U.S. administration began in 1813. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records
- **Use territorial censuses as your starting point.** The 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 Mississippi Territory censuses (at ADAH) name heads of household years before the 1810 federal census and are your best substitute for missing vital records in the first decade of settlement. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records
- **Land records are the primary family-linking source for this era.** Because no civil birth or death registration existed, land transaction chains, estate inventories listing heirs, and federal land patents (GLO) are often the only documents placing individuals in a specific county and linking family members.
- **The three FamilySearch browse-only volumes** (DGS 004512889, 004512890, 004498712) must be examined image by image — there is no name index and no full-text search. Plan time accordingly.
- **Militia rolls and territorial legislative petitions** at ADAH name settlers who do not appear in any other surviving record, especially for the 1800–1813 period before the population surge.

| Alabama Dept. of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery, AL | Territorial censuses 1801, 1805, 1808; militia rolls; county deed books; newspaper microfilm; colonial records copies | In-person; some online finding aids at adah.alabama.gov |
| County probate courts (each county) | Marriage registers, wills, deeds, court minutes | In-person or mail |
| Archdiocese of Mobile Archives | Catholic parish registers from the colonial era onward | Contact the archives directly |
| National Archives (NARA), Southeast Region, Atlanta, GA | Federal territorial records, court records | In-person or written request |
| Library of Congress, Washington, DC | Copies of Spanish colonial records for the Mobile District | In-person; some digitized holdings online |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Original Spanish colonial records (census, land grants, church registers) for the Mobile area pre-1813 | In-person or through Portal de Archivos Españoles (PARES) online |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial records for Mobile (1702–1763) | In-person or written request |
| Mobile Municipal Archives, Mobile, AL | Microfilm of French colonial records for Mobile | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- Territorial censuses for 1801, 1805, and 1808 (ADAH; not digitized online).
- Most county tax lists and territorial tax assessments pre-1810.
- Spanish colonial church registers for Mobile (originals in Seville; partial microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives — not on a major genealogy platform).
- French colonial records for Mobile (originals in Aix-en-Provence; partial microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives).
- County court minute books for the territorial period.

## Known record losses
No tool result returned during this survey specifically identified destroyed or lost record sets for this place and period. The absence of records in a database is a coverage or digitization gap, not necessarily a loss. For confirmed losses (e.g., courthouse fires), consult the ADAH and local historical societies directly.

## Research tips
- **Search under Mississippi Territory, not Alabama**, for any event before 1817. FamilySearch collections and catalog entries filed under 'Alabama' may not surface territorial-era records; explicitly search the Mississippi Territory collections as well (e.g., coll. 1919694 for land records). Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records
- **The Mobile area is a separate research trail.** Records for Mobile before 1813 are in French and Spanish archives (Archivo General de Indias, Seville; Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence; copies at the Library of Congress and Mobile Municipal Archives). Do not confuse this colonial-era record series with the territorial Alabama records filed after U.S. administration began in 1813. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records
- **Use territorial censuses as your starting point.** The 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 Mississippi Territory censuses (at ADAH) name heads of household years before the 1810 federal census and are your best substitute for missing vital records in the first decade of settlement. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records
- **Land records are the primary family-linking source for this era.** Because no civil birth or death registration existed, land transaction chains, estate inventories listing heirs, and federal land patents (GLO) are often the only documents placing individuals in a specific county and linking family members.
- **The three FamilySearch browse-only volumes** (DGS 004512889, 004512890, 004498712) must be examined image by image — there is no name index and no full-text search. Plan time accordingly.
- **Militia rolls and territorial legislative petitions** at ADAH name settlers who do not appear in any other surviving record, especially for the 1800–1813 period before the population surge.

**Pre-1800 Arkansas (Spanish Louisiana) — Locality Guide**

The area that is now Arkansas was not its own jurisdiction before 1800. It was part of **French Louisiana** from the founding of Arkansas Post in 1686, then **Spanish Louisiana** from 1763 until Spain secretly returned it to France in 1800.

**Settlement context:** The only significant European settlement was **Arkansas Post** on the Mississippi River, so nearly every surviving record from before 1800 was created at that one place. Records are written in **French or Spanish**.

**Important Caveat on FamilySearch Indexed Collections**

The three indexed Arkansas collections on FamilySearch all begin **after 1819** (after U.S. territorial organization). None cover the Spanish period.

When you're ready, a sequenced research plan can be drawn up targeting these repositories in priority order based on what is already known about your ancestors.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Arkansas Territory (Pre-1800, French and Spanish Colonial Period)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Arkansas Post established by the French in 1686 as the first European settlement in the lower Mississippi Valley
- **Colonial capitals:** New Orleans (administrative) and Arkansas Post (the only significant local settlement in present-day Arkansas)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** French Louisiana (1686-1763), then Spanish Louisiana (1763-1800); the territory briefly reverted to France in 1800 before the Louisiana Purchase (1803) brought it under U.S. control
- **Population during period:** Extremely sparse — primarily French and Spanish soldiers, traders, missionaries, and a small number of settlers at Arkansas Post; the broader territory was inhabited by Native American nations (Quapaw, Osage, Caddo)
- **Economy:** Fur trade, Mississippi River commerce, small-scale agriculture at Arkansas Post
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creole settlers, Spanish colonial officials and soldiers, Native Americans (especially Quapaw near Arkansas Post); small numbers of enslaved Africans
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic exclusively among European settlers; sacramental registers are the primary vital record equivalent
- **Key historical events:** France ceded Louisiana to Spain by the Treaty of Fontainebleau (1762, effective 1769); Spain ceded it back to France by the Treaty of San Ildefonso (1800); Louisiana Purchase (1803) transferred the territory to the United States

## Boundary changes
- 1686-1762: French Louisiana — Arkansas Post under French colonial administration headquartered at New Orleans
- 1763-1800: Spanish Louisiana — the Treaty of Paris (1763) transferred Louisiana to Spain; Spanish administration continued at New Orleans with the commandant at Arkansas Post managing local affairs
- 1800: Territory reverted to France by Treaty of San Ildefonso (Spain ceded it secretly)
- 1803: Louisiana Purchase — the United States acquired the territory; organized as Orleans Territory and District of Louisiana (later Missouri Territory)
- 1819: Arkansas Territory established as a separate U.S. territory
- 1836: Arkansas admitted to statehood
- **For pre-1800 research:** there is no Arkansas jurisdiction to search. Records are filed under French Louisiana or Spanish Louisiana, with the colonial capital at New Orleans as the administrative hub.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil vital registration existed in this territory before 1800. The FamilySearch Wiki page for Arkansas Vital Records returned only generic content and gave no specific registration start date for the colonial period.
- **What exists:** No civil births, marriages, or deaths were recorded by any government in this territory before 1800. Church sacramental registers (see below) are the only vital record equivalent.
- **Where held:** Not applicable for civil registration in this period
- **Gaps:** The entire pre-1800 period has no civil registration — this is not a loss but a structural absence
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic sacramental registers at Arkansas Post (see Church Records below); Spanish padrones (household censuses)

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic exclusively among European settlers; French Capuchin and Jesuit missionaries served Arkansas Post from the early 1700s
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials — sacramental registers are the equivalent of vital records for this population
- **Where held:** Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock holds surviving original registers; transcribed copies are at the Arkansas History Commission in Little Rock; the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records) confirms both repositories
- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** Image group 008814402 — 64 images of Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial), covering Arkansas Post, 1763-1800. This volume is **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable) and is written in **Spanish**. It must be examined image by image with no search capability.
- **Language:** French (pre-1763 registers), Spanish (1763-1800 registers); a researcher must read the original language or obtain a translation

### Census records
- **Spanish padrones (1763-1800):** Household census lists compiled by Spanish colonial administrators, naming the head of household and family members. These are a key substitute for civil registration. Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records), surviving padrones are at the Arkansas History Commission and the Archivo General de Indias in Seville.
- **Federal/national census:** The first U.S. federal census covering this territory was 1810 (after the Louisiana Purchase). No federal census applies to the pre-1800 period.
- **FamilySearch indexed collection:** 'Arkansas, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1819-1870' (collection 2085124, 178,345 records) — begins in 1819, well after the colonial period; useful only if an ancestor's trail extends into the territorial period.
- **Access:** Padrones are physical-only or microfilm at the repositories listed above; not available as an indexed online collection

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Spanish colonial courts at Arkansas Post handled civil disputes, land matters, and some estate proceedings; records were kept by the commandant of the post
- **Date range:** Spanish period 1769-1800; some French-era records may predate 1763
- **Where held:** Arkansas History Commission (Little Rock) and Archivo General de Indias (Seville); microfilm copies at the Library of Congress, per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Digitization level:** Physical or microfilm only; not available as an indexed online collection on FamilySearch

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Spanish land grants (concessions) used metes and bounds descriptions referencing natural features; French grants preceded them in the same style
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Under Spain, the Governor of Louisiana (New Orleans) issued land concessions; local commandant at Arkansas Post administered smaller grants. The FamilySearch Wiki page for Arkansas Land and Property returned only generic content and gave no Arkansas-specific details.
- **Types:** Spanish land concessions, French land grants; some grants were later confirmed by U.S. land offices after 1803
- **Date range:** French grants from 1686; Spanish concessions from 1769
- **Where held:** Arkansas History Commission; Archivo General de Indias (Seville); confirmed U.S.-era copies are at the Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) for patents issued after 1803
- **Post-1803 angle:** After the Louisiana Purchase, holders of French and Spanish land grants could petition the U.S. for confirmation. These confirmation records at NARA may describe the original colonial grantee and date, making them a bridge source even when the ancestor lived before 1800.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** French-Indian conflicts (early 1700s); American Revolutionary War (Spain was an ally of France against Britain; Spanish forces in Louisiana were involved); Spanish colonial garrison records at Arkansas Post
- **Record types:** Muster rolls and service records for the Spanish garrison at Arkansas Post; Spanish militia records
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias (Seville); Archivo General de Simancas (Valladolid, Spain) for military records; some copies at the Library of Congress on microfilm; Louisiana Historical Center in New Orleans may hold related records
- **Digitization level:** Physical repositories abroad; not available as indexed online collections

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Arkansas Post had a Catholic burial ground associated with the mission church; no formal maintained cemetery records from the pre-1800 period are known to survive separately from sacramental registers
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (findagrave.com) covers later periods; coverage of pre-1800 burials at Arkansas Post is negligible
- **Physical records:** Burial entries are recorded within the sacramental registers (see Church Records above)

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** No newspaper was published in the Arkansas territory before 1800. The first newspaper in Arkansas did not appear until the territorial period (after 1819).
- **Relevant regional papers:** The Louisiana Gazette (New Orleans, founded 1804) and earlier Spanish-era gazettes occasionally reported on events in the broader Louisiana territory, but coverage of Arkansas Post specifically is rare
- **Where held:** Louisiana State University (Baton Rouge) and New Orleans Public Library hold early Louisiana newspaper collections

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans was the principal port of entry for the entire Louisiana territory. All ocean-going arrivals to Arkansas-area settlements passed through or were documented at New Orleans.
- **Record types:** Spanish colonial records of arrivals at New Orleans; passenger manifests for the colonial period are sparse and largely unpublished; naturalization in the modern sense did not apply under colonial administration
- **Where held:** Louisiana Historical Center (New Orleans); Archivo General de Indias (Seville) for official records of colonial appointments and arrivals
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) in the modern sense did not exist for the colonial period in this territory. Arrivals of settlers are sometimes recorded in padrones or in correspondence between Arkansas Post commandants and the Governor of Louisiana at New Orleans.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Spanish colonial tribute and trade records; not equivalent to U.S. property or poll tax records
- **Date range:** Spanish period 1769-1800
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias (Seville); Arkansas History Commission for surviving local copies
- **Substitute value:** Padrones (see Census Records above) function as both census and quasi-tax records in this context

### Other record types
- **Commandant correspondence:** Letters between the Arkansas Post commandant and the Governor of Louisiana at New Orleans frequently named settlers, land claimants, and local events. These are at the Archivo General de Indias and in published transcriptions (the "Papeles Procedentes de Cuba" series).
- **Trade and license records:** Fur trade licenses and commercial permits issued at New Orleans and Arkansas Post named traders operating in the territory. Some are published in Louisiana historical collections.
- **Mission records:** Jesuit and Capuchin mission records occasionally recorded contacts with Native Americans and mixed-heritage individuals not found in parish sacramental registers.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | 1 digitized volume: Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial), Arkansas Post, 1763-1800 (image group 008814402, 64 images, browse-only, Spanish) | Free |
| FamilySearch | Arkansas, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1819-1870 (178,345 records) — post-1800 only | Free |
| BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | U.S.-era land patents, some confirming pre-1803 French/Spanish grants | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Spanish/French land grant confirmation records post-1803; Louisiana territorial records | Free finding aids; some digital |

**Coverage of this survey:** 1 digitized volume matches the Arkansas territory for the pre-1800 period. That single volume is the complete result set for FamilySearch digitized holdings in this period — no additional pages were needed.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|

# Locality Guide: Arkansas Territory (Pre-1800, French and Spanish Colonial Period)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Arkansas Post established by the French in 1686 as the first European settlement in the lower Mississippi Valley
- **Colonial capitals:** New Orleans (administrative) and Arkansas Post (the only significant local settlement in present-day Arkansas)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** French Louisiana (1686-1763), then Spanish Louisiana (1763-1800); the territory briefly reverted to France in 1800 before the Louisiana Purchase (1803) brought it under U.S. control
- **Population during period:** Extremely sparse — primarily French and Spanish soldiers, traders, missionaries, and a small number of settlers at Arkansas Post; the broader territory was inhabited by Native American nations (Quapaw, Osage, Caddo)
- **Economy:** Fur trade, Mississippi River commerce, small-scale agriculture at Arkansas Post
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creole settlers, Spanish colonial officials and soldiers, Native Americans (especially Quapaw near Arkansas Post); small numbers of enslaved Africans
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic exclusively among European settlers; sacramental registers are the primary vital record equivalent
- **Key historical events:** France ceded Louisiana to Spain by the Treaty of Fontainebleau (1762, effective 1769); Spain ceded it back to France by the Treaty of San Ildefonso (1800); Louisiana Purchase (1803) transferred the territory to the United States

## Boundary changes
- 1686-1762: French Louisiana — Arkansas Post under French colonial administration headquartered at New Orleans
- 1763-1800: Spanish Louisiana — the Treaty of Paris (1763) transferred Louisiana to Spain; Spanish administration continued at New Orleans with the commandant at Arkansas Post managing local affairs
- 1800: Territory reverted to France by Treaty of San Ildefonso (Spain ceded it secretly)
- 1803: Louisiana Purchase — the United States acquired the territory; organized as Orleans Territory and District of Louisiana (later Missouri Territory)
- 1819: Arkansas Territory established as a separate U.S. territory
- 1836: Arkansas admitted to statehood
- **For pre-1800 research:** there is no Arkansas jurisdiction to search. Records are filed under French Louisiana or Spanish Louisiana, with the colonial capital at New Orleans as the administrative hub.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil vital registration existed in this territory before 1800. The FamilySearch Wiki page for Arkansas Vital Records returned only generic content and gave no specific registration start date for the colonial period.
- **What exists:** No civil births, marriages, or deaths were recorded by any government in this territory before 1800. Church sacramental registers (see below) are the only vital record equivalent.
- **Where held:** Not applicable for civil registration in this period
- **Gaps:** The entire pre-1800 period has no civil registration — this is not a loss but a structural absence
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic sacramental registers at Arkansas Post (see Church Records below); Spanish padrones (household censuses)

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic exclusively among European settlers; French Capuchin and Jesuit missionaries served Arkansas Post from the early 1700s
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials — sacramental registers are the equivalent of vital records for this population
- **Where held:** Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock holds surviving original registers; transcribed copies are at the Arkansas History Commission in Little Rock; the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records) confirms both repositories
- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** Image group 008814402 — 64 images of Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial), covering Arkansas Post, 1763-1800. This volume is **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable) and is written in **Spanish**. It must be examined image by image with no search capability.
- **Language:** French (pre-1763 registers), Spanish (1763-1800 registers); a researcher must read the original language or obtain a translation

### Census records
- **Spanish padrones (1763-1800):** Household census lists compiled by Spanish colonial administrators, naming the head of household and family members. These are a key substitute for civil registration. Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records), surviving padrones are at the Arkansas History Commission and the Archivo General de Indias in Seville.
- **Federal/national census:** The first U.S. federal census covering this territory was 1810 (after the Louisiana Purchase). No federal census applies to the pre-1800 period.
- **FamilySearch indexed collection:** 'Arkansas, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1819-1870' (collection 2085124, 178,345 records) — begins in 1819, well after the colonial period; useful only if an ancestor's trail extends into the territorial period.
- **Access:** Padrones are physical-only or microfilm at the repositories listed above; not available as an indexed online collection

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Spanish colonial courts at Arkansas Post handled civil disputes, land matters, and some estate proceedings; records were kept by the commandant of the post
- **Date range:** Spanish period 1769-1800; some French-era records may predate 1763
- **Where held:** Arkansas History Commission (Little Rock) and Archivo General de Indias (Seville); microfilm copies at the Library of Congress, per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Digitization level:** Physical or microfilm only; not available as an indexed online collection on FamilySearch

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Spanish land grants (concessions) used metes and bounds descriptions referencing natural features; French grants preceded them in the same style
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Under Spain, the Governor of Louisiana (New Orleans) issued land concessions; local commandant at Arkansas Post administered smaller grants. The FamilySearch Wiki page for Arkansas Land and Property returned only generic content and gave no Arkansas-specific details.
- **Types:** Spanish land concessions, French land grants; some grants were later confirmed by U.S. land offices after 1803
- **Date range:** French grants from 1686; Spanish concessions from 1769
- **Where held:** Arkansas History Commission; Archivo General de Indias (Seville); confirmed U.S.-era copies are at the Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) for patents issued after 1803
- **Post-1803 angle:** After the Louisiana Purchase, holders of French and Spanish land grants could petition the U.S. for confirmation. These confirmation records at NARA may describe the original colonial grantee and date, making them a bridge source even when the ancestor lived before 1800.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** French-Indian conflicts (early 1700s); American Revolutionary War (Spain was an ally of France against Britain; Spanish forces in Louisiana were involved); Spanish colonial garrison records at Arkansas Post
- **Record types:** Muster rolls and service records for the Spanish garrison at Arkansas Post; Spanish militia records
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias (Seville); Archivo General de Simancas (Valladolid, Spain) for military records; some copies at the Library of Congress on microfilm; Louisiana Historical Center in New Orleans may hold related records
- **Digitization level:** Physical repositories abroad; not available as indexed online collections

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Arkansas Post had a Catholic burial ground associated with the mission church; no formal maintained cemetery records from the pre-1800 period are known to survive separately from sacramental registers
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (findagrave.com) covers later periods; coverage of pre-1800 burials at Arkansas Post is negligible
- **Physical records:** Burial entries are recorded within the sacramental registers (see Church Records above)

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** No newspaper was published in the Arkansas territory before 1800. The first newspaper in Arkansas did not appear until the territorial period (after 1819).
- **Relevant regional papers:** The Louisiana Gazette (New Orleans, founded 1804) and earlier Spanish-era gazettes occasionally reported on events in the broader Louisiana territory, but coverage of Arkansas Post specifically is rare
- **Where held:** Louisiana State University (Baton Rouge) and New Orleans Public Library hold early Louisiana newspaper collections

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans was the principal port of entry for the entire Louisiana territory. All ocean-going arrivals to Arkansas-area settlements passed through or were documented at New Orleans.
- **Record types:** Spanish colonial records of arrivals at New Orleans; passenger manifests for the colonial period are sparse and largely unpublished; naturalization in the modern sense did not apply under colonial administration
- **Where held:** Louisiana Historical Center (New Orleans); Archivo General de Indias (Seville) for official records of colonial appointments and arrivals
- **Content note:** Formal passenger lists as known from post-1800 shipping did not exist for this territory in the colonial period. Arrivals of settlers are sometimes recorded in padrones or in correspondence between Arkansas Post commandants and the Governor of Louisiana at New Orleans.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Spanish colonial tribute and trade records; not equivalent to U.S. property or poll tax records
- **Date range:** Spanish period 1769-1800
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias (Seville); Arkansas History Commission for surviving local copies
- **Substitute value:** Padrones (see Census Records above) function as both census and quasi-tax records in this context

- **Commandant correspondence:** Letters between the Arkansas Post commandant and the Governor of Louisiana at New Orleans frequently named settlers, land claimants, and local events. These are at the Archivo General de Indias in the 'Papeles Procedentes de Cuba' series.
- **Trade and license records:** Fur trade licenses and commercial permits issued at New Orleans and Arkansas Post named traders operating in the territory. Some are published in Louisiana historical collections.
- **Mission records:** Jesuit and Capuchin mission records occasionally recorded contacts with Native Americans and mixed-heritage individuals not found in parish sacramental registers.

The area that is now Arkansas was not its own jurisdiction before 1800. It was part of French Louisiana from the founding of Arkansas Post in 1686, and then Spanish Louisiana from 1763 until Spain secretly returned it to France in 1800. None of the three FamilySearch indexed collections for Arkansas cover this period; they all begin after 1819.

When you are ready, a research plan can be drawn up that sequences these repositories and identifies which record classes to search first given what is already known about your ancestors.

- **Content note:** Formal passenger lists as known from post-1800 shipping did not exist for this territory in the colonial period. Arrivals of settlers are sometimes recorded in padrones or in correspondence between Arkansas Post commandants and the Governor of Louisiana at New Orleans.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Spanish colonial tribute and trade records; not equivalent to U.S. property or poll tax records
- **Date range:** Spanish period 1769-1800
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias (Seville); Arkansas History Commission for surviving local copies
- **Substitute value:** Padrones (see Census Records above) function as both census and quasi-tax records in this context

### Other record types
- **Commandant correspondence:** Letters between the Arkansas Post commandant and the Governor of Louisiana at New Orleans frequently named settlers, land claimants, and local events. These are at the Archivo General de Indias in the 'Papeles Procedentes de Cuba' series.
- **Trade and license records:** Fur trade licenses and commercial permits issued at New Orleans and Arkansas Post named traders operating in the territory. Some are published in Louisiana historical collections.
- **Mission records:** Jesuit and Capuchin mission records occasionally recorded contacts with Native Americans and mixed-heritage individuals not found in parish sacramental registers.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | 1 digitized volume: Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial), Arkansas Post, 1763-1800 (image group 008814402, 64 images, browse-only, Spanish) | Free |
| FamilySearch | Arkansas, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1819-1870 (178,345 records) — post-1800 only | Free |
| BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | U.S.-era land patents, some confirming pre-1803 French/Spanish grants | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Spanish/French land grant confirmation records post-1803; Louisiana territorial records | Free finding aids; some digital |
| PARES portal (pares.mcu.es) | Digitized Spanish colonial records from the Archivo General de Indias, including 'Papeles Procedentes de Cuba' series for Louisiana | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** 1 digitized volume matches the Arkansas territory for the pre-1800 period. That single volume is the complete result set for FamilySearch digitized holdings in this period.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Arkansas History Commission (Little Rock, AR) | Spanish colonial records, padrones, land concessions, church register transcripts | In-person; some records available by mail request |
| Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock | Original French and Spanish sacramental registers from Arkansas Post | Contact the Diocese archives directly |
| Library of Congress (Washington, DC) | Microfilm copies of Archivo General de Indias records relating to Spanish Louisiana | In-person at the Library's Manuscript/Microform Reading Room |
| Archivo General de Indias (Seville, Spain) | Primary repository for Spanish colonial administrative, military, land, and civil records for all of Spanish Louisiana including Arkansas Post | In-person or through PARES online portal (pares.mcu.es) for digitized documents |
| Louisiana Historical Center (New Orleans, LA) | Records of the colonial Louisiana territory, including some Arkansas Post-related material | In-person |
| Archivo General de Simancas (Valladolid, Spain) | Military records for Spanish colonial forces in Louisiana | In-person or PARES portal |

## Records NOT online
- Spanish padrones (household censuses) for Arkansas Post — physical only at Arkansas History Commission and Archivo General de Indias
- Spanish land concessions — physical at Archivo General de Indias and Arkansas History Commission (some U.S.-era confirmations are online at BLM GLO)
- Spanish colonial court and civil records — physical at Archivo General de Indias and Arkansas History Commission
- Spanish and French military records — physical at Archivo General de Indias and Archivo General de Simancas
- Commandant correspondence (Papeles Procedentes de Cuba series) — physical at Archivo General de Indias; some published transcriptions exist in historical society publications
- French-era sacramental registers (pre-1763) — physical at Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock and Arkansas History Commission

## Known record losses
No tool result stated that any specific record class was destroyed for this period. The small population of Arkansas Post and the colonial character of its administration mean the surviving record base is inherently thin — empty search results reflect extremely sparse European settlement and limited record creation, not necessarily loss. The FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records) describes the surviving colonial record classes without noting specific losses.

## Research tips
- **Search under Louisiana, not Arkansas.** Before 1800 there was no Arkansas jurisdiction. Colonial records are filed under French Louisiana (pre-1763) or Spanish Louisiana (1763-1800), administered from New Orleans. FamilySearch, NARA, and archive catalogs will catalogue these under Louisiana categories. See https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records.
- **Arkansas Post is the only viable anchor point.** Virtually every pre-1800 European-settler record for the territory was created at Arkansas Post. Begin every search there before looking elsewhere in the territory.
- **The Archivo General de Indias PARES portal** (pares.mcu.es) has digitized a substantial portion of the Spanish colonial records for Louisiana. Search under the 'Papeles Procedentes de Cuba' section, which covers Spanish Louisiana colonial administration.
- **Spanish padrones are your census substitute.** These household enumeration lists name family members and are the closest equivalent to both a census and a family register for the Spanish period (1769-1800). The Arkansas History Commission holds surviving examples.
- **Land grant confirmations bridge the colonial and American periods.** After 1803, former French and Spanish land holders petitioned U.S. courts and the General Land Office for confirmation of colonial grants. These confirmation records at NARA describe the original colonial grantee, the grant date, and sometimes family relationships — search them even if your ancestor died before 1803.
- **The FamilySearch digitized volume (image group 008814402)** covers only 1763-1800 and is 64 images in Spanish with no name index. Browse it completely — it is the only FamilySearch digitized pre-1800 primary source for this territory.
- **Language is a research barrier.** French records (pre-1763) and Spanish records (1763-1800) require reading the original languages. The Arkansas History Commission holds transcribed and translated materials that may help; published volumes such as the Louisiana Historical Society's publications contain some translated colonial material.

Here's what the locality guide found for Ohio around 1790:

---

## Ohio Pre-Statehood (circa 1790): Locality Guide

**Jurisdictional Context — Boundary Changes**

Ohio didn't exist yet in 1790. The land was part of the **Northwest Territory**, organized by federal law in 1787. The two operative counties at that time were:

- **Washington County** (est. 1788) — covered most of the territory
- **Hamilton County** (est. 1790) — covered the southwestern corner

Records were created and filed under *territorial authority*, not state authority. Ohio became a state in 1803, but county offices continued without interruption. This matters for database searching: querying "Ohio" will often miss the pre-1803 territorial period — you need to search by county name instead.

**Two additional jurisdictional splits complicate land records:**
- **Virginia Military District** (between the Scioto and Little Miami rivers): warrants are held in Richmond at the **Virginia State Library**, not Ohio.
- **Connecticut Western Reserve** (northeastern Ohio): records are at the **Western Reserve Historical Society** in Cleveland.

---

## Available Records Despite Early Documentation Gaps

**Vital Records** — Civil registration didn't exist in 1790. The only vital records are **church registers** (baptisms, marriages, burials) kept by Methodist, Presbyterian, and Baptist circuit riders. FamilySearch holds **678,234 records** in a searchable collection going back to 1787.

**Land Records** — The richest primary source for this period:
- FamilySearch has a territorial land record volume (51 images, browse-only)
- A partly-indexed Washington County tax volume
- A larger indexed collection: **Ohio Land Records 1787–1840**

**Court Records** — The Ohio History Connection in Columbus holds core territorial and early county court records not yet fully online.

---

**Bottom line:** Work at the *county* level (Washington or Hamilton), not the state level. Land records and church records are your best tools; Virginia and Connecticut reserve jurisdictions require separate searches outside Ohio. The research-plan agent can build a focused search strategy from here.

The Virginia Military District, between the Scioto and Little Miami rivers, used a metes-and-bounds survey system entirely separate from the federal rectangular survey. Land warrants for this district are held at the Virginia State Library in Richmond, not at Ohio archives — if your ancestor held land here, search Virginia, not Ohio.

The Connecticut Western Reserve in northeastern Ohio used a township-lot survey distinct from both the federal rectangular survey and the Virginia Military District. Records are at the Western Reserve Historical Society in Cleveland.

No statewide civil vital registration existed in 1790 or for decades afterward. Church records are the only vital record source for this period — baptism, marriage, and burial registers kept by Methodist, Presbyterian, and Baptist circuit riders and by German-language congregations.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Ohio / Northwest Territory (around 1790, pre-statehood)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Ohio was not yet a state in 1790. The region was organized as the Northwest Territory by the Northwest Ordinance of 1787. Washington County was organized in 1788 as the first county in the territory; Hamilton County was organized in 1790, carved from Washington County to cover the southwestern region.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Marietta (Washington County seat); Cincinnati (Hamilton County seat)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Northwest Territory (a federal territory under U.S. Congressional authority)
- **Population during period:** No population data was returned by the tool for this period.
- **Economy:** Frontier settlement, subsistence farming, military land grants; Revolutionary War veterans arriving to claim bounty land
- **Ethnic composition:** Anglo-American settlers from Virginia, Pennsylvania, and New England; some German-speaking families; Scots-Irish settlers
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist circuit riders, Presbyterian and Baptist frontier ministers, German Reformed and Lutheran congregations in some areas; no established church infrastructure
- **Key historical events:** Northwest Ordinance 1787; ongoing Northwest Indian War (1785–1795); Ohio statehood 1803

## Boundary changes

Boundary change is the defining challenge for 1790 research in this region:

- **Before 1788:** No organized county structure — the territory was administered directly under the Northwest Ordinance. Almost no non-military American settlement existed.
- **1788:** Washington County organized as the first county of the Northwest Territory, covering essentially all of present-day Ohio.
- **1790:** Hamilton County carved from Washington County, covering the southwestern Ohio region (Cincinnati area and westward).
- **1803:** Ohio statehood. The Northwest Territory counties became Ohio state counties. Records created under the territorial government transferred to the new state.

This is a temporal split: before 1803, every record was created under "Northwest Territory" authority and filed under Washington County or Hamilton County. After 1803, those same county offices continued under Ohio. A researcher must therefore search Washington County or Hamilton County records (not "Ohio" generally) for events in 1790, and understand that those records are part of the same continuous county series that runs through statehood.

In addition, two distinct land districts within the future Ohio created geographically separate record sets that do not follow the county record trail:

- The **Virginia Military District** (between the Scioto and Little Miami rivers) used a metes-and-bounds survey. Land warrants are held at the Virginia State Library in Richmond — not at Ohio archives. Settlers in this zone are researched through Virginia records, not the Northwest Territory's county system.
- The **Connecticut Western Reserve** (northeastern Ohio) used a township-lot survey. Records are held at the Western Reserve Historical Society in Cleveland.

Which of these three systems applies depends on where within the future Ohio the ancestor lived.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths existed in 1790 for the Northwest Territory. The FamilySearch Wiki page for Ohio Vital Records returned only generic content during this survey — a specific year for the start of Ohio civil registration cannot be stated from tool results. Verify at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Vital_Records.
- **What exists for 1790:** None — there was no civil vital registration.
- **Where held:** Not applicable for this period.
- **Gaps:** The entire pre-statehood period is a gap in civil registration.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records are the only vital record source for 1790. FamilySearch collection "Ohio, County Marriages, 1789-2013" (1,523,678 records; collection ID 1803785) begins in 1789 and includes some territorial-era marriage bonds and licenses filed at the county level.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist circuit riders (reaching frontier settlements); German Reformed and Lutheran congregations in areas with German-speaking settlers; Quaker meetings in some communities.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations. Circuit-rider ministers often kept personal registers that were later deposited with denominational archives rather than local churches.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Ohio, Church Records, 1787-1950" (678,234 records, indexed with images; collection ID 2246917). Denominational archives (Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist). Ohio History Connection, Columbus.
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images (FamilySearch collection 2246917)
- **Language:** English for most denominations; German for German Reformed and Lutheran records.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The 1790 federal census enumerated households in some Northwest Territory settlements, but coverage of this frontier region was fragmentary. Many settlers in 1790 Ohio were missed or not yet present.
- **State/provincial census:** None — Ohio was not a state.
- **Other enumerations:** Territorial tax lists (see Tax records below) function as a substitute census for locating individuals between enumerations.
- **Access:** The 1790 federal census is indexed and freely available on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Territorial court records (wills, administrations, guardianships, land dispute proceedings)
- **Testate or intestate:** Probate proceedings for both apply; the territorial court at Marietta (Washington County) was the primary venue in 1790.
- **Date range:** From 1788 (Washington County organization)
- **Where held:** Ohio History Connection in Columbus holds early territorial and county court records (from wiki_search result: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory). Washington County Courthouse in Marietta. No digitized probate volumes for 1790 were returned by volume_search.
- **Digitization level:** Physical only for most pre-statehood probate records.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Three distinct systems: (1) federal rectangular survey (most of Ohio); (2) metes-and-bounds (Virginia Military District); (3) township lots (Connecticut Western Reserve).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Federal government (via the General Land Office) for most of Ohio; Virginia (for the Military District); Connecticut (for the Western Reserve). The FamilySearch Wiki page for Ohio Land and Property returned only generic content during this survey — verify at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Land_and_Property.
- **Types:** Territorial land grants and patents, deed books, bounty land warrants, Virginia Military District warrants, Connecticut Western Reserve proprietor records.
- **Date range:** From 1787 (Northwest Territory organization).
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Ohio, Land Records, 1787-1840" (234,567 records, indexed with images; collection ID 1542187). BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) for federal patents. Virginia State Library for VMD warrants. Western Reserve Historical Society for CWR records. Ohio History Connection for territorial land records.
- **Digitization level — FamilySearch volumes:**
  - Volume 005112233 (51 images): Northwest Territory territorial land records, 1788-1799 — **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable). Must be examined image by image.
  - Volume 005112240 (73 images): Washington County, Ohio tax records, 1799-1803 — **partially indexed** (12% name-indexed, not full-text searchable).
- **Note:** Virginia Military District warrants are at the Virginia State Library in Richmond, not Ohio archives (from wiki_search: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Revolutionary War (service records predate settlement; pension applicants often named Ohio as residence); Northwest Indian War (1785–1795; federal service records).
- **Record types:** Revolutionary War service records, pension files, bounty land warrants (many veterans received land in the Virginia Military District); Northwest Indian War service records.
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington, D.C., and regional); Fold3 (fold3.com) has many indexed military records. Ohio History Connection for state militia records.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Pioneer family plots and small rural cemeteries predominate in 1790 — few organized church cemeteries with sexton records existed.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) — coverage is uneven for early frontier burials; many 1790-era graves are not recorded.
- **Physical records:** Few sexton records survive for this period; family and local histories may be the only source.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Centinel of the North-Western Territory (Cincinnati, founded 1793) was among the earliest newspapers in the region — after the target year of 1790. No newspaper is documented by tool results as existing in this region in 1790.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (subscription); Chronicling America (chroniclingamerica.loc.gov, free) for later territorial-era papers.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, legal notices, land sale announcements, and sheriff's sale notices appear in territorial newspapers from 1793 onward.

Researching ancestors in Ohio around 1790 means working in a place that did not yet exist: the land that became Ohio was part of the Northwest Territory, organized by federal law in 1787. The two counties that had been carved out by 1790 — Washington County (formed 1788, covering most of the territory) and Hamilton County (formed 1790, covering the southwestern corner) — are where records were actually created and filed, under territorial rather than state authority. Ohio statehood came in 1803, at which point those same county offices continued without interruption. This means every record from 1790 belongs to a continuous county series that runs straight through statehood; searching "Ohio" in a database will often miss the pre-1803 portion. Two further complications split the land record trail entirely: the Virginia Military District, between the Scioto and Little Miami rivers, has its warrants held in Richmond at the Virginia State Library, not in Ohio, while the Connecticut Western Reserve in northeastern Ohio has its own records at the Western Reserve Historical Society in Cleveland. No civil vital registration existed in 1790 — church records (baptisms, marriages, burials kept by Methodist, Presbyterian, and Baptist circuit riders) are the only vital record source, and FamilySearch has 678,234 of those in a searchable collection going back to 1787. Land records are the richest primary source for the period: FamilySearch holds a small territorial land record volume (51 images, browse-only) and a partly-indexed Washington County tax volume, plus a larger indexed collection of Ohio land records 1787-1840. The Ohio History Connection in Columbus holds the core of the early territorial and county court records that are not yet online.

# Locality Guide: Ohio / Northwest Territory (around 1790, pre-statehood)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Ohio was not yet a state in 1790. The region was organized as the Northwest Territory by the Northwest Ordinance of 1787. Washington County was organized in 1788 as the first county in the territory; Hamilton County was organized in 1790, carved from Washington County to cover the southwestern region.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Marietta (Washington County seat); Cincinnati (Hamilton County seat)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Northwest Territory (a federal territory under U.S. Congressional authority)
- **Population during period:** No population data was returned by the tool for this period.
- **Economy:** Frontier settlement, subsistence farming, military land grants; Revolutionary War veterans arriving to claim bounty land
- **Ethnic composition:** Anglo-American settlers from Virginia, Pennsylvania, and New England; some German-speaking families; Scots-Irish settlers
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist circuit riders, Presbyterian and Baptist frontier ministers, German Reformed and Lutheran congregations in some areas; no established church infrastructure
- **Key historical events:** Northwest Ordinance 1787; ongoing Northwest Indian War (1785–1795); Ohio statehood 1803

## Boundary changes

Boundary change is the defining challenge for 1790 research in this region:

- **Before 1788:** No organized county structure — the territory was administered directly under the Northwest Ordinance. Almost no non-military American settlement existed.
- **1788:** Washington County organized as the first county of the Northwest Territory, covering essentially all of present-day Ohio.
- **1790:** Hamilton County carved from Washington County, covering the southwestern Ohio region (Cincinnati area and westward).
- **1803:** Ohio statehood. The Northwest Territory counties became Ohio state counties. Records created under the territorial government transferred to the new state.

This is a temporal split: before 1803, every record was created under "Northwest Territory" authority and filed under Washington County or Hamilton County. After 1803, those same county offices continued under Ohio. A researcher must therefore search Washington County or Hamilton County records (not "Ohio" generally) for events in 1790, and understand that those records are part of the same continuous county series that runs through statehood.

In addition, two distinct land districts within the future Ohio created geographically separate record sets that do not follow the county record trail:

- The **Virginia Military District** (between the Scioto and Little Miami rivers) used a metes-and-bounds survey. Land warrants are held at the Virginia State Library in Richmond — not at Ohio archives. Settlers in this zone are researched through Virginia records, not the Northwest Territory's county system.
- The **Connecticut Western Reserve** (northeastern Ohio) used a township-lot survey. Records are held at the Western Reserve Historical Society in Cleveland.

Which of these three systems applies depends on where within the future Ohio the ancestor lived.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths existed in 1790 for the Northwest Territory. The FamilySearch Wiki page for Ohio Vital Records returned only generic content during this survey — a specific year for the start of Ohio civil registration cannot be stated from tool results. Verify at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Vital_Records.
- **What exists for 1790:** None — there was no civil vital registration.
- **Where held:** Not applicable for this period.
- **Gaps:** The entire pre-statehood period is a gap in civil registration.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records are the only vital record source for 1790. FamilySearch collection "Ohio, County Marriages, 1789-2013" (1,523,678 records; collection ID 1803785) begins in 1789 and includes some territorial-era marriage bonds and licenses filed at the county level.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist circuit riders (reaching frontier settlements); German Reformed and Lutheran congregations in areas with German-speaking settlers; Quaker meetings in some communities.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations. Circuit-rider ministers often kept personal registers that were later deposited with denominational archives rather than local churches.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Ohio, Church Records, 1787-1950" (678,234 records, indexed with images; collection ID 2246917). Denominational archives (Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist). Ohio History Connection, Columbus.
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images (FamilySearch collection 2246917)
- **Language:** English for most denominations; German for German Reformed and Lutheran records.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The 1790 federal census enumerated households in some Northwest Territory settlements, but coverage of this frontier region was fragmentary. Many settlers in 1790 Ohio were missed or not yet present.
- **State/provincial census:** None — Ohio was not a state.

| Repository | What's There |
