# Locality Guide: California, United States (1848–1860, Gold Rush Era)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **Formed:** California became a state on September 9, 1850, bypassing territorial status entirely and passing directly from Mexican cession (1848, Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo) to U.S. statehood. (Wikipedia: California Gold Rush)
- **County seat / administrative center:** State capital at Sacramento; San Francisco was the primary commercial and port center throughout the period.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** No territorial period — admitted directly as a state; before 1848, the territory was Mexican Alta California.
- **Population during period:** Population data could not be retrieved from the tool during this survey. Wikipedia records that approximately 300,000 people migrated to California during the Gold Rush.
- **Economy:** Gold mining drove the economy 1848–1855; commerce, shipping, and agriculture grew alongside the mining camps.
- **Ethnic composition:** Highly diverse — American-born migrants from every state, European immigrants (Irish, German, British, French, Italian), Chinese miners, Latin Americans (Chilean, Mexican, Peruvian), and Australian arrivals. (Wikipedia: California Gold Rush)
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (Spanish mission legacy, Irish and Italian immigrants); Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, Episcopal congregations formed during the 1850s settlement wave.
- **Key historical events:** Gold discovered at Sutter's Mill, January 24, 1848; California statehood September 9, 1850; rapid county formation throughout the 1850s as mining districts required administrative organization.

## Boundary Changes
- California organized directly as a state with no territorial phase, so there is no predecessor territorial record set to search before 1850.
- County boundaries shifted frequently throughout the 1850s. Many mining district counties were carved from larger parent counties between 1850 and 1860. Any county-level record search should confirm which county governed a specific locality in the target year.
- If stable, state-level boundaries were unchanged after 1850.

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **What exists:** County-level births and marriages begin in 1850 per FamilySearch collections. FamilySearch holds "California, County Births, 1850–1919" (789,456 indexed records with images, collection 2017276) and "California, County Marriages, 1850–1952" (567,890 records / 1,135,780 persons, indexed with images, collection 1452832).
- **Registration level:** County-level. The specific California Vital Records FamilySearch Wiki page could not be retrieved during this survey (returned only generic content), so the statewide registration requirement and its start year cannot be confirmed from that source. No county death registration collection was returned — deaths in this period were particularly poorly captured for the transient Gold Rush population.
- **Where held:** County clerk/recorder offices; FamilySearch online collections above.
- **Gaps:** Civil registration in the 1850s was inconsistent — the Gold Rush population was heavily transient and male, and many deaths, births, and marriages went unrecorded at the county level.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism/marriage registers; mission records; newspaper notices; probate inventories naming heirs.

### Church Records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic (Franciscan mission system through 1834; then diocesan parishes serving immigrant communities); growing Protestant denominations (Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist, Episcopal) established during the 1850s.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations.
- **Mission Records:** FamilySearch collection "California, Mission Records, 1769–1850" — 98,765 indexed records (collection 1804372). These cover the Spanish/Mexican era and end at the opening of the Gold Rush; most useful for establishing pre-rush California families, not for newly arrived 49ers.
- **Where held:** Diocesan archives (Archdiocese of San Francisco, Diocese of Sacramento); FamilySearch microfilm for mission records. The California Church Records FamilySearch Wiki page returned only generic content and could not confirm specific repository details for Gold Rush-era parish registers.
- **Language:** Mission records are in Latin and Spanish.

### Census Records
- **1852 California State Census:** The most valuable single census for the Gold Rush population. FamilySearch volume DGS 006601001 (522 images) is 88% name-indexed and full-text searchable — **indexed + images** access, free on FamilySearch. This fills the gap between the federal enumerations and captures the population at the height of the rush.
- **1850 Federal Census:** The first federal census taken in California after statehood, but was partially destroyed — some county returns are missing. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Pre-Statehood_Records)
- **1860 Federal Census:** Part of the national decennial series; indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch.
- **Mortality schedules:** Generic wiki pages note mortality schedules exist for 1850–1885; these list persons who died in the year preceding the census — useful given the death-registration gap.
- **Access:** 1852 state census indexed and online at FamilySearch (free). 1850 and 1860 federal censuses indexed on Ancestry.com (subscription).

### Mining Claim Records (Gold Rush–Specific)
- **What exists:** FamilySearch volume DGS 006601002 covers Mining Claim Registers for San Francisco, California, 1849–1855 (340 images). Access level: **browse-only** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable. Must be browsed image by image with no search capability.
- **Additional holdings:** Mining claim records are also held at county recorders' offices for each specific mining county. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records) These are not digitized or indexed for most counties.
- **Physical repositories:** County recorders' offices in the Sierra foothills counties; Bancroft Library at UC Berkeley and California State Library hold additional manuscript mining records.

### Probate and Court Records
- **Types:** Wills, estate administrations, guardianships, inventories, petitions — held at county level.
- **Testate vs. intestate:** Search wills for persons who died with property (testate); search administration files (intestate) for miners who died without a will, which was common.
- **Date range:** From county formation (most foothills mining counties formed 1850–1858).
- **Where held:** County courthouse superior court archives; California State Archives. The California Probate Records FamilySearch Wiki page returned only generic content; specific details about indexed collections could not be confirmed.
- **Court records note:** Pre-1906 naturalization papers (declaration of intention, petition for naturalization) could be filed in any court of record — federal district courts, state superior courts, or county courts. Search at multiple court levels for Gold Rush–era immigrants.

### Land Records
- **Survey system:** California is a federal land state using the rectangular survey system (township and range).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Federal government (Bureau of Land Management) for original federal land patents; the BLM General Land Office (GLO) records website (glorecords.blm.gov) holds searchable federal patents. Spanish and Mexican land grants (ranchos) are relevant for pre-1848 California families and are held at the California State Archives.
- **Types:** Federal land patents; county deed books; Spanish/Mexican land grant documents; county tax records.
- **Where held:** BLM GLO (online) for federal patents; county recorders for deeds; California State Archives for rancho grant documents. The California Land and Property FamilySearch Wiki page returned only generic content.

### Military Records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846–1848) veterans are present in early California — many came to California after the war and joined the Gold Rush. Civil War records are post-period but may identify settlers who stayed.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants (at NARA); California adjutant general records (at California State Archives).
- **Where held:** NARA (archives.gov); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/, subscription) holds indexed service and pension records.

### Cemetery Records
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) is the primary online index; coverage for 1850s California mining camps is uneven — many miners died in remote locations with no marked grave.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records where cemeteries were formally established; Gold Rush–era graves are often in historic pioneer or Catholic cemeteries in the Sierra foothills counties.

### Newspaper Records
- **Local papers:** San Francisco had newspapers from 1846; mining camp papers appeared throughout the Sierra foothills in the early 1850s.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/, subscription) holds a digitized collection. California State Library and Bancroft Library at UC Berkeley hold additional holdings on microfilm.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, ship arrival notices, mining company announcements, legal notices (especially relevant for a transient population), and partner/business notices that identify persons not in any official record.

### Immigration and Arrival Records
- **Port Arrival Registers:** FamilySearch volume DGS 006601003 covers Port Arrival Registers for Sacramento, California, 1849–1858 (298 images). Access level: **browse-only** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable. Must be browsed image by image.
- **Ship passenger manifests (San Francisco):** Arrival manifests for San Francisco are held at the National Archives regional facility in San Bruno, California, and are indexed on Ancestry.com and Fold3. This is the primary indexed source for sea arrivals. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)
- **Overland arrivals:** Overland trail diaries and journals (California State Library, Bancroft Library at UC Berkeley) are manuscript/narrative sources documenting overland routes; not name-indexed. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)
- **Naturalization:** Pre-1906 naturalization papers could be filed in any court of record — federal district courts, California superior courts, or county courts. Search at all three levels.
- **Content note:** Ship passenger manifests record every person aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Great Registers (Voter Registration)
- **What exists:** "California, Great Registers, 1866–1910" — 1,345,678 indexed records with images, free on FamilySearch (collection 1923340, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1923340). These voter registration records name each registrant's birthplace and occupation — extremely valuable for identifying Gold Rush–era settlers who remained in California.
- **Note:** Begins in 1866, so post-1850s. Wikipedia identifies this as a key source for the Gold Rush researcher. Useful for confirming that an ancestor stayed in California after the rush ended.

### Tax Records
- **Types:** County property tax and poll tax records.
- **Where held:** County assessors' offices and California State Archives.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists can confirm presence in a county in years between census enumerations and can substitute for missing census returns.

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | County Births 1850–1919 (789,456 records); County Marriages 1850–1952 (567,890 records); Great Registers 1866–1910 (1,345,678 records); Mission Records 1769–1850 (98,765 records); California State Census 1850–1852 (88% indexed, full-text); Mining Claim Registers 1849–1855 (browse-only); Port Arrival Registers Sacramento 1849–1858 (browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection including 1850 and 1860; ship passenger manifests | Subscription (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) |
| Fold3 | Military records; ship passenger manifests | Subscription (https://www.fold3.com/) |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free (https://www.findagrave.com/) |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Subscription (https://www.newspapers.com/) |
| BLM GLO | Federal land patents | Free (glorecords.blm.gov) |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Ship passenger manifests (San Francisco); naturalization records; military records | Free/in-person (https://www.archives.gov/) |

**Coverage of this survey:** 14 digitized volumes match California for 1848–1870; the 3 detailed above are the first page of results. The remaining 11 volumes were not examined — further pages should be retrieved before concluding the digital coverage is complete. The FamilySearch catalog was not searchable during this survey (tool unavailable) — search it directly at familysearch.org/catalog for microfilmed county records not in the indexed collections above.

### Physical Repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| California State Archives (Sacramento) | State census; adjutant general records; state-level court records; rancho grant documents | In-person / online request |
| National Archives, San Bruno | Ship passenger manifests (San Francisco); federal court naturalization records | In-person / written request |
| Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley | Gold Rush–era manuscripts, diaries, mining records, newspapers, local histories | In-person (appointment) |
| California State Library (Sacramento) | Newspapers; county histories; pioneer biographies; overland trail narratives | In-person / some digital |
| County courthouses (Sierra foothills) | Deed books, mining claim records, probate files, court naturalization papers | In-person / mail |
| Diocesan archives (Archdiocese of San Francisco; Diocese of Sacramento) | Catholic parish registers from the 1850s onward | Contact diocese |

## Records NOT Online
- Mining claim records outside San Francisco (held at individual county recorders' offices) — no known indexed online collection for most foothills counties.
- Overland trail arrival records — held as manuscript diaries and journals at the Bancroft Library and California State Library; not digitized or name-indexed.
- County-level probate inventories and guardianship files for the 1850s — typically held at county courthouses, not digitized.
- Many Catholic parish registers from 1850s Gold Rush–era towns — held at diocesan archives, not fully digitized.
- County tax records for the 1850s — held at county assessors or state archives.
- 11 additional digitized volumes returned by FamilySearch volume search were not examined in this survey.

## Known Record Losses
- The 1850 federal census for California was partially destroyed — some county returns are missing. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Pre-Statehood_Records) The 1852 California State Census is the primary substitute for the missing or incomplete 1850 returns.
- The fate of other specific 1850s record classes could not be confirmed from tool results during this survey; the repositories listed above should be contacted to verify survival rates for specific counties. An empty search result is a coverage gap, not proof of loss.

## Research Tips
- **Start with the 1852 California State Census** — it is 88% name-indexed and full-text searchable on FamilySearch, taken at the height of the Gold Rush population. It captures many 49ers who do not appear in the partially destroyed 1850 federal census. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)
- **Use Great Registers to confirm settlement** — the California Great Registers (starting 1866, indexed on FamilySearch, collection 1923340) name birthplace and occupation and are the best way to verify that a miner stayed in California after the rush ended.
- **Mining claim records require county-level searching** — claims were filed at the county recorder in the mining county. Identify which county governed the mining camp or district your ancestor worked in, then contact that county recorder or check the Bancroft Library. The FamilySearch browse-only volume DGS 006601002 covers San Francisco only. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)
- **For sea arrivals, check Ancestry, Fold3, and NARA San Bruno** — ship passenger manifests for San Francisco arrivals are held at the National Archives in San Bruno and are indexed on Ancestry and Fold3. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)
- **California county boundaries shifted rapidly in the 1850s** — before searching county records, verify which county governed your ancestor's location in the specific year. Many mining district counties were carved from larger parent counties during 1850–1860.
- **Search the Bancroft Library and California State Library** for manuscript sources — these include diaries, journals, overland trail narratives, mining company records, and local histories that name individuals found in no official record series. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)

**Wiki coverage note:** All FamilySearch Wiki place-specific pages for California returned only generic content during this survey. Research guidance specific to California — including vital record registration dates, church record repositories, and probate record details — could not be confirmed from those pages. Check https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy directly before relying on this guide's wiki findings.

## Boundary Changes
- California organized directly as a state with no territorial phase, so there is no predecessor territorial record set to search before 1850.
- County boundaries shifted frequently throughout the 1850s. Many mining district counties were carved from larger parent counties between 1850 and 1860. Any county-level record search should confirm which county governed a specific locality in the target year.
- If stable, state-level boundaries were unchanged after 1850.

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **What exists:** County-level births and marriages begin in 1850 per FamilySearch collections. FamilySearch holds "California, County Births, 1850–1919" (789,456 indexed records with images, collection 2017276) and "California, County Marriages, 1850–1952" (567,890 records / 1,135,780 persons, indexed with images, collection 1452832).
- **Registration level:** County-level. The specific California Vital Records FamilySearch Wiki page could not be retrieved during this survey (returned only generic content), so the statewide registration requirement and its start year cannot be confirmed from that source. No county death registration collection was returned — deaths in this period were particularly poorly captured for the transient Gold Rush population.
- **Where held:** County clerk/recorder offices; FamilySearch online collections above.
- **Gaps:** Civil registration in the 1850s was inconsistent — the Gold Rush population was heavily transient and male, and many deaths, births, and marriages went unrecorded at the county level.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism/marriage registers; mission records; newspaper notices; probate inventories naming heirs.

### Church Records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic (Franciscan mission system through 1834; then diocesan parishes serving immigrant communities); growing Protestant denominations (Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist, Episcopal) established during the 1850s.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations.
- **Mission Records:** FamilySearch collection "California, Mission Records, 1769–1850" — 98,765 indexed records (collection 1804372). These cover the Spanish/Mexican era and end at the opening of the Gold Rush; most useful for establishing pre-rush California families, not for newly arrived 49ers.
- **Where held:** Diocesan archives (Archdiocese of San Francisco, Diocese of Sacramento); FamilySearch microfilm for mission records. The California Church Records FamilySearch Wiki page returned only generic content and could not confirm specific repository details for Gold Rush-era parish registers.
- **Language:** Mission records are in Latin and Spanish.

### Census Records
- **1852 California State Census:** The most valuable single census for the Gold Rush population. FamilySearch volume DGS 006601001 (522 images) is 88% name-indexed and full-text searchable — **indexed + images** access, free on FamilySearch. This fills the gap between the federal enumerations and captures the population at the height of the rush.
- **1850 Federal Census:** The first federal census taken in California after statehood, but was partially destroyed — some county returns are missing. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Pre-Statehood_Records)
- **1860 Federal Census:** Part of the national decennial series; indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch.
- **Mortality schedules:** Generic wiki pages note mortality schedules exist for 1850–1885; these list persons who died in the year preceding the census — useful given the death-registration gap.
- **Access:** 1852 state census indexed and online at FamilySearch (free). 1850 and 1860 federal censuses indexed on Ancestry.com (subscription).

### Mining Claim Records (Gold Rush–Specific)
- **What exists:** FamilySearch volume DGS 006601002 covers Mining Claim Registers for San Francisco, California, 1849–1855 (340 images). Access level: **browse-only** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable. Must be browsed image by image with no search capability.
- **Additional holdings:** Mining claim records are also held at county recorders' offices for each specific mining county. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records) These are not digitized or indexed for most counties.
- **Physical repositories:** County recorders' offices in the Sierra foothills counties; Bancroft Library at UC Berkeley and California State Library hold additional manuscript mining records.

### Probate and Court Records
- **Types:** Wills, estate administrations, guardianships, inventories, petitions — held at county level.
- **Testate vs. intestate:** Search wills for persons who died with property (testate); search administration files (intestate) for miners who died without a will, which was common.
- **Date range:** From county formation (most foothills mining counties formed 1850–1858).
- **Where held:** County courthouse superior court archives; California State Archives. The California Probate Records FamilySearch Wiki page returned only generic content; specific details about indexed collections could not be confirmed.
- **Court records note:** Pre-1906 naturalization papers (declaration of intention, petition for naturalization) could be filed in any court of record — federal district courts, state superior courts, or county courts. Search at multiple court levels for Gold Rush–era immigrants.

### Land Records
- **Survey system:** California is a federal land state using the rectangular survey system (township and range).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Federal government (Bureau of Land Management) for original federal land patents; the BLM General Land Office (GLO) records website (glorecords.blm.gov) holds searchable federal patents. Spanish and Mexican land grants (ranchos) are relevant for pre-1848 California families and are held at the California State Archives.
- **Types:** Federal land patents; county deed books; Spanish/Mexican land grant documents; county tax records.
- **Where held:** BLM GLO (online) for federal patents; county recorders for deeds; California State Archives for rancho grant documents. The California Land and Property FamilySearch Wiki page returned only generic content.

### Military Records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846–1848) veterans are present in early California — many came to California after the war and joined the Gold Rush. Civil War records are post-period but may identify settlers who stayed.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants (at NARA); California adjutant general records (at California State Archives).
- **Where held:** NARA (archives.gov); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/, subscription) holds indexed service and pension records.

### Cemetery Records
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) is the primary online index; coverage for 1850s California mining camps is uneven — many miners died in remote locations with no marked grave.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records where cemeteries were formally established; Gold Rush–era graves are often in historic pioneer or Catholic cemeteries in the Sierra foothills counties.

### Newspaper Records
- **Local papers:** San Francisco had newspapers from 1846; mining camp papers appeared throughout the Sierra foothills in the early 1850s.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/, subscription) holds a digitized collection. California State Library and Bancroft Library at UC Berkeley hold additional holdings on microfilm.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, ship arrival notices, mining company announcements, legal notices (especially relevant for a transient population), and partner/business notices that identify persons not in any official record.

### Immigration and Arrival Records
- **Port Arrival Registers:** FamilySearch volume DGS 006601003 covers Port Arrival Registers for Sacramento, California, 1849–1858 (298 images). Access level: **browse-only** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable. Must be browsed image by image.
- **Ship passenger manifests (San Francisco):** Arrival manifests for San Francisco are held at the National Archives regional facility in San Bruno, California, and are indexed on Ancestry.com and Fold3. This is the primary indexed source for sea arrivals. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)
- **Overland arrivals:** Overland trail diaries and journals (California State Library, Bancroft Library at UC Berkeley) are manuscript/narrative sources documenting overland routes; not name-indexed. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)
- **Naturalization:** Pre-1906 naturalization papers could be filed in any court of record — federal district courts, California superior courts, or county courts. Search at all three levels.
- **Content note:** Ship passenger manifests record every person aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Great Registers (Voter Registration)
- **What exists:** "California, Great Registers, 1866–1910" — 1,345,678 indexed records with images, free on FamilySearch (collection 1923340, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1923340). These voter registration records name each registrant's birthplace and occupation — extremely valuable for identifying Gold Rush–era settlers who remained in California.
- **Note:** Begins in 1866, so post-1850s. Wikipedia identifies this as a key source for the Gold Rush researcher. Useful for confirming that an ancestor stayed in California after the rush ended.

### Tax Records
- **Types:** County property tax and poll tax records.
- **Where held:** County assessors' offices and California State Archives.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists can confirm presence in a county in years between census enumerations and can substitute for missing census returns.

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | County Births 1850–1919 (789,456 records); County Marriages 1850–1952 (567,890 records); Great Registers 1866–1910 (1,345,678 records); Mission Records 1769–1850 (98,765 records); California State Census 1850–1852 (88% indexed, full-text); Mining Claim Registers 1849–1855 (browse-only); Port Arrival Registers Sacramento 1849–1858 (browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection including 1850 and 1860; ship passenger manifests | Subscription (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) |
| Fold3 | Military records; ship passenger manifests | Subscription (https://www.fold3.com/) |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free (https://www.findagrave.com/) |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Subscription (https://www.newspapers.com/) |
| BLM GLO | Federal land patents | Free (glorecords.blm.gov) |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Ship passenger manifests (San Francisco); naturalization records; military records | Free/in-person (https://www.archives.gov/) |

**Coverage of this survey:** 14 digitized volumes match California for 1848–1870; the 3 detailed above are the first page of results. The remaining 11 volumes were not examined — further pages should be retrieved before concluding the digital coverage is complete. The FamilySearch catalog was not searchable during this survey (tool unavailable) — search it directly at familysearch.org/catalog for microfilmed county records not in the indexed collections above.

### Physical Repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| California State Archives (Sacramento) | State census; adjutant general records; state-level court records; rancho grant documents | In-person / online request |
| National Archives, San Bruno | Ship passenger manifests (San Francisco); federal court naturalization records | In-person / written request |
| Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley | Gold Rush–era manuscripts, diaries, mining records, newspapers, local histories | In-person (appointment) |
| California State Library (Sacramento) | Newspapers; county histories; pioneer biographies; overland trail narratives | In-person / some digital |
| County courthouses (Sierra foothills) | Deed books, mining claim records, probate files, court naturalization papers | In-person / mail |
| Diocesan archives (Archdiocese of San Francisco; Diocese of Sacramento) | Catholic parish registers from the 1850s onward | Contact diocese |

## Records NOT Online
- Mining claim records outside San Francisco (held at individual county recorders' offices) — no known indexed online collection for most foothills counties.
- Overland trail arrival records — held as manuscript diaries and journals at the Bancroft Library and California State Library; not digitized or name-indexed.
- County-level probate inventories and guardianship files for the 1850s — typically held at county courthouses, not digitized.
- Many Catholic parish registers from 1850s Gold Rush–era towns — held at diocesan archives, not fully digitized.
- County tax records for the 1850s — held at county assessors or state archives.
- 11 additional digitized volumes returned by FamilySearch volume search were not examined in this survey.

## Known Record Losses
- The 1850 federal census for California was partially destroyed — some county returns are missing. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Pre-Statehood_Records) The 1852 California State Census is the primary substitute for the missing or incomplete 1850 returns.
- The fate of other specific 1850s record classes could not be confirmed from tool results during this survey; the repositories listed above should be contacted to verify survival rates for specific counties. An empty search result is a coverage gap, not proof of loss.

## Research Tips
- **Start with the 1852 California State Census** — it is 88% name-indexed and full-text searchable on FamilySearch, taken at the height of the Gold Rush population. It captures many 49ers who do not appear in the partially destroyed 1850 federal census. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)
- **Use Great Registers to confirm settlement** — the California Great Registers (starting 1866, indexed on FamilySearch, collection 1923340) name birthplace and occupation and are the best way to verify that a miner stayed in California after the rush ended.
- **Mining claim records require county-level searching** — claims were filed at the county recorder in the mining county. Identify which county governed the mining camp or district your ancestor worked in, then contact that county recorder or check the Bancroft Library. The FamilySearch browse-only volume DGS 006601002 covers San Francisco only. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)
- **For sea arrivals, check Ancestry, Fold3, and NARA San Bruno** — ship passenger manifests for San Francisco arrivals are held at the National Archives in San Bruno and are indexed on Ancestry and Fold3. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)
- **California county boundaries shifted rapidly in the 1850s** — before searching county records, verify which county governed your ancestor's location in the specific year. Many mining district counties were carved from larger parent counties during 1850–1860.
- **Search the Bancroft Library and California State Library** for manuscript sources — these include diaries, journals, overland trail narratives, mining company records, and local histories that name individuals found in no official record series. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)

**Wiki coverage note:** All FamilySearch Wiki place-specific pages for California returned only generic content during this survey. Research guidance specific to California — including vital record registration dates, church record repositories, and probate record details — could not be confirmed from those pages. Check https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy directly before relying on this guide's wiki findings.

Locality guide written as **loc_001**. Here's what the agent found:

---

## New York City in the 1700s — Locality Research Guide

**Key context:** No civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths existed in colonial New York. **Church registers are the only vital-event records** for this period. The oldest continuous series — the Dutch Reformed registers covering 1700–1776 — survives on FamilySearch as a browse-only, Dutch-language image volume that must be read page by page in the original Dutch.

---

### Strongest Record Groups for This Period

| Record Type | Where Held |
|---|---|
| Church registers (Dutch Reformed, Anglican, etc.) | FamilySearch (2.3M records indexed), NYGS, NYHS |
| Probate / Wills | Proved at the colony-wide **Prerogative Court of New York**; index in NYHS's published *Abstracts of Wills* |
| Land records & patents | **New York State Archives** |
| Mayor's Court records | NYHS |
| Tax assessment lists (pre-1790 census substitute) | Ward-level, NYHS and NYGS |

---

### Key Repositories

- **New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYG&B)** — indispensable for colonial-era NYC
- **New-York Historical Society (NYHS)** — holds probate abstracts, court records, tax lists
- **New York State Archives** — land patents and colonial-era government records
- **FamilySearch** — indexed collections: church records (2.3M), land (1.6M), probate (988K)

---

### Critical Warning

**"New York City" in the 1700s meant lower Manhattan only.** The Bronx, Brooklyn, Queens, and Staten Island were separate jurisdictions — each requires its own separate research track. Make sure you know exactly which borough your ancestors were in before choosing record sets.

---

### Next Steps

The FamilySearch Wiki page for NYC genealogy ([familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy)) is worth visiting before finalizing a plan. If you'd like a sequenced research plan built on this survey, say the word and the **research-plan** skill can run next.

# Locality Guide: New York City (1700-1799, Colonial Period)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Founded as New Amsterdam in 1624/1626 by the Dutch; seized by England in 1664 and renamed New York City
- **Administrative center:** Lower Manhattan
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Province of New York (British colony) until 1776/1783; then New York State
- **Population during period:** No population data was returned by the place_population tool for this location and period
- **Economy:** Major commercial seaport; trade, shipping, and merchants dominated
- **Ethnic composition:** Dutch, English, German, Scots-Irish, Sephardic Jewish, and West African enslaved persons — among the most ethnically diverse cities in colonial North America; ethnic mix directly shapes which church registers to search
- **Religious denominations:** Dutch Reformed (oldest continuous church records, registers from 1639), Anglican/Church of England (Trinity Church, founded 1697), Presbyterian (First Presbyterian, founded 1716), Lutheran, Quaker, Sephardic Jewish (Shearith Israel, founded 1654)
- **Key historical events:** 1664 English seizure ended Dutch rule; fires of 1776 at the start of British occupation destroyed much of lower Manhattan; British military occupation lasted 1776-1783

## Boundary changes
- During the 1700s, New York City was coextensive with lower Manhattan. The five-borough consolidation (adding the Bronx, Brooklyn, Queens, Staten Island) did not occur until 1898 — records for those areas are under separate jurisdictions and require separate research.
- Local governance was through an elected Common Council under a Crown-appointed governor until 1776.
- Jurisdictional authority for vital events rested entirely with the churches — no civil registration existed.

## Available record types

For each record type, the jurisdictional level is noted as it applies to colonial New York City.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil vital registration existed in New York City during the 1700s. The FamilySearch Wiki returned only generic content during this survey and did not confirm a specific statewide registration date.
- **What exists:** None in the civil sense. All vital-event records for this period are church records.
- **Where held:** See Church Records section below.
- **Gaps:** The entire 1700s is a pre-registration period.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism, marriage, and burial registers are the only source.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Dutch Reformed (continuous registers from 1639), Anglican/Trinity Church (1697), Presbyterian (1716), Lutheran, Quaker, Sephardic Jewish (Shearith Israel, 1654)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations, membership rolls
- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** 1 volume found — image group 007733180, Dutch Reformed Church Registers 1700-1776, 211 images. This volume is 0% name-indexed and NOT full-text searchable — it must be browsed image-by-image. Records are in Dutch. The state-level collection "New York, Church Records, 1640-1940" (FamilySearch collection 1469062, 2,345,678 records) includes church records across the full period at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1469062
- **Other repositories:** The New York Genealogical & Biographical Society and the New-York Historical Society hold extensive colonial-era church collections (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Language:** Dutch Reformed registers are in Dutch through the colonial period; Latin may appear in some Anglican registers.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** None during the 1700s — the first federal census was 1790 (at the very end of / just after this period).
- **State/provincial census:** No provincial census series was identified in tool results for this period.
- **Other enumerations:** Tax assessment lists by ward are the functional substitute for census in 1700-1790 (see Tax Records below).
- **Access:** The 1790 federal census is fully indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, letters of administration, guardianships
- **Key court:** Wills were proved before the Prerogative Court of New York (a colony-wide court, not a local county court) during the colonial period. The FamilySearch Wiki notes that wills are indexed in the *Abstracts of Wills* series published by the New-York Historical Society (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records).
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Probate Records, 1629-1971" (id: 1542780, 987,654 records) covers the full colonial period — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542780
- **Other court records:** The Mayor's Court of New York City is a key source for colonial-period civil and criminal matters (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records). Physical records are at the New York State Archives.
- **Testate vs. intestate:** Testate individuals (with a will) appear in the Prerogative Court's will books; intestate individuals appear in administration files from the same court.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (New York is a state-grant state, not a federal land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Land was granted by the Crown during the colonial period, then by New York State. The FamilySearch Wiki pages did not return place-specific content on the responsible office; the New York State Archives holds colonial patents.
- **Types:** Deeds, land conveyances, grants, land patents; the FamilySearch Wiki names "land conveyances" as a key colonial source (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Land Records, 1630-1975" (id: 2078654, 1,567,890 records) — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078654
- **Other repositories:** New York Colonial Manuscripts at the New York State Archives cover land grants and patents.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Queen Anne's War (1702-1713), King George's War (1744-1748), French and Indian War (1754-1763), American Revolutionary War (1775-1783)
- **Record types:** Colonial militia rolls, Revolutionary War service records and pension files
- **Source from wiki:** "Colonial New York Province maintained militia rolls that list men of military age, useful for identifying residents" (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)
- **Where held:** NARA (archives.gov) holds Revolutionary War records; Fold3 (fold3.com) has military records online; New York State Archives holds colonial militia records.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Trinity Church burial ground (Anglican, one of the oldest in Manhattan), Dutch Reformed churchyards, Shearith Israel cemetery (Sephardic Jewish, founded 1656 — the oldest Jewish cemetery in continuous use in North America)
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (findagrave.com) has indexed some colonial-era burials; coverage is uneven for the 1700s.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records vary by church; some have been published or are on microfilm at the New-York Historical Society.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The New York Gazette (founded 1725) is the first newspaper in the city (Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City); the New York Weekly Journal, New-York Mercury, and others followed.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (newspapers.com) has historical newspaper holdings; the New York Public Library and New-York Historical Society hold originals and microfilm.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, estate and legal notices, runaway slave advertisements, ship arrival lists.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New York Harbor was a primary colonial port of entry.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists, British-era port records, naturalization records before the Prerogative Court or Mayor's Court
- **Where held:** NARA (archives.gov) holds passenger and naturalization records. The Mayor's Court records are cited as a source for colonial-period court proceedings (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Tax assessment lists by ward, personal property assessments
- **Date range:** Some lists survive; FamilySearch collection "New York, Tax Assessment Rolls of Real and Personal Estates, 1799-1804" (id: 1678432, 123,456 records) covers 1799-1804 — just at the end of and after the target period. Earlier 1700s tax lists were not found in indexed online collections.
- **Where held:** Collection 1678432 on FamilySearch. Earlier lists may be held at the New York State Archives or New-York Historical Society.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are the primary substitute for census records for the entire 1700-1790 window before the federal census.

### Other record types
- **Colonial Manuscripts:** The New York Colonial Manuscripts at the New York State Archives cover governance, land grants, and administrative records of the colonial period (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Enslaved persons records:** Bills of sale, estate inventories naming enslaved persons, newspaper advertisements, and manumission registers survive. The New-York Historical Society holds relevant collections.
- **City directories:** New York City directories began in the late 1780s-1790s and are useful for locating residents at the very end of the target period.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | Church Records 1640-1940 (id: 1469062, 2.3M records); Land Records 1630-1975 (id: 2078654, 1.6M records); Probate Records 1629-1971 (id: 1542780, 988K records); Tax Assessment Rolls 1799-1804 (id: 1678432, 123K records); Dutch Reformed Registers 1700-1776 (image group 007733180, browse-only, Dutch) | Free |
| Ancestry (ancestry.com) | U.S. Federal Census and New York state collections | Subscription |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | Military records including colonial and Revolutionary War | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery and burial records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Passenger lists, naturalization, military records | Free/request |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 1 digitized volume specifically for New York City in the 1700-1800 range (the Dutch Reformed Church Registers, image group 007733180). This was the complete result set for that scope. Broadening to state level returned the same single volume.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New York State Archives (Albany) | New York Colonial Manuscripts, land patents, Mayor's Court records | In-person / online request |
| New-York Historical Society (Manhattan) | Abstracts of Wills, church records, colonial manuscripts | In-person / appointment |
| New York Genealogical & Biographical Society | Extensive colonial-era genealogical collections | In-person / membership |
| New York Public Library | Newspapers, city directories, microfilm | In-person |
| Surrogate's Court, New York County | Probate records (originals) | In-person / mail |
| Trinity Church Archives | Anglican burial and baptism registers from 1697 | Contact church |

---

## Records NOT online
- Colonial-period tax assessment lists before 1799 were not found in any indexed online database.
- Mayor's Court records appear to be held physically at the New York State Archives; online availability was not confirmed by any tool result.
- Colonial militia rolls from pre-Revolutionary conflicts are at the New York State Archives, not found as online indexed collections.
- Earlier Dutch Reformed church registers (pre-1700, covering the first generation in New Amsterdam) are on FamilySearch microfilm but were not returned in the 1700-1800 volume search.
- Trinity Church baptism and burial registers predating major digitization projects are physical at Trinity Church Archives.

---

## Known record losses
No specific record losses for New York City were identified in any tool result during this survey. The FamilySearch Wiki returned only generic content and named no specific destroyed collections. The fire of 1776 (at the start of the British occupation) destroyed a significant portion of lower Manhattan; whether specific record sets were lost was not confirmed by any tool result. Consult the New-York Historical Society or New York State Archives directly for information about colonial-period record survivals.

---

- Church registers are the only vital-event record for births, marriages, and deaths throughout the 1700s — there was no civil registration. Begin every family search with church records. (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)

- Wills proved before the Prerogative Court of New York are indexed in the *Abstracts of Wills* series published by the New-York Historical Society — this is a key finding aid for the colonial period. (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)
- Tax assessment lists survive for some years and wards and are the primary substitute for census records before 1790. (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)
- Colonial militia rolls name men of military age and are useful for identifying and locating residents when no other record names them. (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)

- Church registers are the only vital-event record for births, marriages, and deaths throughout the 1700s — there was no civil registration. Begin every family search with church records. (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- The Dutch Reformed Church registers (image group 007733180 on FamilySearch, 1700-1776) are in Dutch and must be browsed image-by-image with no name index. Familiarity with 18th-century Dutch handwriting and language is required.
- Wills proved before the Prerogative Court of New York are indexed in the *Abstracts of Wills* series published by the New-York Historical Society — this is a key finding aid for the colonial period. (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)
- Tax assessment lists survive for some years and wards and are the primary substitute for census records before 1790. (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)
- Colonial militia rolls name men of military age and are useful for identifying and locating residents when no other record names them. (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)
- The FamilySearch Wiki specific pages for New York City, Vital Records, Church Records, and Land Records all returned only generic content during this survey — visit https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy directly for the most current guidance.

**Key Military Records**

- **FamilySearch — "Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783"** (345,678 records, free): Indexed military service records, the best first stop for Virginia soldiers.

Virginia's territory during the war included what are now **Kentucky and West Virginia**. Ancestors living in those areas had their wartime records created under Virginia county courts, so search Virginia county records first.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Virginia, United States (1775-1783)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Virginia operated as the Commonwealth of Virginia from 1776 (declaration of independence), ratifying the U.S. Constitution in 1788; county-level record-keeping dates from the 1630s
- **Administrative structure:** County courts held primary civil record-keeping authority throughout this period
- **Parent jurisdiction:** One of the 13 original colonies; became a U.S. state in 1788
- **Population during period:** No population figures were returned by the place_population tool for 1775-1783
- **Economy:** Tobacco plantation economy; port trade at Norfolk and Alexandria; significant wartime disruption
- **Ethnic composition:** English-descent settlers dominant; large enslaved African population in Tidewater and Piedmont; Scots-Irish and German settlers in the Shenandoah Valley
- **Religious denominations:** Anglican (later Episcopal) was the established colonial church; Baptist and Methodist congregations active during the Revolution; Presbyterian congregations in the Piedmont and Valley
- **Key historical events:** Virginia contributed more soldiers to the Continental Army than any other colony; major British raids through the state; decisive battle at Yorktown (1781) ended major combat operations (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia)

## Boundary changes
- During 1775-1783, Virginia's territory encompassed the present states of Kentucky and West Virginia; records for ancestors in those areas are filed under Virginia county jurisdictions of the period
- Kentucky became a separate state in 1792; West Virginia separated from Virginia in 1863; research in those areas during the Revolutionary War era begins in Virginia county records
- Identifying the specific Virginia county that covered the ancestor's location is prerequisite to finding the relevant court and deed records

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No statewide civil registration existed during 1775-1783; the FamilySearch Wiki Virginia Vital Records page returned only generic content during this survey and did not provide a registration start date with level
- **What exists:** No civil births, marriages, or deaths were registered by the state during this period
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Anglican/Episcopal vestry books; county court marriage bonds and registers; FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Church Records, 1680-1929" (1,234,567 records, id 1598230, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598230)

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Anglican/Episcopal (established colonial church); Baptist and Methodist congregations formed during and after the Revolution; Presbyterian congregations in the Valley and Piedmont
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials (vestry books); pew rents and parish poor relief lists
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Church Records, 1680-1929" (1,234,567 records, id 1598230); originals at individual congregations, the Virginia Episcopal Diocese archives, and the Library of Virginia

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The 1790 Virginia federal census was destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814; the first surviving federal census with Virginia data is 1800 (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands)
- **State enumerations:** Virginia state enumerations and tax lists (1782-1799) are available as digitized volume 005301449 (87 images, full-text searchable but not name-indexed — must be searched as full text, not by name)
- **Substitute:** The 1782 personal property tax lists function as the primary census substitute for the Revolutionary War era and the missing 1790 census gap

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, inventories, guardianships, court order books
- **Date range:** County court records from formation of each county, many predating the Revolution; FamilySearch collection "Virginia, County Court Records, 1650-1920" (1,789,012 records, id 2134567, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134567)
- **Digitized volume:** 005301448, Augusta County court order books, 1775-1795, 158 images, 61% name-indexed — indexed + images; covers western Virginia jurisdiction

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Colonial land grants issued by the Royal Governor before 1776; post-1776 grants by the Commonwealth of Virginia. Warrant and survey records for post-war bounty lands in the Virginia Military District of Ohio are at the Virginia State Library (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands)
- **Types:** Land patents, deeds, bounty land warrants, grants; post-war bounty land warrants for veterans; collection "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900" (2,567,890 records, id 1734285, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1734285)
- **Digitized volume:** 005301447, Revolutionary War land bounty warrants 1779-1800, 341 images, browse-only (0% indexed, not full-text) — must be browsed image by image with no search capability

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** American Revolutionary War (1775-1783)
- **Record types:** Continental Line service records and muster rolls (NARA Record Group 93); Virginia militia records (Library of Virginia, Richmond); pension and bounty-land warrant application files (NARA Record Group 15); Virginia State Navy records — per FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Military Records, 1775-1783" (345,678 records, id 1945678, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678); NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/); Library of Virginia in Richmond for militia records

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Church graveyards associated with Anglican/Episcopal, Baptist, and Presbyterian congregations throughout Virginia
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/)
- **Physical records:** Sexton and burial records vary by congregation and are held at individual churches or denominational archives

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Virginia Gazette (Williamsburg) published through the colonial and early statehood period; papers at Alexandria and Richmond also active during the war
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/); physical holdings at the Library of Virginia
- **Content value:** Obituaries, estate notices, Loyalist notices, and military announcements appear in wartime issues

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Norfolk and Alexandria served as colonial/early statehood ports; major immigration to Virginia preceded the Revolution
- **Record types:** Loyalist emigration records for those departing after the Revolution; some Hessian and British prisoner records for the wartime period; declarations of intention and alien registrations filed inland
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/)
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Personal property tax lists (tithe/levy lists at county level); land tax
- **Date range:** Collection "Virginia, Tax Records, 1782-1850" (456,789 records, id 1456723, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1456723); digitized volume 005301449 (state enumerations/tax lists 1782-1799, full-text searchable, not name-indexed)
- **Substitute value:** 1782 personal property tax lists are the primary substitute for the destroyed 1790 Virginia federal census; they can place a family in a specific county and assess approximate wealth

### Other record types
- **Loyalist claims:** Virginia families who supported the Crown filed loyalist claims with British authorities after the war; records may be at the British National Archives or through published abstracts
- **Pension files:** NARA RG 15 pension application files contain detailed family histories, veterans' own narratives, names of relatives, and sometimes marriage certificates — among the richest genealogical sources for this period

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Virginia, Military Records 1775-1783 (345,678 records); Church Records 1680-1929 (1,234,567); Land, Marriage, and Will Records 1600-1900 (2,567,890); Tax Records 1782-1850 (456,789); County Court Records 1650-1920 (1,789,012) | Free |
| Fold3 | Military records (pension files, service records) | Subscription |
| Ancestry | Census and other Virginia collections | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | National Archives: RG 93 (service records), RG 15 (pensions) | Free/mail request |

**Coverage of this survey:** 3 digitized volumes match Virginia for 1775-1783 in volume_search; all 3 are detailed above. The volume_search response did not include a summary breakdown by record type despite being requested.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Library of Virginia, Richmond | Virginia militia records; state land records; county court records on microfilm | In-person / online catalog |
| National Archives (NARA) | Continental Line service records (RG 93); pension files (RG 15); bounty land warrant files | In-person / mail / Fold3 |
| County courthouses | Deed books, court order books, marriage bonds, will books | In-person / mail |
| Denominational archives | Church vestry books and registers | Varies by denomination |

## Records NOT online
- Virginia militia records at the Library of Virginia are not fully indexed online; many require in-person or mail requests to Richmond
- Pension application files are partially available through Fold3; original paper files at NARA may contain additional pages not digitized
- Revolutionary War land bounty warrants (volume 005301447, 341 images) are browse-only with no name index
- County court order books beyond Augusta County are covered through the broader FamilySearch collection but may not be individually indexed for 1775-1783
- Virginia State Navy records are referenced in the FamilySearch Wiki but no specific online collection was returned by tools for this survey

## Known record losses
- The 1790 federal census for Virginia was destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814; stated in FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands). The 1782 personal property tax lists are the established substitute.
- No other specific record losses for this place and period were returned by the survey tools.

## Research tips
- Begin with NARA pension files (Record Group 15) for any ancestor with known or suspected military service — these files often include the veteran's own narrative, names of family members, and marriage documentation; access via Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) or by written request to NARA (https://www.archives.gov/)
- Use the 1782 Virginia personal property tax lists (FamilySearch digitized volume 005301449, full-text searchable) to place a family in a specific county before and after the period — these are the primary substitute for the missing 1790 census
- Continental Line service records (NARA RG 93) and Virginia militia records (Library of Virginia, Richmond) cover different pools of men; a veteran may appear in one but not the other — search both before concluding no service record exists (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)
- Bounty land warrant records (volume 005301447, browse-only) connect post-war land grants to named veterans; pair with warrant and survey records at the Virginia State Library for land in the Virginia Military District of Ohio (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands)
- For ancestors in the Shenandoah Valley or western Virginia, the Augusta County court order books (volume 005301448, 61% name-indexed) are especially relevant — that county had jurisdiction over much of western Virginia during the Revolution
- The FamilySearch Wiki Virginia-specific pages returned only generic content during this survey; consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Genealogy directly to verify record availability before treating this guide as complete

# Locality Guide: Virginia, United States (1775-1783)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Virginia operated as the Commonwealth of Virginia from 1776 (declaration of independence), ratifying the U.S. Constitution in 1788; county-level record-keeping dates from the 1630s
- **Administrative structure:** County courts held primary civil record-keeping authority throughout this period
- **Parent jurisdiction:** One of the 13 original colonies; became a U.S. state in 1788
- **Population during period:** No population figures were returned by the place_population tool for 1775-1783
- **Economy:** Tobacco plantation economy; port trade at Norfolk and Alexandria; significant wartime disruption
- **Ethnic composition:** English-descent settlers dominant; large enslaved African population in Tidewater and Piedmont; Scots-Irish and German settlers in the Shenandoah Valley
- **Religious denominations:** Anglican (later Episcopal) was the established colonial church; Baptist and Methodist congregations active during the Revolution; Presbyterian congregations in the Piedmont and Valley
- **Key historical events:** Virginia contributed more soldiers to the Continental Army than any other colony; major British raids through the state; decisive battle at Yorktown (1781) ended major combat operations (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia)

## Boundary changes
- During 1775-1783, Virginia's territory encompassed the present states of Kentucky and West Virginia; records for ancestors in those areas are filed under Virginia county jurisdictions of the period
- Kentucky became a separate state in 1792; West Virginia separated from Virginia in 1863; research in those areas during the Revolutionary War era begins in Virginia county records
- Identifying the specific Virginia county that covered the ancestor's location is prerequisite to finding the relevant court and deed records

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No statewide civil registration existed during 1775-1783; the FamilySearch Wiki Virginia Vital Records page returned only generic content during this survey and did not provide a registration start date with level
- **What exists:** No civil births, marriages, or deaths were registered by the state during this period
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Anglican/Episcopal vestry books; county court marriage bonds and registers; FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Church Records, 1680-1929" (1,234,567 records, id 1598230, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598230)

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Anglican/Episcopal (established colonial church); Baptist and Methodist congregations formed during and after the Revolution; Presbyterian congregations in the Valley and Piedmont
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials (vestry books); pew rents and parish poor relief lists
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Church Records, 1680-1929" (1,234,567 records, id 1598230); originals at individual congregations, the Virginia Episcopal Diocese archives, and the Library of Virginia

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The 1790 Virginia federal census was destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814; the first surviving federal census with Virginia data is 1800 (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands)
- **State enumerations:** Virginia state enumerations and tax lists (1782-1799) are available as digitized volume 005301449 (87 images, full-text searchable but not name-indexed — must be searched as full text, not by name)
- **Substitute:** The 1782 personal property tax lists function as the primary census substitute for the Revolutionary War era and the missing 1790 census gap

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, inventories, guardianships, court order books
- **Date range:** County court records from formation of each county, many predating the Revolution; FamilySearch collection "Virginia, County Court Records, 1650-1920" (1,789,012 records, id 2134567, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134567)
- **Digitized volume:** 005301448, Augusta County court order books, 1775-1795, 158 images, 61% name-indexed — indexed + images; covers western Virginia jurisdiction

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Colonial land grants issued by the Royal Governor before 1776; post-1776 grants by the Commonwealth of Virginia. Warrant and survey records for post-war bounty lands in the Virginia Military District of Ohio are at the Virginia State Library (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands)
- **Types:** Land patents, deeds, bounty land warrants, grants; post-war bounty land warrants for veterans; collection "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900" (2,567,890 records, id 1734285, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1734285)
- **Digitized volume:** 005301447, Revolutionary War land bounty warrants 1779-1800, 341 images, browse-only (0% indexed, not full-text) — must be browsed image by image with no search capability

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** American Revolutionary War (1775-1783)
- **Record types:** Continental Line service records and muster rolls (NARA Record Group 93); Virginia militia records (Library of Virginia, Richmond); pension and bounty-land warrant application files (NARA Record Group 15); Virginia State Navy records — per FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Virginia, Military Records, 1775-1783" (345,678 records, id 1945678, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678); NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/); Library of Virginia in Richmond for militia records

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Church graveyards associated with Anglican/Episcopal, Baptist, and Presbyterian congregations throughout Virginia
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/)
- **Physical records:** Sexton and burial records vary by congregation and are held at individual churches or denominational archives

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Virginia Gazette (Williamsburg) published through the colonial and early statehood period; papers at Alexandria and Richmond also active during the war
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/); physical holdings at the Library of Virginia
- **Content value:** Obituaries, estate notices, Loyalist notices, and military announcements appear in wartime issues

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Norfolk and Alexandria served as colonial/early statehood ports; major immigration to Virginia preceded the Revolution
- **Record types:** Loyalist emigration records for those departing after the Revolution; some Hessian and British prisoner records for the wartime period; declarations of intention and alien registrations filed inland
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/)
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Personal property tax lists (tithe/levy lists at county level); land tax
- **Date range:** Collection "Virginia, Tax Records, 1782-1850" (456,789 records, id 1456723, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1456723); digitized volume 005301449 (state enumerations/tax lists 1782-1799, full-text searchable, not name-indexed)
- **Substitute value:** 1782 personal property tax lists are the primary substitute for the destroyed 1790 Virginia federal census; they can place a family in a specific county and assess approximate wealth

### Other record types
- **Loyalist claims:** Virginia families who supported the Crown filed loyalist claims with British authorities after the war; records may be at the British National Archives or through published abstracts
- **Pension files:** NARA RG 15 pension application files contain detailed family histories, veterans' own narratives, names of relatives, and sometimes marriage certificates — among the richest genealogical sources for this period

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Virginia, Military Records 1775-1783 (345,678 records); Church Records 1680-1929 (1,234,567); Land, Marriage, and Will Records 1600-1900 (2,567,890); Tax Records 1782-1850 (456,789); County Court Records 1650-1920 (1,789,012) | Free |
| Fold3 | Military records (pension files, service records) | Subscription |
| Ancestry | Census and other Virginia collections | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | National Archives: RG 93 (service records), RG 15 (pensions) | Free/mail request |

**Coverage of this survey:** 3 digitized volumes match Virginia for 1775-1783 in volume_search; all 3 are detailed above. The volume_search response did not include a summary breakdown by record type despite being requested.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Library of Virginia, Richmond | Virginia militia records; state land records; county court records on microfilm | In-person / online catalog |
| National Archives (NARA) | Continental Line service records (RG 93); pension files (RG 15); bounty land warrant files | In-person / mail / Fold3 |
| County courthouses | Deed books, court order books, marriage bonds, will books | In-person / mail |
| Denominational archives | Church vestry books and registers | Varies by denomination |

## Records NOT online
- Virginia militia records at the Library of Virginia are not fully indexed online; many require in-person or mail requests to Richmond
- Pension application files are partially available through Fold3; original paper files at NARA may contain additional pages not digitized
- Revolutionary War land bounty warrants (volume 005301447, 341 images) are browse-only with no name index
- County court order books beyond Augusta County are covered through the broader FamilySearch collection but may not be individually indexed for 1775-1783
- Virginia State Navy records are referenced in the FamilySearch Wiki but no specific online collection was returned by tools for this survey

## Known record losses
- The 1790 federal census for Virginia was destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814; stated in FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands). The 1782 personal property tax lists are the established substitute.
- No other specific record losses for this place and period were returned by the survey tools.

## Research tips
- Begin with NARA pension files (Record Group 15) for any ancestor with known or suspected military service — these files often include the veteran's own narrative, names of family members, and marriage documentation; access via Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) or by written request to NARA (https://www.archives.gov/)
- Use the 1782 Virginia personal property tax lists (FamilySearch digitized volume 005301449, full-text searchable) to place a family in a specific county before and after the period — these are the primary substitute for the missing 1790 census
- Continental Line service records (NARA RG 93) and Virginia militia records (Library of Virginia, Richmond) cover different pools of men; a veteran may appear in one but not the other — search both before concluding no service record exists (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)
- Bounty land warrant records (volume 005301447, browse-only) connect post-war land grants to named veterans; pair with warrant and survey records at the Virginia State Library for land in the Virginia Military District of Ohio (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands)
- For ancestors in the Shenandoah Valley or western Virginia, the Augusta County court order books (volume 005301448, 61% name-indexed) are especially relevant — that county had jurisdiction over much of western Virginia during the Revolution
- The FamilySearch Wiki Virginia-specific pages returned only generic content during this survey; consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Genealogy directly to verify record availability before treating this guide as complete
