---

Old New Orleans in the early 1800s is one of the most disaster-complicated places to research in the United States. Here is what the locality guide found:

**What was destroyed**
- The fires of **1788 and 1794** burned most of the French Quarter and wiped out many colonial-era records before this period even begins.
- Yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and floods continued damaging archives throughout the 1800s.

**What survived and where to find it**

1. **Sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral** — Baptisms, marriages, and burials from 1731 (with gaps). These are the primary substitute for civil vital records, which barely exist for this era. FamilySearch has indexed collections covering Louisiana church records.

2. **Notarial Archives** — A Louisiana-specific record type unlike anything in most other states. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds 30+ million pages of property transfers, estate inventories, marriage contracts, and civil acts dating to 1734. FamilySearch has digitized one browse-only (unindexed) volume of Orleans Parish Notarial Acts, 1803–1820, in French and English; the rest require an in-person visit.

3. **Cabildo records** — Records of the Spanish colonial governing body, now held at the Louisiana State Museum. These cover the late Spanish period that bleeds into the early American territorial era.

**Practical search path**
- FamilySearch has indexed collections for Louisiana church records, probate, and a death index — start there.
- For anything beyond those indexed collections, plan for a visit to New Orleans (Notarial Archives Research Center) or Baton Rouge (Louisiana State Archives).

The next step would be building a research plan targeting your specific ancestors using these surviving record types as the foundation. Let me know who you are tracing and I can help scope that plan.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana (1800–1850)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** New Orleans founded 1718 by France; Spanish control 1763; returned to France 1800; Louisiana Purchase transferred it to the United States 1803; Louisiana became a state 1812
- **Administrative unit:** Orleans Parish (Louisiana uses parishes instead of counties; New Orleans is coterminous with Orleans Parish)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Louisiana Territory 1803–1812, then State of Louisiana
- **Population during period:** Population data could not be retrieved through the place_population tool for this period
- **Economy:** Major Mississippi River port; cotton and sugar commerce; large enslaved population throughout the period
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creole, Spanish Creole, Anglo-American newcomers post-1803, free people of color, enslaved Africans, and growing Irish and German immigrant communities by the 1830s–1840s
- **Religious denominations:** Predominantly Roman Catholic (St. Louis Cathedral the central parish); Protestant denominations established by mid-period
- **Key historical events:** Louisiana Purchase (1803); Louisiana statehood (1812); Battle of New Orleans (1815); multiple yellow fever epidemics and flooding throughout the period; fires of 1788 and 1794 (pre-period but their effect on the record base persists throughout the 1800s)

## Boundary changes
- New Orleans / Orleans Parish boundaries were stable across the 1800–1850 period
- The critical jurisdictional shift was the Louisiana Purchase (1803): records before that date were created under French or Spanish authority; from 1803 onward under US territorial then state authority
- Louisiana became a state in 1812, transforming the record-keeping hierarchy from territorial to state

## Record survival after disasters

This is the central research challenge for early 1800s New Orleans and must be understood before searching any other record type.

**What was destroyed:** The fires of 1788 and 1794 "destroyed most of the French Quarter and many colonial records" (FamilySearch Wiki, [New Orleans Genealogy — Records Surviving Disasters](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)). Repeated yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and floods further damaged archival holdings throughout the city's history (Wikipedia, New Orleans).

**What survived — and where copies or substitutes are held:**

1. **St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers** — Baptisms, marriages, and burials from 1731 survive with gaps ([New Orleans Genealogy — Records Surviving Disasters](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)). These are the primary source for vital events in the early 1800s before civil registration. FamilySearch has indexed records in "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (collection 1612905, ~987,654 records).

2. **Notarial records** — Survived the fires and are the backbone of Louisiana legal documentation. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds over 30 million pages of notarial acts dating to 1734 ([New Orleans Genealogy — Records Surviving Disasters](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)). FamilySearch has digitized one browse-only volume: Orleans Parish Notarial Acts, 1803–1820 (image group 004990115, 167 images, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable, in French and English — must be browsed image by image).

3. **Cabildo records** — Records of the Spanish colonial governing body also survived ([New Orleans Genealogy — Records Surviving Disasters](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)). Held at the Louisiana State Museum (Cabildo building, Jackson Square).

4. **Louisiana State Archives** — Holds territorial and early state records from 1803 onward ([Louisiana Genealogy — Parish System](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System)), Baton Rouge.

## Available record types

For each record type, the jurisdictional level at which records were created is noted. For early 1800s New Orleans, the parish (Orleans Parish) is the primary civil unit.

### Vital records (civil registration)

Old New Orleans in the early 1800s is one of the most disaster-complicated places to research in the United States. The great fires of 1788 and 1794 destroyed most of the French Quarter and many colonial-era records before this period even begins, and yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and floods continued damaging archives throughout the 1800s. The next step would be to build a research plan targeting the specific ancestors you are tracing, using the surviving record types identified in this guide as the foundation.

# Locality Guide: Boston, Massachusetts — Port of Entry (1840s)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Boston founded 1630; Suffolk County established 1643
- **County seat / administrative center:** Boston (city and county seat are the same)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Suffolk County, Massachusetts
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the tool for this query. Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston) notes that by 1850 over a quarter of Boston's residents were Irish-born, reflecting the surge from the Great Famine (1845–1852).
- **Economy:** Major seaport and commercial hub; construction, domestic service, and textile mills absorbed immigrant labor
- **Ethnic composition:** Heavy Irish immigration in the 1840s driven by the Great Famine; also German, British, and Canadian arrivals at the port
- **Religious denominations:** Congregationalist, Episcopal, Catholic (growing rapidly with Irish immigration), Methodist, Baptist
- **Key historical events:** The Irish Potato Famine (1845–1852) made Boston one of the highest-volume ports for Irish arrivals in the United States

## Boundary changes
- place_search_all returned no historical boundary change records for this place and period.
- Boston was incorporated as a city in 1822; Suffolk County boundaries were stable in the 1840s.

## Available record types

Note: Massachusetts recorded vital events at the **town** level, not the county level. Route searches to the specific Boston town clerk records, not a county-level index.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki's Massachusetts Vital Records page returned only generic content during this survey; specific Massachusetts statewide registration start dates cannot be confirmed from tool results. Records do exist: FamilySearch collection 2061550 (Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890, 3,456,789 records) covers this period.
- **What exists:** Births, marriages, and deaths recorded at the town level through 1890 in collection 2061550
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 2061550 (free); originals at Boston City Archives and Massachusetts State Archives
- **Gaps:** Civil registration for immigrant families in the 1840s may be incomplete; church records are the preferred supplement
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic parish registers (see Church Records); The Pilot's Missing Persons column

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (rapidly expanding with Irish and German immigration); Congregationalist; Episcopal; Methodist
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Where held:** The FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston) states Catholic parish registers — especially those of the Cathedral of the Holy Cross and St. Patrick's — document baptisms, marriages, and burials of Irish immigrants from the 1840s onward, and that the Archdiocese of Boston Archives holds these records. FamilySearch collection 1921657 (Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920, 987,654 records) also covers this period.
- **Language:** English; some Latin in Catholic sacramental registers

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1840 (heads of household listed by name; other members as tick-marks by age bracket — immigrants may be unnamed) and 1850 (first census to name every individual with age, sex, and birthplace). Both are indexed and available free on FamilySearch and by subscription on Ancestry.
- **State census:** No Massachusetts state census in the 1840s was returned by the survey tools.
- **Other enumerations:** Mortality schedules began with the 1850 census and record deaths in the prior year.
- **Access:** 1840 and 1850 federal censuses are indexed + images on FamilySearch (free)

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, petitions
- **Date range:** Suffolk County Probate Court records from 1636; FamilySearch collection 1678901 (Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991, 567,890 records)
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1678901 (free); Suffolk County Probate Court (originals)

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Massachusetts is not a federal land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The FamilySearch Wiki's Massachusetts Land and Property page returned only generic content during this survey; the specific granting office cannot be confirmed from tool results.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, tax records
- **Where held:** Suffolk County Registry of Deeds (originals); some indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846–1848); many recent Irish immigrants served
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, draft records
- **Where held:** National Archives (NARA); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/, subscription) is a curated external link for military records for this place

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Catholic cemeteries expanded in the 1840s to serve the Irish immigrant community
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) is a curated external link for this place
- **Physical records:** Sexton registers; church burial records (see Church Records)

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston) notes that *The Pilot*, an Irish Catholic newspaper published in Boston, ran arrival notices and Missing Persons advertisements valuable for tracing 1840s Irish immigrants. Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) is a curated external link.
- **Where held:** Boston Public Library; digital coverage on Newspapers.com (subscription)
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, immigrant arrival notices, legal notices, and Missing Persons columns are particularly useful for 1840s arrivals

### Immigration and naturalization records (PRIMARY focus)
- **Relevant port:** Port of Boston was the primary entry point for 1840s arrivals.
- **Passenger lists:** The FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston) confirms customs passenger lists (1820–1891) for the Port of Boston are in NARA Record Group 36 and have been indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry. FamilySearch collection 1784312 (Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891, 1,234,567 records). 1 digitized volume found: DGS 003345210 (389 images, 1840–1850), **3% name-indexed, full-text searchable** — not fully accessible via standard name search; must text-search AND browse images for complete coverage.
- **Naturalization records:** FamilySearch collection 1459213 (Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906, 345,678 records). The process had multiple steps — declaration of intention, petition, final certificate — each potentially in a different court's records, any of which may supply arrival date, country of origin, or birthplace.
- **Where held:** Originals at National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA), per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston); also indexed on FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry (subscription).
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest for all family members when researching a family.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Town property and poll tax lists
- **Where held:** Boston City Archives; Massachusetts State Archives
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists name heads of household and can place an immigrant in Boston between census years

### Other record types
- **City directories:** Boston city directories listing residents, occupations, and addresses are useful between census years; some held at Boston Public Library and partially digitized
- **Almshouse and institutional records:** Many newly arrived immigrants in the 1840s entered public institutions; Boston almshouse records may survive in city archives

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Passenger Lists 1820–1891 (coll. 1784312); Town Vital Records 1620–1890 (coll. 2061550); Church Records 1630–1920 (coll. 1921657); Naturalization Records 1790–1906 (coll. 1459213); Probate Records 1635–1991 (coll. 1678901) | Free |
| Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/) | U.S. Federal Census; overlapping Boston passenger list coverage | Subscription |
| Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) | Military Records | Subscription |
| FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Cemetery Records | Free |
| Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Historical Newspapers including The Pilot | Subscription |
| NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) | National Archives finding aids; some digitized originals | Free online / In-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned 1 digitized volume matching the Port of Boston passenger lists for 1840–1850 (DGS 003345210, 389 images). This is the complete result set for the specific place and years queried. The FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891" (collection 1784312) covers a broader date range and returned 1,234,567 records from collections_search.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA) | Original customs passenger lists (NARA RG 36); naturalization records | In-person / written request; some digitized online |
| Massachusetts State Archives (Boston) | State vital records, court records | In-person / online request |
| Archdiocese of Boston Archives | Catholic parish registers from 1840s onward | Contact archives directly |
| Suffolk County Registry of Deeds (Boston) | Deed books, mortgages | In-person / online index |
| Suffolk County Probate Court (Boston) | Probate files from 1636 | In-person |
| Boston Public Library | City directories; The Pilot on microfilm; local newspaper archives | In-person; some digital |

## Records NOT online
- Original customs passenger list volumes at NARA Waltham for years beyond what is digitized in DGS 003345210
- Almshouse and poorhouse registers (city-level institutional records)
- Full Boston city directory runs for the 1840s (coverage on digital platforms is uneven)
- Archdiocese of Boston Catholic parish registers not yet microfilmed or digitized beyond what appears in FamilySearch collection 1921657

## Known record losses
No specific record losses for the Port of Boston or Boston-area repositories were reported in any tool result returned during this survey. An empty search result is a coverage gap, not evidence of destruction. Contact NARA Waltham or the Massachusetts State Archives to confirm the status of any apparently missing series.

## Research tips
- **Start with the passenger list.** The FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston) confirms customs passenger lists for the Port of Boston (1820–1891) are indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry. The 1 digitized volume (DGS 003345210) is only 3% name-indexed but full-text searchable — search by text AND browse images, since automated indexing missed most names.
- **1840s manifests give minimal origin detail.** Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston), 1840s customs manifests typically record only name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin — not the specific Irish townland or parish. Combine passenger list evidence with Catholic church records and the 1850 census (which asks birthplace) to narrow the origin.
- **Use The Pilot's Missing Persons columns.** Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston) notes that The Pilot published arrival notices and Missing Persons advertisements that often name the townland of origin — a recognized supplement to sparse passenger list data.
- **Follow up with naturalization records.** FamilySearch collection 1459213 (Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906) may supply the immigrant's arrival date and country of origin. Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court, so search federal district, Suffolk County, and Boston Municipal Court records.
- **Catholic church records are essential** for 1840s Irish arrivals. The FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston) identifies the Cathedral of the Holy Cross and St. Patrick's as key parishes; registers are held at the Archdiocese of Boston Archives.
- **Search adjoining counties at the town level.** Many immigrants who arrived through Boston settled in Middlesex, Norfolk, and Essex Counties. The wiki_place_page home section returned only generic content for Boston, so the Neighboring Counties table was not retrieved — but check those surrounding counties as well. Massachusetts recorded vital events at the town level, so search specific town records within those counties rather than just a county index.

- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (rapidly expanding with Irish and German immigration); Congregationalist; Episcopal; Methodist
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Where held:** The FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston) states Catholic parish registers — especially those of the Cathedral of the Holy Cross and St. Patrick's — document baptisms, marriages, and burials of Irish immigrants from the 1840s onward, and that the Archdiocese of Boston Archives holds these records. FamilySearch collection 1921657 (Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920, 987,654 records) also covers this period.
- **Language:** English; some Latin in Catholic sacramental registers

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1840 (heads of household listed by name; other members as tick-marks by age bracket — immigrants may be unnamed) and 1850 (first census to name every individual with age, sex, and birthplace). Both are indexed and available free on FamilySearch and by subscription on Ancestry.
- **State census:** No Massachusetts state census in the 1840s was returned by the survey tools.
- **Other enumerations:** Mortality schedules began with the 1850 census and record deaths in the prior year.
- **Access:** 1840 and 1850 federal censuses are indexed + images on FamilySearch (free)

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, petitions
- **Date range:** Suffolk County Probate Court records from 1636; FamilySearch collection 1678901 (Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991, 567,890 records)
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1678901 (free); Suffolk County Probate Court (originals)

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Massachusetts is not a federal land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The FamilySearch Wiki's Massachusetts Land and Property page returned only generic content during this survey; the specific granting office cannot be confirmed from tool results.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, tax records
- **Where held:** Suffolk County Registry of Deeds (originals); some indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846–1848); many recent Irish immigrants served
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, draft records
- **Where held:** National Archives (NARA); Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/, subscription) is a curated external link for military records for this place

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Catholic cemeteries expanded in the 1840s to serve the Irish immigrant community
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) is a curated external link for this place
- **Physical records:** Sexton registers; church burial records (see Church Records)

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston) notes that *The Pilot*, an Irish Catholic newspaper published in Boston, ran arrival notices and Missing Persons advertisements valuable for tracing 1840s Irish immigrants. Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) is a curated external link.
- **Where held:** Boston Public Library; digital coverage on Newspapers.com (subscription)
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, immigrant arrival notices, legal notices, and Missing Persons columns are particularly useful for 1840s arrivals

### Immigration and naturalization records (PRIMARY focus)
- **Relevant port:** Port of Boston was the primary entry point for 1840s arrivals.
- **Passenger lists:** The FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston) confirms customs passenger lists (1820–1891) for the Port of Boston are in NARA Record Group 36 and have been indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry. FamilySearch collection 1784312 (Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891, 1,234,567 records). 1 digitized volume found: DGS 003345210 (389 images, 1840–1850), **3% name-indexed, full-text searchable** — not fully accessible via standard name search; must text-search AND browse images for complete coverage.
- **Naturalization records:** FamilySearch collection 1459213 (Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906, 345,678 records). The process had multiple steps — declaration of intention, petition, final certificate — each potentially in a different court's records, any of which may supply arrival date, country of origin, or birthplace.
- **Where held:** Originals at National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA), per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston); also indexed on FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry (subscription).
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest for all family members when researching a family.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Town property and poll tax lists
- **Where held:** Boston City Archives; Massachusetts State Archives
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists name heads of household and can place an immigrant in Boston between census years

### Other record types
- **City directories:** Boston city directories listing residents, occupations, and addresses are useful between census years; some held at Boston Public Library and partially digitized
- **Almshouse and institutional records:** Many newly arrived immigrants in the 1840s entered public institutions; Boston almshouse records may survive in city archives

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Passenger Lists 1820–1891 (coll. 1784312); Town Vital Records 1620–1890 (coll. 2061550); Church Records 1630–1920 (coll. 1921657); Naturalization Records 1790–1906 (coll. 1459213); Probate Records 1635–1991 (coll. 1678901) | Free |
| Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/) | U.S. Federal Census; overlapping Boston passenger list coverage | Subscription |
| Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) | Military Records | Subscription |
| FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Cemetery Records | Free |
| Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Historical Newspapers including The Pilot | Subscription |
| NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) | National Archives finding aids; some digitized originals | Free online / In-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned 1 digitized volume matching the Port of Boston passenger lists for 1840–1850 (DGS 003345210, 389 images). This is the complete result set for the specific place and years queried. The FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891" (collection 1784312) covers a broader date range and returned 1,234,567 records from collections_search.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA) | Original customs passenger lists (NARA RG 36); naturalization records | In-person / written request; some digitized online |
| Massachusetts State Archives (Boston) | State vital records, court records | In-person / online request |
| Archdiocese of Boston Archives | Catholic parish registers from 1840s onward | Contact archives directly |
| Suffolk County Registry of Deeds (Boston) | Deed books, mortgages | In-person / online index |
| Suffolk County Probate Court (Boston) | Probate files from 1636 | In-person |
| Boston Public Library | City directories; The Pilot on microfilm; local newspaper archives | In-person; some digital |

## Records NOT online
- Original customs passenger list volumes at NARA Waltham for years beyond what is digitized in DGS 003345210
- Almshouse and poorhouse registers (city-level institutional records)
- Full Boston city directory runs for the 1840s (coverage on digital platforms is uneven)
- Archdiocese of Boston Catholic parish registers not yet microfilmed or digitized beyond what appears in FamilySearch collection 1921657

## Known record losses
No specific record losses for the Port of Boston or Boston-area repositories were reported in any tool result returned during this survey. An empty search result is a coverage gap, not evidence of destruction. Contact NARA Waltham or the Massachusetts State Archives to confirm the status of any apparently missing series.

## Research tips
- **Start with the passenger list.** The FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston) confirms customs passenger lists for the Port of Boston (1820–1891) are indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry. The 1 digitized volume (DGS 003345210) is only 3% name-indexed but full-text searchable — search by text AND browse images, since automated indexing missed most names.
- **1840s manifests give minimal origin detail.** Per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston), 1840s customs manifests typically record only name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin — not the specific Irish townland or parish. Combine passenger list evidence with Catholic church records and the 1850 census (which asks birthplace) to narrow the origin.
- **Use The Pilot's Missing Persons columns.** Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston) notes that The Pilot published arrival notices and Missing Persons advertisements that often name the townland of origin — a recognized supplement to sparse passenger list data.
- **Follow up with naturalization records.** FamilySearch collection 1459213 (Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906) may supply the immigrant's arrival date and country of origin. Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court, so search federal district, Suffolk County, and Boston Municipal Court records.
- **Catholic church records are essential** for 1840s Irish arrivals. The FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston) identifies the Cathedral of the Holy Cross and St. Patrick's as key parishes; registers are held at the Archdiocese of Boston Archives.
- **Search adjoining counties at the town level.** Many immigrants who arrived through Boston settled in Middlesex, Norfolk, and Essex Counties. The wiki_place_page home section returned only generic content for Boston, so the Neighboring Counties table was not retrieved — but check those surrounding counties as well. Massachusetts recorded vital events at the town level, so search specific town records within those counties rather than just a county index.

Locality guide written as **loc_001**. Here's what the agent found:

---

## Oklahoma / Indian Territory — Mid-1800s Native American Research

Oklahoma was designated **Indian Territory** in the mid-1800s, set aside for the **Five Civilized Tribes** (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek, and Seminole) relocated under the Indian Removal Act of 1830. Because there was no county-level civil government, records fall into four systems:

### Key Record Systems

| System | What It Covers |
|---|---|
| **Tribal governments** | Enrollment rolls, tribal court records |
| **Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA)** | Agency records, annuity payment rolls, school census rolls |
| **Missionary records** | Baptism, marriage, and burial registers from Christian missionaries |
| **Federal government** | Treaty documents, removal emigration lists |

### Important Caution About the Dawes Rolls

The **Dawes Rolls (1898–1914)** are the most widely indexed tribal records online — but they **postdate the mid-1800s entirely**. For that earlier period you need:

- **Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851)**
- **Drennen Roll (1852)**
- **Annuity rolls** and BIA agency correspondence

Most of this earlier material is **physical, undigitized** and held at:

> **National Archives Southwest Region — Fort Worth, Texas**

### Federal Census Gap

The standard federal census **did not cover Indian Territory residents** in 1850–1880. A blank result in those census years is expected and normal — not a dead end.

### FamilySearch Collections

FamilySearch has **three relevant indexed collections** covering this area with hundreds of thousands of records. These are the best starting point for digitized material.

---

### Next Step

Identify **which of the Five Tribes** your ancestors belonged to — Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek, or Seminole — then target that tribe's specific roll series on FamilySearch and at NARA Fort Worth. That determination drives everything else in the research plan.

quirks: During the mid-1800s this region was Indian Territory, not an organized U.S. state or territory with standard civil government — records were created by tribal governments, the Bureau of Indian Affairs, missionaries, and the federal government, not county courthouses.

Oklahoma statehood was 1907; county-level civil records (marriages, deeds, probate) begin only after county organization, which occurred mainly after the Curtis Act of 1898 began dissolving tribal governments.
The Dawes Rolls (1898-1914) are the most widely used enrollment records but postdate the mid-1800s target period — work backward from them to find families present in the 1850s-1880s.

Earlier tribal rolls covering the mid-1800s include the Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851) and the Drennen Roll (1852) for Cherokee; each of the Five Tribes maintained its own enrollment series — search the specific tribe first.
Annuity payment rolls list heads of household eligible for treaty payments and are among the best pre-Dawes census substitutes for Indian Territory families.
The National Archives Southwest Region in Fort Worth, Texas is the primary physical repository for Bureau of Indian Affairs agency records, tribal court records, and Indian Territory records.
Tribal records were kept in the tribe's own language in some cases; Cherokee records used the Sequoyah syllabary — a researcher unfamiliar with it will need a specialist or a transcription.

The standard U.S. federal decennial census (1850, 1860, 1870, 1880) did not enumerate Indian Territory residents on the standard population schedules — look instead for the separate Indian censuses and special BIA-administered enumerations.
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Indian Territory (Five Civilized Tribes), Oklahoma (1830-1890)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Indian Territory established under the Indian Removal Act of 1830; the Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek/Muscogee, and Seminole) were relocated there primarily 1830-1842 via the Trail of Tears
- **Administrative center:** Each tribe maintained its own capital: Tahlequah (Cherokee), Tishomingo (Chickasaw), Doaksville then Tuskahoma (Choctaw), Okmulgee (Creek), Wewoka (Seminole)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Federal (U.S. government); no organized territorial legislature; governed by tribal governments and the Office of Indian Affairs
- **Population during period:** Population figures from standard census tools were not returned for this jurisdiction; the standard federal census did not enumerate Indian Territory on regular population schedules during this period
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, ranching, and later cotton cultivation in the southern nations; some enslaved persons held by tribal members; trade and commerce regulated through tribal governments
- **Ethnic composition:** Five Civilized Tribes as the dominant groups; freedmen (formerly enslaved persons) enrolled separately after the Civil War; a growing non-Indian (white and Black) population entered illegally or as licensed traders
- **Religious denominations:** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missionaries active from the 1820s; each maintained schools and churches and kept their own registers
- **Key historical events:** Trail of Tears relocations (1830-1842); U.S. Civil War divided the tribes (1861-1865), causing massive record loss and population displacement; Reconstruction treaties (1866) reorganized tribal governments and enrolled freedmen

## Boundary changes
- Indian Territory boundaries shifted with successive treaties; Oklahoma Territory was carved from the western portion in 1890 and opened to non-Indian settlement by land runs
- The Five Civilized Tribes occupied the eastern portion throughout the mid-1800s; the western portion was home to Plains tribes under separate agencies
- Oklahoma statehood 1907 merged Indian Territory and Oklahoma Territory; county governments replaced tribal governments after the Curtis Act (1898) began dissolving them
- Records created before statehood under tribal or federal authority remain at NARA Fort Worth and in tribal archives, not at county courthouses

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Oklahoma Vital Records were not available during this survey; no specific statewide registration date can be confirmed from tool results. Oklahoma became a state in 1907; statewide civil registration most likely began at or near that date.

- **Where held:** FamilySearch indexes the collection "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820-1965" (collection 1654321, 123,456 records); originals are dispersed among denominational archives and NARA
- **Language:** Primarily English; some Cherokee-language records used the Sequoyah syllabary

### Census records
- **Standard federal census:** The 1850, 1860, 1870, and 1880 federal censuses did NOT enumerate Indian Territory residents on standard population schedules
- **Tribal and Indian censuses:** FamilySearch collection "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851-1959" (collection 1987432, 567,890 records) covers tribal enrollments and BIA-administered counts; this is the primary census-type source for the mid-1800s
- **Annuity rolls:** Heads of household receiving treaty payment annuities were listed by name; these function as intercensal substitutes and are part of the BIA agency records at NARA Fort Worth
- **Access:** Collection 1987432 is indexed and searchable at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Tribal courts (not county courts) handled probate-equivalent matters; estate records, guardianship of orphans, and land disputes went before tribal district courts
- **Date range:** Tribal court records from the mid-1800s onward
- **Where held:** NARA Southwest Region, Fort Worth, Texas; some are microfilmed by FamilySearch
- **Note:** Because there were no county courts in Indian Territory, do not search Oklahoma county probate indexes for this period

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Tribal land was held communally under treaty; individual allotment did not begin until the Dawes Allotment era (1887-1907)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Land grants and patents for the allotment era are at the Bureau of Land Management and NARA; pre-allotment communal land records are in tribal archives and BIA records at NARA Fort Worth. The FamilySearch Wiki Land and Property page for Oklahoma was not returned with specific content during this survey.
- **Types:** Allotment files, BIA improvement permits, tribal land use records; FamilySearch collection "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834-1907" (collection 1541872, 234,567 records) at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Five Tribes service in the Confederate and Union armies (1861-1865); U.S.-Indian Wars
- **Record types:** Service and pension records for tribal members who served are at NARA Washington, D.C.; the Civil War pension files for Indian veterans are especially useful for family relationships
- **Where held:** NARA; available via Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com) for service records; FamilySearch for some pension indexes

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Tribal and mission cemeteries are scattered throughout the Five Nations; many are unmarked or unrecorded
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com) has some Indian Territory cemetery listings, though coverage is uneven
- **Physical records:** Sexton records were rarely kept systematically; mission burial registers are the best alternative

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Cherokee Nation published the *Cherokee Phoenix* (1828-1834) and later the *Cherokee Advocate* (1844 onward); Choctaw and other nations had their own presses
- **Where held:** Some issues digitized; check the Oklahoma Historical Society and university libraries
- **Content value:** Obituaries, legal notices, tribal government announcements, treaty summaries

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant movements:** The Trail of Tears removals (1830s-1840s) generated federal removal records including muster rolls, emigration lists, and subsistence claims
- **Record types:** Removal emigration rolls name heads of household and family members; treaty documents at NARA and published in Kappler's *Indian Affairs: Laws and Treaties* (freely available online)
- **Where held:** NARA Washington D.C. and Fort Worth; Kappler's compilation is freely accessible
- **Content note:** Emigration rolls often list all family members present during removal, including children — examine the full record for every household member

### Tax records
- **Types:** No standard county tax records exist for Indian Territory in the mid-1800s; tribes levied their own taxes and collected fees, documented in tribal council records
- **Date range:** Tribal revenue and license records from the mid-1800s
- **Where held:** NARA Fort Worth; tribal archives
- **Substitute value:** Annuity rolls and improvement permits serve the tax-list substitute function here

### Tribal rolls (primary record type)
- **What they are:** Periodic enumerations of tribal citizens used to determine eligibility for treaty benefits, annuity payments, and later land allotments
- **Mid-1800s rolls:** Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851), Drennen Roll (1852) for the Eastern Cherokees; each of the Five Tribes maintained its own series with varying completeness (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls)
- **Dawes Rolls (1898-1914):** Most widely indexed series; too late for the mid-1800s target period but essential for working backward — a Dawes enrollee's card lists approximate birth year and blood quantum
- **Where held and access:** FamilySearch collection 1987432 ("Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851-1959") is the primary online source; NARA Fort Worth holds originals; Ancestry also indexes Dawes and related rolls

### BIA agency records
- **What they contain:** Annual reports of agents, correspondence with tribal leaders, school census records, trader license files, and police records — naming thousands of individuals not in any roll
- **Date range:** BIA agency records for Indian Territory run from the 1830s through statehood (1907)
- **Where held:** NARA Southwest Region, Fort Worth, Texas (Record Group 75); some correspondence also in NARA Washington D.C.
- **Access:** Primarily physical only; a researcher visit or NARA reproduction order is needed for most volumes

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851-1959 (coll. 1987432; 567,890 records); Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834-1907 (coll. 1541872; 234,567 records); Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820-1965 (coll. 1654321; 123,456 records) | Free |
| Ancestry | Dawes Rolls and related allotment records; U.S. Federal Census collection | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military service and pension records for tribal members | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Record Group 75 (Bureau of Indian Affairs); finding aids online, most records physical | Free finding aids; reproduction fees for records |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 1 digitized volume for Indian Territory 1830-1890 (DGS 002298871, Tribal Enrollment Cards, 940 images, 99% name-indexed and full-text searchable). The collections_search returned 4 indexed collections. The FamilySearch catalog was not queried in this run; a catalog search for "Indian Territory" or "Oklahoma" would likely surface additional microfilm volumes.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| NARA Southwest Region, Fort Worth, TX | BIA agency records (RG 75), tribal court records, Indian Territory land records, Dawes enrollment files | In-person or reproduction request via archives.gov |
| Oklahoma Historical Society, Oklahoma City | Tribal records, Oklahoma newspapers, local history | In-person; some digitized |
| Tribal archives (Cherokee National History Society, Choctaw Nation, etc.) | Tribe-specific rolls, council minutes, court records | Contact each tribe directly |
| Denominational archives (American Baptist Historical Society, etc.) | Mission church registers and school records | Contact each archive |

## Records NOT online
- Most BIA agency correspondence and annual reports (Record Group 75) are physical at NARA Fort Worth
- Tribal district court records for the mid-1800s are largely physical at NARA Fort Worth
- Pre-1898 tribal roll originals not covered by the FamilySearch collection
- Mission school enrollment registers not captured in collection 1654321
- Annuity payment rolls (available on microfilm at NARA; not fully indexed online)

## Known record losses
- No tool result in this survey specified the confirmed destruction of a particular record set. The U.S. Civil War caused significant disruption to tribal governments and their records; some records were lost or damaged. When no tool result confirms the fate of a specific record, treat the absence as a coverage gap rather than a confirmed loss, and contact NARA Fort Worth or the relevant tribal archive.

## Research tips
- Begin with the Dawes Rolls even though they postdate the target period: a Dawes enrollment card gives the enrollee's approximate birth year and blood quantum, which can anchor a family to the mid-1800s and point to the right tribal roll series. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls)
- Work through each tribe's own roll series in sequence: for Cherokee, the Old Settler Roll (1851) and Drennen Roll (1852) are the main mid-1800s sources; each tribe had its own enrollment timeline. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls)
- For families of mixed ancestry (Indian and white, or Indian and freedmen), search both the tribal citizen rolls and the separate freedmen rolls — the 1866 Reconstruction treaties required each tribe to enroll its freedmen as a separate class.
- Annuity rolls name heads of household eligible for treaty payments and are among the best pre-Dawes census substitutes; request them through NARA Fort Worth under Record Group 75.
- Missionary records (FamilySearch collection 1654321) can supply baptism and burial dates unavailable in any tribal roll, especially for infants and children. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records)
- The standard U.S. federal census did not enumerate Indian Territory on its standard population schedules; near-zero results in the 1850-1880 census indexes for tribal citizens are expected, not evidence the family did not exist.

Locality guide written as `loc_001`. Here's the full guide:

---

Pennsylvania Quaker communities in the late 1700s left some of the richest religious records in early American genealogy, and those records are the primary stand-in for civil vital registration, which Pennsylvania did not require at the state level until 1906.

**Key record types to focus on:**
- **Monthly meeting registers** — births, marriages, and deaths
- **Certificates of removal** — issued when families relocated between meetings, invaluable for tracing migration
- **Disownment minutes** — especially relevant for the Revolutionary War era, when many Quakers were formally expelled for taking oaths or bearing arms

**Primary repositories:**
- **Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College** — the largest collection of Pennsylvania Quaker records
- **Haverford College's Quaker and Special Collections**
- **FamilySearch** has digitized one notable volume: *Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750–1800* (145 images), but it must be browsed image by image with no name index

**Best name index available:**
- **William Wade Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy*** (6 volumes) — abstracts Pennsylvania meeting records and is widely held in research libraries. This is the fastest way to locate an ancestor in Quaker records.

**For pre-1790 research (before the first federal census):**
- County tax lists are the primary population name lists for this period.

**Recommended next step:**
Identify which specific monthly meeting your ancestors attended, then contact the Friends Historical Library directly to confirm which of that meeting's registers survive and arrange access.

Quaker records are organized by monthly meeting, not by civil township or county. Identify which monthly meeting the family attended before searching meeting-specific registers.

Certificates of Removal move with the family from one monthly meeting to another and name family members — the best single source for tracing Quaker migration across Pennsylvania and into neighboring states.

Many Quakers were disowned 1775-1783 for participation in the American Revolution (oath-taking, bearing arms, supplying war goods). An ancestor who disappears from meeting records after the mid-1770s should be searched in monthly meeting disownment minutes.
The SYNTH-PA-CHURCH collection returned by FamilySearch collections_search is labeled 'synthetic test fixture' in its title and should not be treated as a real collection.

The FamilySearch wiki pages for Pennsylvania (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) returned only generic content during this survey — consult them directly at familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Genealogy for current Pennsylvania-specific guidance.
County boundaries changed frequently throughout the late 1700s. If an ancestor's county did not yet exist, records were created in the parent county from which it was later carved.
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania, United States — Quaker Communities (c. 1750–1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Pennsylvania was granted to William Penn in 1681 and became a U.S. state in 1787.
- **Administrative center:** Philadelphia (colonial and state capital through this period).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** British Crown (pre-1776); then the United States (post-1787).
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the place_population tool for this query.
- **Economy:** Mixed agriculture in Chester, Bucks, and Lancaster counties; mercantile trade centered on Philadelphia.
- **Ethnic composition:** English Quakers formed the founding demographic; Welsh, German, Scots-Irish, and other groups joined throughout the 1700s.
- **Religious denominations:** Society of Friends (Quakers) dominant among original settlers; also Presbyterian, Lutheran, German Reformed, Anglican/Episcopal, Mennonite, and Baptist communities.
- **Key historical events:** American Revolution (1775–1783) created severe internal tensions within Quaker communities due to their pacifist testimony; large numbers were disowned for war-related activities, generating a significant body of disownment records.

## Boundary changes
- Pennsylvania's outer boundaries were largely fixed by the 1760s–1780s. County formations changed substantially throughout the 1700s — by 1800, many counties had been carved from earlier ones. Records before a county's formation date are filed under the parent county that then held authority.
- If the specific county did not yet exist in the target year, search the predecessor county's deeds, probate, and court records.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No statewide civil registration for births, marriages, or deaths existed during the late 1700s. Per the FamilySearch Pennsylvania Church Records wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records), Pennsylvania did not mandate statewide registration until 1906. The entire period 1750–1800 predates statewide civil registration.
- **What exists:** No civil births, marriages, or deaths for this period. Quaker meeting records are the primary — and often the only — substitute.
- **Where held:** No state-level civil registration office for this period. Vital events are recorded in church/meeting records and, secondarily, in probate and land records.
- **Gaps:** The entire 1750–1800 period is pre-civil registration.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Quaker meeting registers (see below), other denominational registers, newspaper marriage and death notices, probate inventories naming heirs.

### Church records — Quaker (Society of Friends)
- **Overview:** Quaker monthly meeting records are among the most detailed religious records in Pennsylvania. Per the FamilySearch Pennsylvania Church Records wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records), monthly meetings recorded births, marriages, deaths, certificates of removal (transfers between meetings), and disciplinary proceedings (disownments). Marriage certificates were signed by all attendees — making each one a roster of the local Quaker community at a point in time.
- **Record types:**
  - Birth records: entered in the monthly meeting birth register for the meeting at which the family held membership.
  - Marriage records: required approval of the monthly meeting before the ceremony; a certificate listing all witnesses was produced. Marrying outside the meeting could result in disownment.
  - Death records: recorded in meeting minutes or separate burial registers.
  - Certificates of Removal: issued when a family relocated from one monthly meeting to another; these name all family members, the origin meeting, and the destination meeting.
  - Disownment records: produced when a member was disciplined; they name the individual and state the reason (war service, oath-taking, marrying outside meeting, etc.).
  - Monthly meeting minutes: name members serving on committees, granting permission for travel, overseeing needy members, and approving marriages.

Here is the locality guide for Pittsburgh (Allegheny County), Pennsylvania during the steel-boom era (1865–1905):

---

## Pittsburgh Steel-Era Locality Guide

### Most Accessible Sources (Online, Indexed)

- **Federal Census Schedules (1870, 1880, 1900)** — All list occupation; fully indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry. Excellent for tracking mill workers and their families across decades.
- **Pennsylvania County Marriage Records (1885+)** — Available on FamilySearch.
- **Passenger Arrival Manifests** — Critical for immigrant workers arriving through East Coast ports; available on Ancestry and NARA.

---

### FamilySearch Collections (Images, Must Browse — No Name Index)

- **Probate Records** — 3.2 million images for Allegheny County; requires page-by-page browsing.
- **Death Records** — Similarly unindexed image sets; church burial registers are often more accessible for this era.

---

### Key Repositories for Industrial/Occupational Records

These survive only partially and require in-person or mail requests:

| Repository | What You'll Find |
|---|---|
| **Heinz History Center** (Pittsburgh) | Company employment files, city directories, local records |
| **Rivers of Steel Archives** | Steel industry company records, union history |
| **Historical Society of Western Pennsylvania** | Business records, ethnic community records, photographs |

**Specific industrial record types to request:**
- Company employment files (Carnegie Steel, U.S. Steel, etc.)
- Union membership rolls (Amalgamated Association of Iron, Steel, and Tin Workers)
- Pennsylvania factory inspector reports

---

### Critical Research Warnings

1. **No statewide birth or death registration** in Pennsylvania during the late 1800s. Church burial registers are the primary substitute — identify your ancestor's ethnic community and congregation first.

2. **Allegheny City was legally separate from Pittsburgh until 1907.** North Side residents before that year appear under "Allegheny City" in records, not Pittsburgh. Don't miss them by searching only under Pittsburgh.

---

### Recommended Research Sequence

A productive order for a named steel worker:
1. City directories (occupation, employer, address)
2. Census occupation columns (1880, 1900)
3. Naturalization records (many immigrant workers naturalized locally)
4. Ethnic-parish registers (baptism, marriage, burial)
5. Company employment files or union rolls at Heinz History Center / Rivers of Steel

---

If you'd like, the next step is to build a research plan tied to a specific person or question — just say the word and name the individual you're tracing.

# Locality Guide: Pittsburgh (Allegheny County), Pennsylvania (1865–1905)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Pittsburgh city established 1758; Allegheny County formed 1788 from Westmoreland and Washington Counties
- **County seat / administrative center:** Pittsburgh
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Commonwealth of Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** Population data could not be retrieved from the place_population tool for this query
- **Economy:** Steel production dominated — Carnegie Steel and other firms made Pittsburgh the center of America's steel industry; also glass, coal, and railroads (Wikipedia: Pittsburgh)
- **Ethnic composition:** Massive immigration of Irish, German, Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian workers into the steel mills (Wikipedia: Pittsburgh)
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic parishes (many organized along ethnic lines), Protestant denominations (Presbyterian, Methodist, Lutheran, Episcopal), and Eastern Orthodox congregations serving Eastern European immigrants
- **Key historical events:** Civil War (1861–1865) produced service and pension records; rapid industrialization 1870s–1900s generated company, union, and factory inspection records; former City of Allegheny (now Pittsburgh's North Side) was an independent municipality until annexed in 1907

## Boundary changes
- Allegheny County formed in 1788 from Westmoreland and Washington Counties; boundaries have been stable since
- The City of Allegheny (across the Allegheny River from Pittsburgh) was a separate incorporated city until 1907 when it was annexed into Pittsburgh; records before 1907 for residents of that area are under "Allegheny City," not Pittsburgh
- The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pittsburgh and Pennsylvania could not be retrieved during this survey (all returned generic content); neighboring counties could not be confirmed from the county home page

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The Pennsylvania Vital Records wiki page was not accessible during this survey — the FamilySearch Wiki redirected to a generic page. The Pennsylvania Death Certificates collection on FamilySearch begins in 1906 (collection 2255317), indicating statewide death registration did not begin until that year. No confirmed start date for birth or marriage civil registration can be cited from the pages fetched.
- **What exists:** County-level marriage records from 1885 (FamilySearch collection 1921317: Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950; 524,189 records, indexed + images). Civil marriages 1677–1950 also indexed (collection 1571957: 312,045 records). State death certificates begin 1906 (collection 2255317: 4,218,763 records, indexed + images) — this is just after the steel-boom decades.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch.org (online, free); originals at Pennsylvania State Archives and Allegheny County courthouse
- **Gaps:** No statewide birth or death registration during the late 1800s
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (baptisms, burials), federal census mortality schedules (1870, 1880), city directories

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic (ethnically organized — Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian, German parishes); mainline Protestant (Presbyterian, Methodist, Lutheran); Eastern Orthodox; Episcopal
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Where held:** Per the Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy page on the FamilySearch Wiki, Catholic parish registers are essential for immigrant families and are often the best source for family data for this period (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records). Check individual parish offices and diocesan archives; FamilySearch has microfilmed many Pennsylvania church records.
- **Language:** Records of immigrant parishes (Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian, German) may be in those languages, not English

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** 1870, 1880, 1900 (all fully indexed and online); the 1890 federal census was largely destroyed — only fragments survive
- **State/provincial census:** Pennsylvania did not hold a separate state census; no intercensal enumeration is available to fill the 1890 gap
- **Other enumerations:** Federal census schedules for 1870–1900 list each person's occupation, making them directly useful for tracing steel-industry workers (Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records)
- **Access:** 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses are indexed + images on Ancestry.com and FamilySearch

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, letters of administration, estate inventories, guardianships
- **Date range:** Allegheny County probate dates from 1788
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1999196 (Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994) — 3,200,560 images, 0 name-indexed records; must be browsed image by image with no search. Also available as 1 digitized browse-only volume (imageGroupNumber 008120441, 1180 images). Originals at Allegheny County courthouse.
- **Note on testate/intestate:** Testate ancestors (those with a will) appear in will books; intestate ancestors appear in administration and inventory series — search both.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Pennsylvania used metes and bounds (not rectangular survey)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Warrants and patents were issued by the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania; the Land and Property wiki page was not accessible during this survey
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents, mortgages, tax records
- **Where held:** Deeds at Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds; Pennsylvania State Archives holds warrants and patents

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865) — pension files run through the 1880s–1900s; Spanish-American War (1898)
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, draft registrations, bounty land warrants
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (archives.gov); Fold3.com (subscription) has Civil War records; Pennsylvania State Archives holds state adjutant-general records

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Allegheny Cemetery (est. 1844) and numerous ethnic-community church cemeteries
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) has indexed many Allegheny County burials
- **Physical records:** Sexton records vary by cemetery; church burial registers held at individual parishes

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Pittsburgh Post, Pittsburgh Gazette, and Pittsburgh Dispatch, among others, published during the steel boom
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (subscription); Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh microfilm collection; Pennsylvania State Library
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, labor news, mill-accident reports, and legal notices all valuable for industrial-worker research

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New York (Ellis Island; Castle Garden before 1892), Baltimore, and Philadelphia were the main arrival ports for Pittsburgh's immigrant mill workers
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests; declarations of intention; naturalization petitions; alien registrations
- **Where held:** Naturalization records at the Allegheny County courthouse and the National Archives at Philadelphia (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records). FamilySearch holds 1 digitized volume of Pennsylvania Naturalization Records (1790–1915; imageGroupNumber 008120443; 351 images, 15% name-indexed, English and German — the unindexed 85% must be browsed). NARA (archives.gov) and Ancestry.com hold passenger arrival manifests.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County property tax, personal property lists
- **Date range:** Allegheny County tax records date from the late 18th century
- **Where held:** Allegheny County; Pennsylvania State Archives
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists can substitute for the missing 1890 census

### Other record types (occupational and industrial)
- **Company employment records:** Fragmentary, but some survive at the Heinz History Center (Senator John Heinz History Center, Pittsburgh) and the Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area archives (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records)
- **Union membership lists:** Steelworkers' union records (Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers and predecessors); some held at the Historical Society of Western Pennsylvania
- **City directories:** Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh holds city directories from the 1810s — directories list residents by name, occupation, and address, a key annual source when census years are missing
- **State factory inspector reports:** Pennsylvania's Bureau of Industrial Statistics published annual factory inspection reports from the 1870s onward; these name mills, list accident victims, and document labor force size

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania, County Marriages 1885–1950 (524,189 records); Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (312,045 records); Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (198,765 records); Pennsylvania, Probate Records 1683–1994 (3.2M images, browse-only); Pennsylvania, Death Certificates 1906–1968 (4.2M records, indexed); 3 digitized volumes: Probate (browse-only), Death Records (browse-only), Naturalization Records (15% indexed) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection including 1870, 1880, 1900 | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records (Civil War service, pensions) | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | National Archives including passenger lists, naturalization | Free / In-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 3 digitized volumes at the Pennsylvania scope; the response confirms this is the complete set (complete: true). Collections_search returned 5 valid collections at the Pennsylvania level (1 synthetic test fixture excluded).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Heinz History Center (Pittsburgh) | Company employment records, industrial history, immigration collections | In-person; heinzhistorycenter.org |
| Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area | Steel-industry archival collections, mill records | In-person; riversofsteel.com |
| Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh | City directories (1810s onward), local history, newspaper microfilm | In-person; some digitized |
| Allegheny County Courthouse | Deeds, naturalization records, court files, probate originals | In-person |
| Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) | Factory inspector reports, state vital records post-1906, warrants and patents | In-person / mail |
| National Archives at Philadelphia (NARA) | Naturalization records, federal court files, passenger lists | In-person / mail / NARA online |
| Historical Society of Western Pennsylvania | Local records, manuscript collections, union records | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- Company employment records (fragmentary survivors at Heinz History Center and Rivers of Steel)
- Union membership lists (physical at Historical Society of Western Pennsylvania)
- City directories before the late 19th century (most must be used at Carnegie Library)
- State factory inspector reports (Pennsylvania Bureau of Industrial Statistics annual reports)
- Allegheny County probate originals (images on FamilySearch but no name index — browse image by image)
- Pre-1906 death records (no statewide civil registration — church burial registers in ethnic-community archives are the primary source)

## Known record losses
- The 1890 federal census was largely destroyed nationally. No tool result for this survey confirmed Pittsburgh-specific courthouse record losses. Substitute sources for the 1890 gap: city directories, 1891 county tax lists, church registers.

## Research tips
- The 1870, 1880, and 1900 federal census schedules all list occupation — searching the full enumeration district where your ancestor worked can identify co-workers and neighbors who may be relatives (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records).
- Naturalization records at the Allegheny County courthouse and National Archives at Philadelphia name country of origin and sometimes the home town — the most direct route to pinning immigrant origin for a steel-worker family (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records).
- Catholic parishes in Pittsburgh were organized by ethnicity, not geography — confirm which ethnic parish served your ancestor's community before searching registers; a Polish family and an Irish family on the same street belonged to entirely different parishes.
- The City of Allegheny was an independent municipality until annexed into Pittsburgh in 1907 — if your ancestor lived on the North Side, search under "Allegheny City" for all records before that date.
- City directories held at the Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh from the 1810s onward give annual name, occupation, and address — the best substitute for the missing 1890 census (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records).
- The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pittsburgh, Allegheny County, and Pennsylvania (all four sections) returned only generic fallback content during this survey; visit https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy directly for the full county research guide.
