- **Parent jurisdiction:** Commonwealth of Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** Population data could not be retrieved from the place_population tool for this query
- **Economy:** Steel production dominated — Carnegie Steel and other firms made Pittsburgh the center of America's steel industry; also glass, coal, and railroads (Wikipedia: Pittsburgh)
- **Ethnic composition:** Massive immigration of Irish, German, Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian workers into the steel mills (Wikipedia: Pittsburgh)
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic parishes (many organized along ethnic lines), Protestant denominations (Presbyterian, Methodist, Lutheran, Episcopal), and Eastern Orthodox congregations serving Eastern European immigrants
- **Key historical events:** Civil War (1861–1865) produced service and pension records; rapid industrialization 1870s–1900s generated company, union, and factory inspection records; former City of Allegheny (now Pittsburgh's North Side) was an independent municipality until annexed in 1907

## Boundary changes
- Allegheny County formed in 1788 from Westmoreland and Washington Counties; boundaries have been stable since
- The City of Allegheny (across the Allegheny River from Pittsburgh) was a separate incorporated city until 1907 when it was annexed into Pittsburgh; records before 1907 for residents of that area are under "Allegheny City," not Pittsburgh
- The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pittsburgh and Pennsylvania could not be retrieved during this survey (all returned generic content); neighboring counties could not be confirmed from the county home page

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The Pennsylvania Vital Records wiki page was not accessible during this survey — the FamilySearch Wiki redirected to a generic page. The Pennsylvania Death Certificates collection on FamilySearch begins in 1906 (collection 2255317), indicating statewide death registration did not begin until that year. No confirmed start date for birth or marriage civil registration can be cited from the pages fetched.
- **What exists:** County-level marriage records from 1885 (FamilySearch collection 1921317: Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950; 524,189 records, indexed + images). Civil marriages 1677–1950 also indexed (collection 1571957: 312,045 records). State death certificates begin 1906 (collection 2255317: 4,218,763 records, indexed + images) — this is just after the steel-boom decades.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch.org (online, free); originals at Pennsylvania State Archives and Allegheny County courthouse
- **Gaps:** No statewide birth or death registration during the late 1800s
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (baptisms, burials), federal census mortality schedules (1870, 1880), city directories

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic (ethnically organized — Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian, German parishes); mainline Protestant (Presbyterian, Methodist, Lutheran); Eastern Orthodox; Episcopal
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Where held:** Per the Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy page on the FamilySearch Wiki, Catholic parish registers are essential for immigrant families and are often the best source for family data for this period (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records). Check individual parish offices and diocesan archives; FamilySearch has microfilmed many Pennsylvania church records.
- **Language:** Records of immigrant parishes (Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian, German) may be in those languages, not English

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** 1870, 1880, 1900 (all fully indexed and online); the 1890 federal census was largely destroyed — only fragments survive
- **State/provincial census:** Pennsylvania did not hold a separate state census; no intercensal enumeration is available to fill the 1890 gap
- **Other enumerations:** Federal census schedules for 1870–1900 list each person's occupation, making them directly useful for tracing steel-industry workers (Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records)
- **Access:** 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses are indexed + images on Ancestry.com and FamilySearch

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, letters of administration, estate inventories, guardianships
- **Date range:** Allegheny County probate dates from 1788
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1999196 (Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994) — 3,200,560 images, 0 name-indexed records; must be browsed image by image with no search. Also available as 1 digitized browse-only volume (imageGroupNumber 008120441, 1180 images). Originals at Allegheny County courthouse.
- **Note on testate/intestate:** Testate ancestors (those with a will) appear in will books; intestate ancestors appear in administration and inventory series — search both.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Pennsylvania used metes and bounds (not rectangular survey)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Warrants and patents were issued by the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania; the Land and Property wiki page was not accessible during this survey
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents, mortgages, tax records
- **Where held:** Deeds at Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds; Pennsylvania State Archives holds warrants and patents

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865) — pension files run through the 1880s–1900s; Spanish-American War (1898)
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, draft registrations, bounty land warrants
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (archives.gov); Fold3.com (subscription) has Civil War records; Pennsylvania State Archives holds state adjutant-general records

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Allegheny Cemetery (est. 1844) and numerous ethnic-community church cemeteries
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) has indexed many Allegheny County burials
- **Physical records:** Sexton records vary by cemetery; church burial registers held at individual parishes

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Pittsburgh Post, Pittsburgh Gazette, and Pittsburgh Dispatch, among others, published during the steel boom
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (subscription); Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh microfilm collection; Pennsylvania State Library
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, labor news, mill-accident reports, and legal notices all valuable for industrial-worker research

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New York (Ellis Island; Castle Garden before 1892), Baltimore, and Philadelphia were the main arrival ports for Pittsburgh's immigrant mill workers
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests; declarations of intention; naturalization petitions; alien registrations
- **Where held:** Naturalization records at the Allegheny County courthouse and the National Archives at Philadelphia (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records). FamilySearch holds 1 digitized volume of Pennsylvania Naturalization Records (1790–1915; imageGroupNumber 008120443; 351 images, 15% name-indexed, English and German — the unindexed 85% must be browsed). NARA (archives.gov) and Ancestry.com hold passenger arrival manifests.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County property tax, personal property lists
- **Date range:** Allegheny County tax records date from the late 18th century
- **Where held:** Allegheny County; Pennsylvania State Archives
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists can substitute for the missing 1890 census

### Other record types (occupational and industrial)
- **Company employment records:** Fragmentary, but some survive at the Heinz History Center (Senator John Heinz History Center, Pittsburgh) and the Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area archives (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records)
- **Union membership lists:** Steelworkers' union records (Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers and predecessors); some held at the Historical Society of Western Pennsylvania
- **City directories:** Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh holds city directories from the 1810s — directories list residents by name, occupation, and address, a key annual source when census years are missing
- **State factory inspector reports:** Pennsylvania's Bureau of Industrial Statistics published annual factory inspection reports from the 1870s onward; these name mills, list accident victims, and document labor force size

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania, County Marriages 1885–1950 (524,189 records); Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (312,045 records); Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (198,765 records); Pennsylvania, Probate Records 1683–1994 (3.2M images, browse-only); Pennsylvania, Death Certificates 1906–1968 (4.2M records, indexed); 3 digitized volumes: Probate (browse-only), Death Records (browse-only), Naturalization Records (15% indexed) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection including 1870, 1880, 1900 | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records (Civil War service, pensions) | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | National Archives including passenger lists, naturalization | Free / In-person |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 3 digitized volumes at the Pennsylvania scope; the response confirms this is the complete set (complete: true). Collections_search returned 5 valid collections at the Pennsylvania level (1 synthetic test fixture excluded).

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Heinz History Center (Pittsburgh) | Company employment records, industrial history, immigration collections | In-person; heinzhistorycenter.org |
| Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area | Steel-industry archival collections, mill records | In-person; riversofsteel.com |
| Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh | City directories (1810s onward), local history, newspaper microfilm | In-person; some digitized |
| Allegheny County Courthouse | Deeds, naturalization records, court files, probate originals | In-person |
| Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) | Factory inspector reports, state vital records post-1906, warrants and patents | In-person / mail |
| National Archives at Philadelphia (NARA) | Naturalization records, federal court files, passenger lists | In-person / mail / NARA online |
| Historical Society of Western Pennsylvania | Local records, manuscript collections, union records | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- Company employment records (fragmentary survivors at Heinz History Center and Rivers of Steel)
- Union membership lists (physical at Historical Society of Western Pennsylvania)
- City directories before the late 19th century (most must be used at Carnegie Library)
- State factory inspector reports (Pennsylvania Bureau of Industrial Statistics annual reports)
- Allegheny County probate originals (images on FamilySearch but no name index — browse image by image)
- Pre-1906 death records (no statewide civil registration — church burial registers in ethnic-community archives are the primary source)

## Known record losses
- The 1890 federal census was largely destroyed nationally. No tool result for this survey confirmed Pittsburgh-specific courthouse record losses. Substitute sources for the 1890 gap: city directories, 1891 county tax lists, church registers.

## Research tips
- The 1870, 1880, and 1900 federal census schedules all list occupation — searching the full enumeration district where your ancestor worked can identify co-workers and neighbors who may be relatives (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records).
- Naturalization records at the Allegheny County courthouse and National Archives at Philadelphia name country of origin and sometimes the home town — the most direct route to pinning immigrant origin for a steel-worker family (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records).
- Catholic parishes in Pittsburgh were organized by ethnicity, not geography — confirm which ethnic parish served your ancestor's community before searching registers; a Polish family and an Irish family on the same street belonged to entirely different parishes.
- The City of Allegheny was an independent municipality until annexed into Pittsburgh in 1907 — if your ancestor lived on the North Side, search under "Allegheny City" for all records before that date.
- City directories held at the Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh from the 1810s onward give annual name, occupation, and address — the best substitute for the missing 1890 census (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records).
- The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pittsburgh, Allegheny County, and Pennsylvania (all four sections) returned only generic fallback content during this survey; visit https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy directly for the full county research guide.

output.text_response:
Locality survey written as `loc_001`.

---

Philadelphia in 1793 was a city of roughly 50,000 people without any civil registration system — no government office recorded births, marriages, or deaths. The epidemic killed approximately 5,000 people between August and November of that year, and the records that survive it fall into three overlapping groups:

**1. Church Burial Registers**
Especially Christ Church and Gloria Dei/Old Swedes'. These are the primary documentation of deaths during the epidemic.

**2. Published Account by Mathew Carey**
Carey published a list naming the dead — an invaluable resource for this specific event.

**3. Citizens' Committee Records**
Minutes and reports of the committee that managed epidemic relief, documenting affected families.

**Where records are held:**
- **Historical Society of Pennsylvania** and **Philadelphia City Archives** — hold the core manuscript sources; none are searchable in an online genealogy database
- **Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania** — compiled indexes to many Philadelphia church registers; this is the fastest route to identifying which register to examine in person

**Online / indexed sources:**
- **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting (Quaker) minutes, 1750–1800** — available on FamilySearch, but browse-only (no name index)
- **Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994** (FamilySearch collection 1999196) — over three million browse-only images; estates filed 1793–1794 are the highest-priority window, since epidemic deaths drove a surge in filings
- **1790 and 1800 federal censuses** — both free and indexed on FamilySearch; bracketing the epidemic lets you spot who disappeared from a household between enumerations

**Key caveat:** No civil registration existed in this period — births, marriages, and deaths were not recorded by any government office. Church registers are the primary substitute.

If you'd like a research plan built for a specific family or question in Philadelphia around 1793, let me know.

quirks: No Pennsylvania civil registration existed in 1793 — church records are the only vital records source for births, marriages, and deaths. Statewide death registration began in 1906.

The 1793 yellow fever epidemic killed approximately 5,000 residents (one-tenth of the population) between August and November 1793; Mathew Carey's published list of the dead is the nearest equivalent to a death register for that event.
Thousands of Philadelphians fled the city during the epidemic; records of persons in August–November 1793 may be found in neighboring counties or further afield.

The Committee appointed by citizens of Philadelphia left minutes and reports naming relief recipients and providers — held at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania and Philadelphia City Archives (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793).
Bush Hill hospital records (the epidemic's primary hospital) may survive at the Philadelphia City Archives but are not digitized.
Philadelphia Yearly Meeting (Quaker) minutes 1750–1800 are on FamilySearch (image group 001188322, 145 images) but are browse-only — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania (1793 — Yellow Fever Epidemic)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Philadelphia County established 1682 as one of the original three Pennsylvania counties under William Penn's charter
- **County seat / administrative center:** Philadelphia (city and county were coextensive in this period; full legal consolidation came with the Act of Consolidation in 1854)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Commonwealth of Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** Approximately 50,000 residents in 1793; approximately 5,000 died in the epidemic (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793). The place_population tool returned no data for this location and period.
- **Economy:** Major seaport and mercantile center; printing, manufacturing, and artisan trades
- **Ethnic composition:** English Quakers, German immigrants, Scots-Irish, free Black community, and recent arrivals from the Caribbean (a source of the epidemic's introduction)
- **Religious denominations:** Quakers (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting), Anglican/Episcopal (Christ Church), Swedish Lutheran (Gloria Dei/Old Swedes'), Presbyterian, German Reformed, Lutheran, Catholic, Methodist, and others
- **Key historical events:** 1793 yellow fever epidemic — approximately 5,000 deaths between August and November 1793; thousands more fled the city. Philadelphia was the U.S. national capital during this period. (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793)

## Boundary changes
- Philadelphia County was established in 1682 and remained territorially stable throughout the target period.
- The city of Philadelphia and Philadelphia County were coextensive geographically by the 1790s, though distinct legal entities until 1854.
- No boundary changes affected the county during 1793.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** None for 1793. Pennsylvania had no statewide civil registration during the epidemic. The FamilySearch Wiki states that "Philadelphia's church records are the primary source of vital information before Pennsylvania's statewide registration in 1906" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records).
- **What exists:** No civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths existed in Philadelphia in 1793. Church registers are the substitute.
- **Where held:** See Church Records below.
- **Gaps:** The entire 1793 period predates civil registration by over 100 years.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church burial registers — especially those of Christ Church and Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') — are the primary death record source. The published account by Mathew Carey listing names of the dead, the Committee's minutes, and Bush Hill hospital records are unique epidemic-era substitutes (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793).

### Church records (PRIMARY source for 1793)

---

Researching Chicago families around the Great Fire of 1871 is primarily a problem of **record loss**: the fire destroyed the Cook County Courthouse on October 8–10, 1871, taking with it deeds, birth and death registers, court records, and tax rolls.

**Where to look for pre-fire records (originals survived elsewhere):**
- **1860 and 1870 federal census** — originals held in Washington, so they survived
- **City directories from the 1840s onward** — held at the Newberry Library
- **Church baptism and burial registers** — many congregations kept their own records
- **Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance records** — now at the Chicago History Museum

**Post-fire reconstruction records:**
- Cook County began recording vital events anew after 1871; FamilySearch holds Cook County **birth, marriage, and death collections** each starting in 1871 (combined ~3 million records)
- The **Burnt Record Act of 1872** required property owners to re-register deeds — these re-registrations are themselves a valuable source
- FamilySearch holds two small digitized volumes of court and property records from the transition window; one is browse-only with no name index

**Two important caveats:**
1. The **1890 federal census does not exist** anywhere in the US — not just Chicago
2. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Illinois and Cook County were unreachable during this survey; visit [Cook County, Illinois Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy) directly before treating any absence as final

If you'd like to build a research plan for a specific family using this guide, that's the natural next step.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Chicago, Cook County, Illinois (1860–1890)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Chicago incorporated as a city in 1837; Cook County established 1831
- **County seat / administrative center:** Chicago
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Cook County, Illinois, United States
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the population tool for this query. Wikipedia notes more than 100,000 residents were left homeless by the 1871 fire alone, confirming a large and rapidly growing mid-19th-century city.
- **Economy:** Major railroad hub, meatpacking, lumber, and grain trade — industries that drew large immigrant labor populations
- **Ethnic composition:** Heavy Irish, German, and Scandinavian immigration in the 1850s–1870s; Polish and Eastern European influx followed in the 1880s onward
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (Archdiocese of Chicago), Lutheran, Methodist, Baptist, Episcopal, Presbyterian, and Jewish congregations
- **Key historical events:** The Great Chicago Fire, October 8–10, 1871, destroyed roughly 3.3 square miles of the city, killed approximately 300 people, left more than 100,000 residents homeless, and destroyed the Cook County Courthouse along with deeds, birth and death registers, court records, and tax rolls (Wikipedia: Great Chicago Fire, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire)

## Boundary changes
- Cook County boundaries have been stable throughout the target period.
- Pre-1831 records (territorial period) would fall under Illinois Territory jurisdiction.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** County-level vital registration (Cook County Clerk) began in 1871, the year of the Great Fire — pre-fire vital records at the county level were largely destroyed. The Illinois statewide registration date was not confirmed from tool results in this survey. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Cook County, Illinois Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories
- **What exists:** FamilySearch holds indexed collections — births 1871–1940 (1,450,000 records, ID 2024189), deaths 1871–1947 (980,000 records, ID 1913456), marriages 1871–1920 (620,000 records, ID 1756321) — all at county level and all post-fire.
- **Gaps:** Pre-1871 vital records were largely destroyed in the fire. No indexed collection for births, deaths, or marriages before 1871 exists in this survey's results.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (baptisms, marriages, burials) are the primary pre-fire vital substitute; city directories establish residence and approximate dates.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic, Lutheran, German Reformed, Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, Episcopal, and Jewish congregations active in Chicago during this period
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Where held:** FamilySearch indexes 285,000 records in "Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833–1925" (ID 1803978). The Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives holds Catholic parish registers. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories. Note that many church registers were destroyed in 1871; surviving and re-established registers post-1871 are the main source.
- **Language:** Some German Lutheran and German Catholic registers may be in German.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1860 and 1870 schedules survived the fire because originals were held in Washington — the 1870 census is especially critical as the last complete pre-fire snapshot of Chicago families. The 1880 and 1900 federal censuses also cover the period. The 1890 census was destroyed nationally — no schedule exists for Chicago or anywhere else.
- **State census:** Illinois conducted state censuses in 1865 and 1885, which can fill gaps around the fire period.
- **Other enumerations:** Mortality schedules (1850–1880) record deaths in the year preceding each census.
- **Access:** Federal census schedules are indexed and searchable on FamilySearch and Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/).

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, petitions
- **Date range:** Pre-fire probate records were largely destroyed when the Cook County Courthouse burned. Post-1871 records survive. FamilySearch holds a browse-only volume of reconstructed pre-fire Cook County Court Records (DGS 009982110, 38 images, 1865–1871, 0% indexed — must be browsed image by image with no name search).
- **Where held:** Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD) at Northeastern Illinois University for post-1871 Cook County records (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories); Cook County Circuit Court for original holdings.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Rectangular (federal land survey) — Illinois is a federal land state
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Bureau of Land Management General Land Office for original patents; Cook County Recorder of Deeds for subsequent transfers. The Illinois Vital Records and Land and Property wiki pages were not accessible during this survey (redirected to generic content).
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents, mortgages, tax records; crucially, Burnt Record Act (1872) reconstructed deed filings post-fire
- **Date range:** Post-fire re-recordings from 1872 onward; FamilySearch holds a partially indexed volume of Post-fire Property Re-recordings (DGS 009982111, 112 images, 1871–1880, 41% indexed — some records searchable by name, the remainder must be browsed).
- **Where held:** Cook County Recorder of Deeds; the Chicago History Museum holds the Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance collection, a vital substitute for pre-fire property ownership records. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865) falls within the target period; veterans active in Chicago through the 1880s
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, draft registrations (Civil War draft), bounty land warrants, Grand Army of the Republic (GAR) records
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) holds service records and pension files; Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) provides online access to many Civil War records; Illinois State Archives holds adjutant general records.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Graceland Cemetery (incorporated 1860) and Rosehill Cemetery (1859) are major Chicago cemeteries from the period; denominational cemeteries also operated.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) provides searchable memorials for Chicago-area burials.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records held by individual cemeteries; some may be microfilmed.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Chicago Tribune (founded 1847, continuous through the period); Chicago Times; Illinois Staats-Zeitung (German-language). Papers reported fire victims, missing persons, and survivors in October–November 1871.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) provides digitized historical papers; the Newberry Library holds extensive newspaper holdings for Chicago.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, survivor lists, legal notices, and fire-victim accounts; fire-period coverage (October 1871) is especially valuable for identifying affected families.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Chicago is inland; immigrants typically arrived via New York, Baltimore, New Orleans, or Quebec, then traveled by rail or water to Chicago.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests (at ports of entry), declarations of intention and naturalization petitions (filed at Cook County Circuit Court or federal courts in Chicago), alien registrations. Passenger lists record every person aboard including infants — examine the full manifest when researching a traveling family.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) holds passenger lists and post-1906 naturalization records; pre-1906 naturalization records may be in Cook County Circuit Court files at IRAD. Ancestry indexes major passenger list series.
- **Content note:** Pre-1906 naturalizations can appear in any court of record; search Cook County Circuit Court naturalization records as well as federal court records.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Property tax rolls, personal property lists
- **Date range:** Pre-fire tax rolls largely destroyed in 1871; post-fire records survive at the county level.
- **Where held:** Cook County; some records at IRAD.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists substitute for missing census years; city directories and the 1865/1885 Illinois state censuses fill the 1860–1870 and 1880–1890 intercensal gaps.

### Other record types
- **City directories:** Chicago city directories from the 1840s onward survived the fire and are held at the Newberry Library — a primary substitute for census years and for establishing residence and occupation. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire
- **Insurance/title records:** The Chicago Title and Trust Company collection at the Chicago History Museum documents pre-fire property ownership and is a key substitute for destroyed deed records. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire
- **Relief records:** The Chicago Relief and Aid Society compiled lists of disaster victims receiving aid after the 1871 fire — these may identify families and their circumstances; held at the Chicago History Museum.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Church Records 1833–1925 (285,000); Birth Certs 1871–1940 (1,450,000); Death Records 1871–1947 (980,000); Marriage Records 1871–1920 (620,000); 2 digitized volumes of court/property records (DGS 009982110, 009982111) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records (Civil War service, pension, draft) — https://www.fold3.com/ | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers including Chicago Tribune — https://www.newspapers.com/ | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery memorials — https://www.findagrave.com/ | Free |
| NARA | National Archives finding aids; some records online — https://www.archives.gov/ | Free/Varies |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 2 total matching volumes for Chicago in this period; both are detailed above and represent the complete result set for 1855–1895.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Newberry Library, Chicago | City directories (1840s+), maps, manuscripts, newspapers | In-person; some materials online |
| Chicago History Museum | Insurance records (Chicago Title and Trust Co.), photographs, personal papers, relief records | In-person research center |
| IRAD at Northeastern Illinois University | Cook County records post-1871, Circuit Court naturalization files | In-person / contact for access |
| Archdiocese of Chicago, Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives | Catholic parish registers | Contact archives |
| Cook County Clerk's Office | Vital records from 1871 onward | In-person / written request |
| Illinois State Archives, Springfield | State-level records, adjutant general military records | In-person / some online |
| NARA Chicago Field Office | Federal court and naturalization records | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- Pre-fire (pre-1871) vital records: largely destroyed; surviving church registers are not all digitized
- Pre-fire deed and property records: destroyed; Burnt Record Act reconstructions (1872) are partially digitized but the browse-only pre-fire court records volume (DGS 009982110) is not name-indexed
- Chicago Relief and Aid Society relief lists (1871): held at the Chicago History Museum; not known to be digitized from this survey
- Full run of Cook County Circuit Court naturalization records: held at IRAD; not fully digitized
- Sexton and burial records for individual cemeteries: physical at each cemetery

## Known record losses
The Great Chicago Fire (October 8–10, 1871) destroyed the Cook County Courthouse, which housed deeds, birth and death registers, court records, and tax rolls. Sources: Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire); FamilySearch Wiki, Cook County Genealogy (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire). The loss was catastrophic for pre-1871 genealogical documentation. Many church registers also burned. The 1890 federal census was destroyed nationally. Post-fire reconstructed records — Burnt Record Act deeds, re-established church registers, insurance company records — partially compensate.

## Research tips
- Start with the 1870 federal census — it is the last complete pre-fire snapshot of Chicago families and survived because originals were held in Washington, not at the Cook County Courthouse. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire
- Treat 1871 as a research split, not a dead end: before the fire, work backward from church records and city directories; from 1871 onward, use county vital records, Burnt Record Act deeds, and re-established church registers as one continuous trail.
- City directories are essential between federal censuses. The Newberry Library holds directories from the 1840s onward; they establish residence, occupation, and neighbors for years without a census. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire
- Search the Chicago History Museum's Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance records for pre-fire property ownership — these are a key substitute for destroyed deed records. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire
- For pre-1906 naturalization, search Cook County Circuit Court records at IRAD as well as federal court records — naturalizations could be filed in any court of record.
- Check the FamilySearch Church Records collection (ID 1803978, 285,000 records, 1833–1925) for baptisms and marriages on both sides of 1871 — parishes that survived or were re-established continued their registers, providing vital evidence the county clerk's records cannot give for pre-1871 events.

The 1890 federal census was destroyed nationally — no 1890 schedule exists for Chicago or anywhere in the United States. The 1885 Illinois state census and city directories partially fill this gap.
added.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Chicago, Cook County, Illinois (1860–1890)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Chicago incorporated as a city in 1837; Cook County established 1831
- **County seat / administrative center:** Chicago
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Cook County, Illinois, United States
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the population tool for this query. Wikipedia notes more than 100,000 residents were left homeless by the 1871 fire alone, confirming a large and rapidly growing mid-19th-century city.
- **Economy:** Major railroad hub, meatpacking, lumber, and grain trade — industries that drew large immigrant labor populations
- **Ethnic composition:** Heavy Irish, German, and Scandinavian immigration in the 1850s–1870s; Polish and Eastern European influx followed in the 1880s onward
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (Archdiocese of Chicago), Lutheran, Methodist, Baptist, Episcopal, Presbyterian, and Jewish congregations
- **Key historical events:** The Great Chicago Fire, October 8–10, 1871, destroyed roughly 3.3 square miles of the city, killed approximately 300 people, left more than 100,000 residents homeless, and destroyed the Cook County Courthouse along with deeds, birth and death registers, court records, and tax rolls (Wikipedia: Great Chicago Fire, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire)

## Boundary changes
- Cook County boundaries have been stable throughout the target period.
- Pre-1831 records (territorial period) would fall under Illinois Territory jurisdiction.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** County-level vital registration (Cook County Clerk) began in 1871, the year of the Great Fire — pre-fire vital records at the county level were largely destroyed. The Illinois statewide registration date was not confirmed from tool results in this survey. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Cook County, Illinois Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories
- **What exists:** FamilySearch holds indexed collections — births 1871–1940 (1,450,000 records, ID 2024189), deaths 1871–1947 (980,000 records, ID 1913456), marriages 1871–1920 (620,000 records, ID 1756321) — all at county level and all post-fire.
- **Gaps:** Pre-1871 vital records were largely destroyed in the fire. No indexed collection for births, deaths, or marriages before 1871 exists in this survey's results.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (baptisms, marriages, burials) are the primary pre-fire vital substitute; city directories establish residence and approximate dates.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic, Lutheran, German Reformed, Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, Episcopal, and Jewish congregations active in Chicago during this period
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Where held:** FamilySearch indexes 285,000 records in "Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833–1925" (ID 1803978). The Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives holds Catholic parish registers. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories. Note that many church registers were destroyed in 1871; surviving and re-established registers post-1871 are the main source.
- **Language:** Some German Lutheran and German Catholic registers may be in German.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1860 and 1870 schedules survived the fire because originals were held in Washington — the 1870 census is especially critical as the last complete pre-fire snapshot of Chicago families. The 1880 and 1900 federal censuses also cover the period. The 1890 census was destroyed nationally — no schedule exists for Chicago or anywhere else.
- **State census:** Illinois conducted state censuses in 1865 and 1885, which can fill gaps around the fire period.
- **Other enumerations:** Mortality schedules (1850–1880) record deaths in the year preceding each census.
- **Access:** Federal census schedules are indexed and searchable on FamilySearch and Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/).

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, petitions
- **Date range:** Pre-fire probate records were largely destroyed when the Cook County Courthouse burned. Post-1871 records survive. FamilySearch holds a browse-only volume of reconstructed pre-fire Cook County Court Records (DGS 009982110, 38 images, 1865–1871, 0% indexed — must be browsed image by image with no name search).
- **Where held:** Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD) at Northeastern Illinois University for post-1871 Cook County records (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories); Cook County Circuit Court for original holdings.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Rectangular (federal land survey) — Illinois is a federal land state
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Bureau of Land Management General Land Office for original patents; Cook County Recorder of Deeds for subsequent transfers. The Illinois Vital Records and Land and Property wiki pages were not accessible during this survey (redirected to generic content).
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents, mortgages, tax records; crucially, Burnt Record Act (1872) reconstructed deed filings post-fire
- **Date range:** Post-fire re-recordings from 1872 onward; FamilySearch holds a partially indexed volume of Post-fire Property Re-recordings (DGS 009982111, 112 images, 1871–1880, 41% indexed — some records searchable by name, the remainder must be browsed).
- **Where held:** Cook County Recorder of Deeds; the Chicago History Museum holds the Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance collection, a vital substitute for pre-fire property ownership records. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865) falls within the target period; veterans active in Chicago through the 1880s
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, draft registrations (Civil War draft), bounty land warrants, Grand Army of the Republic (GAR) records
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) holds service records and pension files; Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) provides online access to many Civil War records; Illinois State Archives holds adjutant general records.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Graceland Cemetery (incorporated 1860) and Rosehill Cemetery (1859) are major Chicago cemeteries from the period; denominational cemeteries also operated.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) provides searchable memorials for Chicago-area burials.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records held by individual cemeteries; some may be microfilmed.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Chicago Tribune (founded 1847, continuous through the period); Chicago Times; Illinois Staats-Zeitung (German-language). Papers reported fire victims, missing persons, and survivors in October–November 1871.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) provides digitized historical papers; the Newberry Library holds extensive newspaper holdings for Chicago.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, survivor lists, legal notices, and fire-victim accounts; fire-period coverage (October 1871) is especially valuable for identifying affected families.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Chicago is inland; immigrants typically arrived via New York, Baltimore, New Orleans, or Quebec, then traveled by rail or water to Chicago.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests (at ports of entry), declarations of intention and naturalization petitions (filed at Cook County Circuit Court or federal courts in Chicago), alien registrations. Passenger lists record every person aboard including infants — examine the full manifest when researching a traveling family.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) holds passenger lists and post-1906 naturalization records; pre-1906 naturalization records may be in Cook County Circuit Court files at IRAD. Ancestry indexes major passenger list series.
- **Content note:** Pre-1906 naturalizations can appear in any court of record; search Cook County Circuit Court naturalization records as well as federal court records.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Property tax rolls, personal property lists
- **Date range:** Pre-fire tax rolls largely destroyed in 1871; post-fire records survive at the county level.
- **Where held:** Cook County; some records at IRAD.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists substitute for missing census years; city directories and the 1865/1885 Illinois state censuses fill the 1860–1870 and 1880–1890 intercensal gaps.

### Other record types
- **City directories:** Chicago city directories from the 1840s onward survived the fire and are held at the Newberry Library — a primary substitute for census years and for establishing residence and occupation. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire
- **Insurance/title records:** The Chicago Title and Trust Company collection at the Chicago History Museum documents pre-fire property ownership and is a key substitute for destroyed deed records. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire
- **Relief records:** The Chicago Relief and Aid Society compiled lists of disaster victims receiving aid after the 1871 fire — these may identify families and their circumstances; held at the Chicago History Museum.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Church Records 1833–1925 (285,000); Birth Certs 1871–1940 (1,450,000); Death Records 1871–1947 (980,000); Marriage Records 1871–1920 (620,000); 2 digitized volumes of court/property records (DGS 009982110, 009982111) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records (Civil War service, pension, draft) — https://www.fold3.com/ | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers including Chicago Tribune — https://www.newspapers.com/ | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery memorials — https://www.findagrave.com/ | Free |
| NARA | National Archives finding aids; some records online — https://www.archives.gov/ | Free/Varies |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 2 total matching volumes for Chicago in this period; both are detailed above and represent the complete result set for 1855–1895.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Newberry Library, Chicago | City directories (1840s+), maps, manuscripts, newspapers | In-person; some materials online |
| Chicago History Museum | Insurance records (Chicago Title and Trust Co.), photographs, personal papers, relief records | In-person research center |
| IRAD at Northeastern Illinois University | Cook County records post-1871, Circuit Court naturalization files | In-person / contact for access |
| Archdiocese of Chicago, Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives | Catholic parish registers | Contact archives |
| Cook County Clerk's Office | Vital records from 1871 onward | In-person / written request |
| Illinois State Archives, Springfield | State-level records, adjutant general military records | In-person / some online |
| NARA Chicago Field Office | Federal court and naturalization records | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- Pre-fire (pre-1871) vital records: largely destroyed; surviving church registers are not all digitized
- Pre-fire deed and property records: destroyed; Burnt Record Act reconstructions (1872) are partially digitized but the browse-only pre-fire court records volume (DGS 009982110) is not name-indexed
- Chicago Relief and Aid Society relief lists (1871): held at the Chicago History Museum; not known to be digitized from this survey
- Full run of Cook County Circuit Court naturalization records: held at IRAD; not fully digitized
- Sexton and burial records for individual cemeteries: physical at each cemetery

## Known record losses
The Great Chicago Fire (October 8–10, 1871) destroyed the Cook County Courthouse, which housed deeds, birth and death registers, court records, and tax rolls. Sources: Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire); FamilySearch Wiki, Cook County Genealogy (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire). The loss was catastrophic for pre-1871 genealogical documentation. Many church registers also burned. The 1890 federal census was destroyed nationally. Post-fire reconstructed records — Burnt Record Act deeds, re-established church registers, insurance company records — partially compensate.

## Research tips
- Start with the 1870 federal census — it is the last complete pre-fire snapshot of Chicago families and survived because originals were held in Washington, not at the Cook County Courthouse. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire
- Treat 1871 as a research split, not a dead end: before the fire, work backward from church records and city directories; from 1871 onward, use county vital records, Burnt Record Act deeds, and re-established church registers as one continuous trail.
- City directories are essential between federal censuses. The Newberry Library holds directories from the 1840s onward; they establish residence, occupation, and neighbors for years without a census. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire
- Search the Chicago History Museum's Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance records for pre-fire property ownership — these are a key substitute for destroyed deed records. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire
- For pre-1906 naturalization, search Cook County Circuit Court records at IRAD as well as federal court records — naturalizations could be filed in any court of record.
- Check the FamilySearch Church Records collection (ID 1803978, 285,000 records, 1833–1925) for baptisms and marriages on both sides of 1871 — parishes that survived or were re-established continued their registers, providing vital evidence the county clerk's records cannot give for pre-1871 events.

Locality guide written as **loc_001**.

---

The survey covers Louisiana from roughly 1699 through 1803 — the full French and early Spanish colonial period, ending at the Louisiana Purchase. The most important thing to understand about this era is that no civil registration existed: **the Catholic Church kept all births (baptisms), marriages, and burials**, and those registers are your vital records. FamilySearch has an indexed, searchable collection ("Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925") that is the natural first stop.

Beyond the church, the **Superior Council** — the colonial civil and legal body — produced contracts, estate inventories, land concessions, and court proceedings. FamilySearch holds a small browse-only digitized volume of those records (1699–1769), and the **Louisiana Historical Center in New Orleans** holds the broader collection.

Colonial census rolls (*recensements*) and administrative correspondence live in France at the **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM)** and are not in any indexed online database.

**Two chief obstacles to be aware of:**

1. **Language** — All colonial records are in French or Spanish, with no name-indexing in the original volumes.
2. **The 1762 territorial split** — France gave land west of the Mississippi to Spain but handed the east side to Britain. Families east of the river after 1762 must be traced through British West Florida records rather than Spanish Louisiana ones.

---

The next step is to identify the specific individual or family and parish you are researching so a focused research plan can be built from this survey.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Louisiana, United States — French Colonial Period (1700–1803)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **Formed:** French colony established ca. 1682/1699; New Orleans founded 1718; colony operated under French rule until 1762 (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Louisiana)
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans (founded 1718)
- **Colonial periods:** French colony 1699–1762; ceded to Spain by Treaty of Fontainebleau (1762); Spanish colony 1769–1803; Louisiana Purchase 1803
- **Population during period:** Population data were not returned by tools for this period
- **Economy:** Fur trade, indigo and tobacco plantations; enslaved African labor central to the plantation economy
- **Ethnic composition:** French settlers, Acadian refugees (from 1755), German Coast settlers, enslaved Africans, Native American nations; Spanish administrators and settlers after 1762
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic Church exclusively recognized under both French and Spanish rule; Code Noir (1724) required the baptism of all enslaved persons
- **Key historical events:** 1724 Code Noir; 1762 Treaty of Fontainebleau (split territory between Spain and Britain); 1755–1760s Acadian deportation and resettlement; 1803 Louisiana Purchase

## Boundary Changes
- Under the 1762 Treaty of Fontainebleau, France ceded land **west** of the Mississippi River to Spain and the **eastern** portion to Britain (British West Florida). This is a geographic split: which colonial power holds a family's records depends on exactly which side of the Mississippi they lived on. Do not assume all 1762–1803 Louisiana records are under Spanish administration — search British West Florida records for families east of the river.
- Spain formally administered the colony from 1769; records shift to Spanish from that point though French continued in church registers.
- Louisiana became a U.S. territory in 1803 and a state in 1812.
- Louisiana uses civil **parishes** (not counties), dating from its Catholic colonial heritage. Records are filed at the parish level.

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **Start date:** No civil registration existed in Louisiana during the 1700s. The Louisiana Vital Records FamilySearch wiki page was not reachable (redirected to generic content), so no statewide start year can be stated from tools. Catholic church sacramental registers ARE the functional vital records for this period.
- **What exists:** No civil births, marriages, or deaths were registered by any governmental authority during the colonial period.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic sacramental registers from 1720 — see Church Records below.

### Church Records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic Church — the only legally recognized church under both French and Spanish colonial rule. The Code Noir (1724) required the baptism of all enslaved persons, making Catholic registers the primary source for enslaved individuals as well as free settlers. (Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Louisiana)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials (sacramental registers)
- **FamilySearch holdings:**

# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (1860-1910)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1811 (from place_search, dateRange +1811/)
- **County seat:** Pottsville
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** No population data returned by tools for this query.
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining; expanded dramatically in the 1820s-1870s drawing mass immigration (Wikipedia: Coal Region)
- **Ethnic composition:** Irish, Welsh, German, Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, Italian, and Ukrainian immigrants (Wikipedia: Coal Region)
- **Religious denominations:** Irish Catholic, Welsh Congregational, Polish Catholic, Lithuanian Catholic ethnic parishes, among others (FamilySearch Wiki: Pennsylvania Occupational Records, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining)
- **Key historical events:** Rapid industrial expansion drove mass immigration; Pennsylvania Mine Inspector system established 1870; United Mine Workers of America founded 1890

## Boundary changes
- Schuylkill County formed 1811 and appears stable through the target period (place_search_all returned no additional historical jurisdictions).
- Lackawanna County, to the north, is a neighboring coal county whose colliery payroll ledgers in the volume_search begin in 1878 -- suggesting formation around that date, though the specific split from Luzerne County was not confirmed by a fetched wiki page.

## FamilySearch Wiki coverage note
All four wiki_place_page sections (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) and all wiki_read calls to the Pennsylvania Vital Records, Schuylkill County, and Pennsylvania Occupational Records pages returned only a generic fallback page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Research_Guide), not jurisdiction-specific content. Claims below come from wiki_search results, collections_search, volume_search, Wikipedia, and external_links_search only. Visit the FamilySearch Wiki directly for Pennsylvania and Schuylkill County pages to supplement this guide.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki Pennsylvania_Vital_Records page returned only generic content -- specific registration dates cannot be confirmed from tool results. The Pennsylvania Death Certificates collection (id 2255317) covers 1906-1968, indicating statewide death registration began around 1906 -- after the late 1800s target window.
- **What exists:** Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885-1950 (collection 1921317): 524,189 records indexed, 312,045 images. Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677-1950 (collection 1571957): 312,045 records. Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700-1900 (collection 1502909): 198,765 records (no images). Death certificates begin only in 1906 (collection 2255317, 4,218,763 indexed records) -- outside the late 1800s window.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (online, indexed). County courthouse records for the original certificates.
- **Gaps:** No statewide birth or death registration in the late 1800s. For the target period, births and deaths were recorded only by churches and sometimes by local undertakers.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptismal, marriage, and burial registers are the primary alternative. Mine Inspector fatal accident reports (from 1870) also document deaths of miners.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Irish Catholic, Welsh Congregational, Polish Catholic, Lithuanian Catholic ethnic parishes confirmed by wiki_search (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining). Other Protestant denominations (Methodist, Presbyterian, Episcopal) also served the region.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations. Wiki_search states these registers "often contain the most detailed family data" for mining communities.
- **Where held:** Individual parishes hold originals; FamilySearch has microfilmed many Pennsylvania church registers. A collection labeled 'Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records (synthetic test fixture)' appeared in collections_search output but is a test artifact and should not be cited.
- **Language:** Irish and Welsh records in English; Polish and Lithuanian registers often in Latin or the respective native language.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Available 1870, 1880, 1900 (1890 mostly destroyed). Lists occupation as 'miner', useful for identifying mining families (wiki_search). The 1880 census includes a Defective, Dependent, and Delinquent schedule relevant for accident survivors.
- **Mortality schedules:** 1850-1885 record deaths in the year preceding the census -- relevant for miners who died before formal death certificates.
- **State census:** No Pennsylvania state census is confirmed by tool results for this period.
- **Access:** Federal census fully indexed on Ancestry.com (subscription) and FamilySearch (free). Mortality schedules on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### Occupational records (critical for coal mining families)
- **Mine Worker Employment Cards, Schuylkill County, 1870-1900** (volume 002240015): 410 images, 95% name-indexed, full-text searchable. Digitization level: **indexed + images**.
- **Mine Accident Reports, Luzerne County, 1870-1895** (volume 002240016): 287 images, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable. Digitization level: **browse-only images** (must be browsed image by image).
- **Colliery Payroll Ledgers, Lackawanna County, 1878-1900** (volume 002240017): 199 images, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable. Digitization level: **browse-only images**.
- **Pennsylvania State Mine Inspector reports** (from 1870): List fatal accidents with names, ages, nationalities, and cause of death. At the Pennsylvania State Archives. (wiki_search, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining)
- **UMWA membership rolls and grievance files** (from 1890): At relevant union archives. (wiki_search, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources)
- **Coverage note:** 23 digitized volumes match the coal region for 1860-1910 in this search; only the 3 volumes above were detailed (first page). The remaining 20 volumes were not examined in this survey.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, guardianship files, letters of administration, court minute books.
- **Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994** (collection 1999196): 3,200,560 images, 0 indexed records. Digitization level: **browse-only images** (must be browsed without name index).
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County Courthouse (originals); FamilySearch (browse-only digital images).
- **Court minute books** name people involved in county business, road maintenance, poor relief, and civil suits -- valuable for people not found in other records.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is a state-land state, not a public-land state; the BLM GLO website does not apply).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The FamilySearch Wiki Pennsylvania_Land_and_Property page was not retrieved (returned generic content only) -- the specific office holding original grants cannot be confirmed from tool results. County deed books are held at the Schuylkill County Recorder of Deeds.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, tax records.
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County Recorder of Deeds (originals); Pennsylvania State Archives (some early records).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861-1865), Spanish-American War (1898). Miners served in large numbers.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, draft registrations, bounty land warrants.
- **Where held:** NARA (service records and pensions); Fold3 (online, subscription) for digitized military records.
- **Content note:** Civil War pension files often contain family affidavits naming spouses, children, and places of birth -- valuable for immigrant miners who naturalized after the war.

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) is the primary online index for Schuylkill County cemeteries (external_links_search result).
- **Physical records:** Individual cemetery sexton records vary by institution; local historical societies may hold transcriptions.

### Newspaper records
- **Online access:** Newspapers.com (newspapers.com, subscription) covers historical Pennsylvania newspapers (external_links_search result).
- **Content value:** Mining-town papers routinely published accident and fatality notices, obituaries, marriage announcements, and legal notices. These are especially valuable for the pre-death-certificate period.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia and New York were the primary ports of entry for coal region immigrants (wiki_search, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources).
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests, declarations of intention, naturalization petitions, certificates of citizenship. Pre-1906 naturalizations filed in any court of record -- county Court of Common Pleas, orphans' court, or U.S. district court.
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County naturalization records 1840s-1906 at Pennsylvania State Archives (wiki_search). NARA holds passenger lists (archives.gov).
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) list every person aboard including infants and children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest for all family members when researching an immigrant family.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County property tax, personal property tax, poll tax.
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County; Pennsylvania State Archives holds some series.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists can fill gaps left by the missing 1890 federal census and by the absence of vital registration before 1906.

### Other record types
- **Occupational/union records:** UMWA membership rolls and grievance files from 1890 (wiki_search); company employment records (payrolls, accident reports) survive fragmentarily at Pennsylvania State Archives and local historical societies.
- **School records:** May exist at local school district or township level.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for Schuylkill County | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | Mine Worker Employment Cards 1870-1900 (indexed+images, vol. 002240015); Probate Records 1683-1994 (browse-only, 3.2M images); County Marriages 1885-1950 (indexed); Civil Marriages 1677-1950 (indexed); Compiled Marriages 1700-1900 | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection (indexed+images, 1870-1910) | Subscription |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | Military Records | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Pennsylvania newspapers | Subscription |
| FindAGrave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery records | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Passenger lists, federal naturalization records | Free (some) |

**Coverage of this survey:** 23 digitized volumes match the coal region for 1860-1910 in the FamilySearch volume search; only the 3 volumes detailed above were examined (first page of results). The remaining volumes were not reviewed in this survey.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) | Schuylkill County naturalization records 1840s-1906; Mine Inspector reports from 1870; some county records | In-person or online request via phmc.pa.gov |
| Schuylkill County Courthouse (Pottsville) | Original deeds, court records, probate files | In-person or mail |
| Historical Society of Schuylkill County | Local mining collections, local history materials | In-person (Pottsville) |
| Anthracite Heritage Museum (Scranton) | Mining community records for the coal region | In-person |
| Local ethnic parishes | Original baptismal, marriage, and burial registers | Contact individual parish |

## Records NOT online
- Pennsylvania State Mine Inspector reports (1870+): Physical at Pennsylvania State Archives; not fully digitized.
- UMWA membership rolls and grievance files: Physical at relevant union archives.
- Most ethnic parish registers: Many not yet digitized; must contact individual parishes or diocesan archives.
- Mine accident reports for Schuylkill County specifically: Only Luzerne County Mine Accident Reports appeared in volume_search; Schuylkill equivalents were not found in this survey.
- County tax records: Held at the county level; not confirmed online.

## Known record losses
No specific record losses for Schuylkill County were stated in any tool result retrieved during this survey. An empty search result is a coverage gap, not a confirmed loss. Contact the Schuylkill County Courthouse and Historical Society of Schuylkill County to confirm the status of any series before concluding it does not exist.

## Research tips
- Pennsylvania State Mine Inspector reports (from 1870) name accident victims with age and nationality -- a primary source for miners who died before death certificates were required. At the Pennsylvania State Archives. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining)
- Identify the ancestor's ethnic community first, then search for the matching ethnic parish (Irish, Welsh, Polish, Lithuanian). Ethnic parish registers are described as holding the most detailed family data for coal mining communities. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining)
- Naturalization records for Schuylkill County (1840s-1906) are at the Pennsylvania State Archives -- a critical source for immigrant miners who naturalized before 1906. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources)
- Federal census records 1870-1900 list occupation as 'miner', useful for locating families between vital records events. Cross-reference census mortality schedules (1850-1885) for miners who died in the year preceding each census.
- Pre-1906 naturalizations appear in any court of record -- search county court minute books, not just dedicated naturalization indexes, since many pre-1906 naturalizations are only in the minutes.
- 23 digitized volumes match the coal region for 1860-1910 in FamilySearch; only 3 were reviewed. Run a fresh volume_search for Schuylkill County to identify all available volumes before concluding a record type is absent.
