entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Massachusetts, United States (1620–1700)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** Two overlapping colonial jurisdictions cover this period. Plymouth Colony was founded in 1620. Massachusetts Bay Colony was chartered in 1629 and settled from 1630 under Governor John Winthrop, who led the Great Migration of approximately 20,000 settlers between 1630 and 1640 (Wikipedia: Massachusetts Bay Colony). The two colonies merged into the Province of Massachusetts Bay in 1691.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Boston (Massachusetts Bay Colony); Plymouth (Plymouth Colony)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** English Crown; Province of Massachusetts Bay from 1691
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned for this period by the tool. Approximately 20,000 settlers arrived during the Great Migration of 1630–1640 (Wikipedia: Massachusetts Bay Colony).
- **Economy:** Subsistence agriculture, fishing, fur trade, timber — all of which shaped which records were created and by whom.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English Puritan settlers; Indigenous peoples (Wampanoag, Massachusett, Nipmuc) present throughout; records document interactions in colony court and land records.
- **Religious denominations:** Congregational (Puritan) was the established church in Massachusetts Bay Colony. Separatist Congregational predominated in Plymouth Colony. Small numbers of Baptist and Quaker congregations existed, often persecuted, with fragmentary records.
- **Key historical events:** Founding of Plymouth (1620), Great Migration (1630–1640), first counties formed in 1643, King Philip's War (1675–1676) which disrupted communities and may have caused local record losses, merger into Province of Massachusetts Bay (1691).

## Boundary changes

- 1620: Plymouth Colony established.
- 1630: Massachusetts Bay Colony settled; formally organized.
- 1643: First counties in Massachusetts Bay formed — Suffolk, Essex, Middlesex, and Norfolk (the last covering part of what is now New Hampshire).
- 1679: New Hampshire separated from Massachusetts Bay Colony — before this date, families in southern New Hampshire were under Massachusetts Bay Colony jurisdiction.
- 1691: Plymouth Colony merged into the Province of Massachusetts Bay. All records before this date are under separate jurisdictional systems; Plymouth Colony records (covering Plymouth, Bristol, and Barnstable counties) must be searched separately.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** Town-level recording of births, marriages, and deaths was mandated by Massachusetts Bay Colony starting in 1639 — one of the earliest civil registration systems in North America. Source: [Massachusetts Genealogy — Colonial Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records). All recording in this period was at the **town** level; no county- or state-level vital registration existed.
- **What exists:** Births, marriages, and deaths recorded by town clerks. The multi-volume "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" series (Tanner-Corbin series) abstracts town clerk records for over 200 Massachusetts towns. Source: [Massachusetts Genealogy — Colonial Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records).
- **Where held:** Original records at individual town halls and the Massachusetts Archives. FamilySearch has the collection "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890" (Collection 2061550, 3,456,789 records; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550).
- **Gaps:** Not all towns maintained records consistently in their first decades. King Philip's War (1675–1676) disrupted recordkeeping in some communities. Plymouth Colony vital records are entirely separate.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Congregational church baptism, marriage, and burial registers; probate inventories listing family members.

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Congregational (the established church of Massachusetts Bay Colony, whose records are the most complete); Separatist Congregational in Plymouth Colony; small numbers of Baptist and Quaker congregations.
- **Record types:** Church member admission lists, baptisms, marriages, ecclesiastical disciplinary proceedings (admonishments, excommunications), and burial records. Disciplinary records often name family members and document relationships.
- **Where held:** Many records published in the Colonial Society of Massachusetts series and by local historical societies. FamilySearch has "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920" (Collection 1921657, 987,654 records; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657). One digitized FamilySearch volume covers Suffolk County Congregational church admissions and baptisms 1630–1700 (DGS 007612045, 121 images; full-text searchable but NOT name-indexed — must be searched as text, not by name). Source: [Massachusetts Church Records — Congregational](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational).
- **Language:** English.

### Census records

- **Federal/national census:** The first federal census is 1790 — entirely after this period. No federal census applies to 1620–1700.
- **Colonial enumerations:** No standard colonial census exists. The Massachusetts Bay Colony conducted periodic militia musters and town rates (tax lists) naming inhabitants. Town meeting records and proprietors' records serve as partial substitutes.
- **Other enumerations:** Town meeting records and proprietors' lists name householders. FamilySearch has one browse-only volume covering Massachusetts town meeting and proprietors' records 1620–1698 (DGS 007612044, 188 images; 0% name-indexed, NOT full-text searchable — must be browsed image by image with no search capability).
- **Access:** DGS 007612044 — browse-only; images must be examined page by page.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, letters of administration, guardianship orders.
- **Date range:** From the 1630s for Massachusetts Bay Colony; Plymouth Colony probate records run from the 1630s and are published separately.
- **Where held:** County probate courts (formed 1643). FamilySearch has "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991" (Collection 1678901, 567,890 records; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901). Original records remain at county probate courts and the Massachusetts Archives. Source: [Massachusetts Church Records — Congregational](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational).

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Town proprietors granted land within each town's bounds; county deed registries recorded deeds from the 1630s. Massachusetts is a state-land (original-grant) state — there are no federal land office records.
- **Types:** Town proprietors' grants, deeds, mortgages. The town meeting and proprietors' records volume (DGS 007612044) on FamilySearch also covers land grants.
- **Date range:** Deed books survive from the 1630s in remarkably complete runs at county registries of deeds. Source: [Massachusetts Church Records — Congregational](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational).
- **Where held:** County registries of deeds (in-person or through microfilm); Massachusetts Archives for colony-level grants.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** King Philip's War (1675–1676) is the dominant military event of this period; colonial militia musters run from the 1630s onward.
- **Record types:** Militia muster rolls, colonial court orders related to military service. King Philip's War service lists survive in the Massachusetts Archives.
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives (Boston); published transcriptions through the Massachusetts Historical Society and NEHGS.

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** Burial grounds were typically adjacent to Congregational meetinghouses. Physical grave markers from before 1700 are fragmentary and many have not survived.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com) has entries for some early colonial graves.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records were rarely kept systematically in this era; church burial registers are the best substitute.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** No newspapers were published in Massachusetts before 1704 (the Boston News-Letter, begun 1704). Newspaper research does not apply to 1620–1700.

### Immigration/emigration records

- **Relevant ports:** Boston and Plymouth were the primary ports of entry for 1620–1700.
- **Record types:** The "Great Migration" study series (Robert Charles Anderson, NEHGS) documents every known settler arriving 1620–1643 with English origins and family relationships — the primary compiled source for arrival research. Formal passenger lists as a record class did not exist in this era; ship manifests are fragmentary.
- **Where held:** Great Migration volumes available through NEHGS / AmericanAncestors.org and research libraries. Colonial-era ship records survive mainly in English port records (National Archives of the United Kingdom) and scattered Massachusetts sources.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) in this era record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed. For 1620–1643, the Great Migration study is more reliable than any surviving list.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Town rates (local property and poll assessments); colonial tax lists mandated by the General Court.
- **Date range:** From the 1630s, though survival is uneven by town.
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives; individual town clerk offices. Some published transcriptions exist in local town histories.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists name heads of household by name and can locate families in years with no other record, particularly given the absence of census records for this period.

### Other record types

- **Town meeting records:** Town meetings (the fundamental governing unit of colonial New England) kept minutes recording land allotments, town officers, fines, and residents' petitions. FamilySearch's browse-only volume DGS 007612044 (Massachusetts, 1620–1698, 188 images) covers these. This record type has no equivalent in most other American jurisdictions.
- **Colonial court records:** The Court of Assistants and county courts adjudicated civil and criminal matters; their records (held at the Massachusetts Archives) name ordinary settlers, frequently in contexts that reveal relationships and residence.
- **Plymouth Colony records:** Entirely separate from Massachusetts Bay Colony for the entire 1620–1691 period. Published and indexed in various Mayflower-focused genealogical series available through NEHGS.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890 (3,456,789 records; Collection 2061550) | Free |
| FamilySearch | Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920 (987,654 records; Collection 1921657) | Free |
| FamilySearch | Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991 (567,890 records; Collection 1678901) | Free |
| FamilySearch | Town meeting and proprietors' records 1620–1698 (DGS 007612044, 188 images, browse-only) | Free |
| FamilySearch | Suffolk Co. Congregational church admissions/baptisms 1630–1700 (DGS 007612045, 121 images, full-text searchable, not name-indexed) | Free |
| NEHGS / AmericanAncestors.org | Great Migration study series; Tanner-Corbin vital records series | Membership |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery Records (https://www.findagrave.com) | Free |
| NARA | National Archives records (https://www.archives.gov) | Free/varies |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned all 2 matching digitized volumes for Massachusetts 1620–1700 — the complete result set for that date range. The 5 indexed collections returned by collections_search represent all collections held at the Massachusetts state scope; note that 2 of them (Passenger Lists 1820–1891, Naturalization Records 1790–1906) start well after the target period.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Massachusetts Archives, Boston | Original colony records, court records, land records, governor's correspondence from the 1620s onward | In-person; some records microfilmed |
| New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS), Boston | Manuscript collections, published genealogies, Great Migration series, Tanner-Corbin vital records series | In-person; online via AmericanAncestors.org membership |
| Massachusetts Historical Society, Boston | Manuscript collections, early church records, town histories | In-person; some digital |
| County Registries of Deeds | Deed books from the 1630s onward | In-person at each county registry |
| County Probate Courts | Probate case files from the 1630s | In-person; some digitized via FamilySearch |
| Individual Town Clerks | Original town vital records and meeting minutes | In-person or mail |

## Records NOT online

- **Colonial militia muster rolls** (King Philip's War and earlier musters): held at the Massachusetts Archives; not in any online searchable database as of this survey.
- **Many town meeting minute books**: the single FamilySearch volume (DGS 007612044) is a partial holding; most individual town records are at town halls or the Massachusetts Archives, not online.
- **Non-Congregational church records** (Baptist, Quaker): fragmentary and mostly undigitized; held at denominational archives or local historical societies.
- **Plymouth Colony records** (pre-1691): available in published print transcriptions through NEHGS and research libraries, but not all are name-indexed online.
- **County deed books** from the 1630s–1690s: held at county registries of deeds; FamilySearch collections_search returned no collection covering colonial deed books.

## Known record losses

No tool result returned in this survey specifically names a destroyed or lost record series for Massachusetts in this period. The Wikipedia article notes King Philip's War (1675–1676) as a disruption to communities, which is associated with some local record losses in historical literature, but no specific record series was confirmed lost by any tool result. When a physical search at a town hall or the Massachusetts Archives turns up nothing for 1675–1676 specifically, the war's disruption is a plausible explanation — but absence of a record is a coverage gap, not confirmed destruction, unless a repository states it.

## Research tips

- **Start with the Great Migration study** (Robert Charles Anderson, NEHGS): the multi-volume series documents every known settler arriving 1620–1643 with English origins and family reconstructions — the most reliable starting point for colonial Massachusetts research. Available through NEHGS / AmericanAncestors.org. Source: [Massachusetts Genealogy — Colonial Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records).
- **Search the Tanner-Corbin vital records series**: The "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" series abstracts records for over 200 towns and is searchable at NEHGS and many library databases — the fastest path to colonial-era birth, marriage, and death entries. Source: [Massachusetts Genealogy — Colonial Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records).
- **Determine which colony before searching**: Plymouth Colony records (1620–1691) are entirely separate from Massachusetts Bay Colony records. Plymouth Colony territory covers Plymouth, Barnstable, and Bristol counties. If your ancestor was there, use Plymouth Colony-specific published series, not Massachusetts Bay colony or court records.
- **Town is the key unit**: vital records, town meetings, land allotments, and local governance all operated at the town level — identify the specific town first, then go to county and colony records. Source: [Massachusetts Genealogy — Colonial Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records).
- **Use Congregational church records to fill vital-record gaps**: not all vital events appear in town records for the first decades; church baptism, marriage, and member admission lists are the primary alternative and often name children, spouses, and ages. Source: [Massachusetts Church Records — Congregational](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational).
- **For the 1675–1676 period**, expect gaps caused by King Philip's War: some towns were abandoned and re-settled; surviving records may contain no entries for these years.

added.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Massachusetts, United States (1620–1700)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** Two overlapping colonial jurisdictions cover this period. Plymouth Colony was founded in 1620. Massachusetts Bay Colony was chartered in 1629 and settled from 1630 under Governor John Winthrop, who led the Great Migration of approximately 20,000 settlers between 1630 and 1640 (Wikipedia: Massachusetts Bay Colony). The two colonies merged into the Province of Massachusetts Bay in 1691.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Boston (Massachusetts Bay Colony); Plymouth (Plymouth Colony)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** English Crown; Province of Massachusetts Bay from 1691
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned for this period by the tool. Approximately 20,000 settlers arrived during the Great Migration of 1630–1640 (Wikipedia: Massachusetts Bay Colony).
- **Economy:** Subsistence agriculture, fishing, fur trade, timber — all of which shaped which records were created and by whom.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English Puritan settlers; Indigenous peoples (Wampanoag, Massachusett, Nipmuc) present throughout; records document interactions in colony court and land records.
- **Religious denominations:** Congregational (Puritan) was the established church in Massachusetts Bay Colony. Separatist Congregational predominated in Plymouth Colony. Small numbers of Baptist and Quaker congregations existed, often persecuted, with fragmentary records.
- **Key historical events:** Founding of Plymouth (1620), Great Migration (1630–1640), first counties formed in 1643, King Philip's War (1675–1676) which disrupted communities and may have caused local record losses, merger into Province of Massachusetts Bay (1691).

## Boundary changes

- 1620: Plymouth Colony established.
- 1630: Massachusetts Bay Colony settled; formally organized.
- 1643: First counties in Massachusetts Bay formed — Suffolk, Essex, Middlesex, and Norfolk (the last covering part of what is now New Hampshire).
- 1679: New Hampshire separated from Massachusetts Bay Colony — before this date, families in southern New Hampshire were under Massachusetts Bay Colony jurisdiction.
- 1691: Plymouth Colony merged into the Province of Massachusetts Bay. All records before this date are under separate jurisdictional systems; Plymouth Colony records (covering Plymouth, Bristol, and Barnstable counties) must be searched separately.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** Town-level recording of births, marriages, and deaths was mandated by Massachusetts Bay Colony starting in 1639 — one of the earliest civil registration systems in North America. Source: [Massachusetts Genealogy — Colonial Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records). All recording in this period was at the **town** level; no county- or state-level vital registration existed.
- **What exists:** Births, marriages, and deaths recorded by town clerks. The multi-volume "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" series (Tanner-Corbin series) abstracts town clerk records for over 200 Massachusetts towns. Source: [Massachusetts Genealogy — Colonial Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records).
- **Where held:** Original records at individual town halls and the Massachusetts Archives. FamilySearch has the collection "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890" (Collection 2061550, 3,456,789 records; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550).
- **Gaps:** Not all towns maintained records consistently in their first decades. King Philip's War (1675–1676) disrupted recordkeeping in some communities. Plymouth Colony vital records are entirely separate.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Congregational church baptism, marriage, and burial registers; probate inventories listing family members.

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Congregational (the established church of Massachusetts Bay Colony, whose records are the most complete); Separatist Congregational in Plymouth Colony; small numbers of Baptist and Quaker congregations.
- **Record types:** Church member admission lists, baptisms, marriages, ecclesiastical disciplinary proceedings (admonishments, excommunications), and burial records. Disciplinary records often name family members and document relationships.
- **Where held:** Many records published in the Colonial Society of Massachusetts series and by local historical societies. FamilySearch has "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920" (Collection 1921657, 987,654 records; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657). One digitized FamilySearch volume covers Suffolk County Congregational church admissions and baptisms 1630–1700 (DGS 007612045, 121 images; full-text searchable but NOT name-indexed — must be searched as text, not by name). Source: [Massachusetts Church Records — Congregational](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational).
- **Language:** English.

### Census records

- **Federal/national census:** The first federal census is 1790 — entirely after this period. No federal census applies to 1620–1700.
- **Colonial enumerations:** No standard colonial census exists. The Massachusetts Bay Colony conducted periodic militia musters and town rates (tax lists) naming inhabitants. Town meeting records and proprietors' records serve as partial substitutes.
- **Other enumerations:** Town meeting records and proprietors' lists name householders. FamilySearch has one browse-only volume covering Massachusetts town meeting and proprietors' records 1620–1698 (DGS 007612044, 188 images; 0% name-indexed, NOT full-text searchable — must be browsed image by image with no search capability).
- **Access:** DGS 007612044 — browse-only; images must be examined page by page.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, letters of administration, guardianship orders.
- **Date range:** From the 1630s for Massachusetts Bay Colony; Plymouth Colony probate records run from the 1630s and are published separately.
- **Where held:** County probate courts (formed 1643). FamilySearch has "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991" (Collection 1678901, 567,890 records; https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901). Original records remain at county probate courts and the Massachusetts Archives. Source: [Massachusetts Church Records — Congregational](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational).

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Town proprietors granted land within each town's bounds; county deed registries recorded deeds from the 1630s. Massachusetts is a state-land (original-grant) state — there are no federal land office records.
- **Types:** Town proprietors' grants, deeds, mortgages. The town meeting and proprietors' records volume (DGS 007612044) on FamilySearch also covers land grants.
- **Date range:** Deed books survive from the 1630s in remarkably complete runs at county registries of deeds. Source: [Massachusetts Church Records — Congregational](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational).
- **Where held:** County registries of deeds (in-person or through microfilm); Massachusetts Archives for colony-level grants.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** King Philip's War (1675–1676) is the dominant military event of this period; colonial militia musters run from the 1630s onward.
- **Record types:** Militia muster rolls, colonial court orders related to military service. King Philip's War service lists survive in the Massachusetts Archives.
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives (Boston); published transcriptions through the Massachusetts Historical Society and NEHGS.

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** Burial grounds were typically adjacent to Congregational meetinghouses. Physical grave markers from before 1700 are fragmentary and many have not survived.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com) has entries for some early colonial graves.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records were rarely kept systematically in this era; church burial registers are the best substitute.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** No newspapers were published in Massachusetts before 1704 (the Boston News-Letter, begun 1704). Newspaper research does not apply to 1620–1700.

### Immigration/emigration records

- **Relevant ports:** Boston and Plymouth were the primary ports of entry for 1620–1700.
- **Record types:** The "Great Migration" study series (Robert Charles Anderson, NEHGS) documents every known settler arriving 1620–1643 with English origins and family relationships — the primary compiled source for arrival research. Formal passenger lists as a record class did not exist in this era; ship manifests are fragmentary.
- **Where held:** Great Migration volumes available through NEHGS / AmericanAncestors.org and research libraries. Colonial-era ship records survive mainly in English port records (National Archives of the United Kingdom) and scattered Massachusetts sources.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) in this era record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed. For 1620–1643, the Great Migration study is more reliable than any surviving list.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Town rates (local property and poll assessments); colonial tax lists mandated by the General Court.
- **Date range:** From the 1630s, though survival is uneven by town.
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives; individual town clerk offices. Some published transcriptions exist in local town histories.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists name heads of household by name and can locate families in years with no other record, particularly given the absence of census records for this period.

### Other record types

- **Town meeting records:** Town meetings (the fundamental governing unit of colonial New England) kept minutes recording land allotments, town officers, fines, and residents' petitions. FamilySearch's browse-only volume DGS 007612044 (Massachusetts, 1620–1698, 188 images) covers these. This record type has no equivalent in most other American jurisdictions.
- **Colonial court records:** The Court of Assistants and county courts adjudicated civil and criminal matters; their records (held at the Massachusetts Archives) name ordinary settlers, frequently in contexts that reveal relationships and residence.
- **Plymouth Colony records:** Entirely separate from Massachusetts Bay Colony for the entire 1620–1691 period. Published and indexed in various Mayflower-focused genealogical series available through NEHGS.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890 (3,456,789 records; Collection 2061550) | Free |
| FamilySearch | Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920 (987,654 records; Collection 1921657) | Free |
| FamilySearch | Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991 (567,890 records; Collection 1678901) | Free |
| FamilySearch | Town meeting and proprietors' records 1620–1698 (DGS 007612044, 188 images, browse-only) | Free |
| FamilySearch | Suffolk Co. Congregational church admissions/baptisms 1630–1700 (DGS 007612045, 121 images, full-text searchable, not name-indexed) | Free |
| NEHGS / AmericanAncestors.org | Great Migration study series; Tanner-Corbin vital records series | Membership |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery Records (https://www.findagrave.com) | Free |
| NARA | National Archives records (https://www.archives.gov) | Free/varies |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned all 2 matching digitized volumes for Massachusetts 1620–1700 — the complete result set for that date range. The 5 indexed collections returned by collections_search represent all collections held at the Massachusetts state scope; note that 2 of them (Passenger Lists 1820–1891, Naturalization Records 1790–1906) start well after the target period.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Massachusetts Archives, Boston | Original colony records, court records, land records, governor's correspondence from the 1620s onward | In-person; some records microfilmed |
| New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS), Boston | Manuscript collections, published genealogies, Great Migration series, Tanner-Corbin vital records series | In-person; online via AmericanAncestors.org membership |
| Massachusetts Historical Society, Boston | Manuscript collections, early church records, town histories | In-person; some digital |
| County Registries of Deeds | Deed books from the 1630s onward | In-person at each county registry |
| County Probate Courts | Probate case files from the 1630s | In-person; some digitized via FamilySearch |
| Individual Town Clerks | Original town vital records and meeting minutes | In-person or mail |

## Records NOT online

- **Colonial militia muster rolls** (King Philip's War and earlier musters): held at the Massachusetts Archives; not in any online searchable database as of this survey.
- **Many town meeting minute books**: the single FamilySearch volume (DGS 007612044) is a partial holding; most individual town records are at town halls or the Massachusetts Archives, not online.
- **Non-Congregational church records** (Baptist, Quaker): fragmentary and mostly undigitized; held at denominational archives or local historical societies.
- **Plymouth Colony records** (pre-1691): available in published print transcriptions through NEHGS and research libraries, but not all are name-indexed online.
- **County deed books** from the 1630s–1690s: held at county registries of deeds; FamilySearch collections_search returned no collection covering colonial deed books.

## Known record losses

No tool result returned in this survey specifically names a destroyed or lost record series for Massachusetts in this period. The Wikipedia article notes King Philip's War (1675–1676) as a disruption to communities, which is associated with some local record losses in historical literature, but no specific record series was confirmed lost by any tool result. When a physical search at a town hall or the Massachusetts Archives turns up nothing for 1675–1676 specifically, the war's disruption is a plausible explanation — but absence of a record is a coverage gap, not confirmed destruction, unless a repository states it.

## Research tips

- **Start with the Great Migration study** (Robert Charles Anderson, NEHGS): the multi-volume series documents every known settler arriving 1620–1643 with English origins and family reconstructions — the most reliable starting point for colonial Massachusetts research. Available through NEHGS / AmericanAncestors.org. Source: [Massachusetts Genealogy — Colonial Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records).
- **Search the Tanner-Corbin vital records series**: The "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" series abstracts records for over 200 towns and is searchable at NEHGS and many library databases — the fastest path to colonial-era birth, marriage, and death entries. Source: [Massachusetts Genealogy — Colonial Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records).
- **Determine which colony before searching**: Plymouth Colony records (1620–1691) are entirely separate from Massachusetts Bay Colony records. Plymouth Colony territory covers Plymouth, Barnstable, and Bristol counties. If your ancestor was there, use Plymouth Colony-specific published series, not Massachusetts Bay colony or court records.
- **Town is the key unit**: vital records, town meetings, land allotments, and local governance all operated at the town level — identify the specific town first, then go to county and colony records. Source: [Massachusetts Genealogy — Colonial Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records).
- **Use Congregational church records to fill vital-record gaps**: not all vital events appear in town records for the first decades; church baptism, marriage, and member admission lists are the primary alternative and often name children, spouses, and ages. Source: [Massachusetts Church Records — Congregational](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational).
- **For the 1675–1676 period**, expect gaps caused by King Philip's War: some towns were abandoned and re-settled; surviving records may contain no entries for these years.

# Locality Guide: Oklahoma (1889–1910 — Land Run and Territorial Era)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** The Land Run of 1889 (April 22) opened the Unassigned Lands; Oklahoma Territory formally organized May 2, 1890, by the Organic Act; statehood November 16, 1907, combining Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory
- **Capital:** Guthrie (territorial capital); Oklahoma City (after statehood)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Federal public domain / Indian Territory before 1890; U.S. territory 1890–1907
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by tools for this period
- **Economy:** Homestead agriculture, cattle ranching; oil discovered in Indian Territory in 1897
- **Ethnic composition:** Settlers from Kansas, Texas, Missouri, and other states (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts); Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek, Seminole) in Indian Territory; Freedmen (formerly enslaved people of the Five Tribes)
- **Religious denominations:** Protestant denominations (Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian) established congregations sporadically from 1889; missionary churches had operated in Indian Territory for decades prior (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts)
- **Key historical events:** Land Run of 1889 (April 22); subsequent runs 1891, 1892, 1893, 1895; Oklahoma Territory organized 1890; Dawes Commission allotment 1898–1907; statehood 1907

## Boundary changes
- **Pre-1889:** Unassigned Lands were part of Indian Territory under federal control
- **1890:** Oklahoma Territory created by Organic Act; Indian Territory remained a separate jurisdiction to the east
- **1898–1907:** Dawes Commission enrolled members of the Five Civilized Tribes; Indian Territory transitioned toward county government
- **1907:** Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory merged into the state of Oklahoma

This is a critical research split: records created before 1907 for people in Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory belong to two different federal/tribal jurisdictions. A family's records will be in one system or the other depending on where they lived. Indian Territory records follow the tribal and Dawes Commission systems; Oklahoma Territory records follow the standard U.S. territorial system.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki specific pages for Oklahoma Vital Records were not successfully retrieved during this survey (all returned only generic content). No registration start year can be stated from tool results for births or deaths.
- **What exists:** County marriages from 1890 — FamilySearch collection "Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890-1995" (id: 2134789, 456,789 records / 913,578 persons, indexed + images, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134789)
- **Gaps:** No statewide birth or death registration is documented in tool results for the 1889–1907 territorial period. Church records and homestead proof files are the primary substitutes.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism and burial records; homestead final proof files (include claimant's age, family composition, and settlement length)

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Protestant denominations (Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian) began establishing congregations from 1889; missionary churches had operated in Indian Territory for decades before 1889 (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820-1965" (id: 1654321, 123,456 records, indexed + images, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321); original records at denominational archives
- **Language:** English

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** 1880 (pre-Land Run, covers Indian Territory residents); 1890 federal census largely destroyed nationally — but see the Oklahoma 1890 special territorial census below; 1900 and 1910 cover both former territories
- **Oklahoma 1890 special territorial census:** The Oklahoma Historical Society holds this, described as one of the few surviving 1890 census records in the nation (per wiki_search result https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run)
- **Indian Territory censuses:** FamilySearch collection "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851-1959" (id: 1987432, 567,890 records, indexed + images, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432) — covers tribal census records including the Dawes Rolls
- **Other enumerations:** County-level tax rolls from the 1890s (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts)
- **Access:** FamilySearch collections above are indexed. The 1890 special territorial census at the Oklahoma Historical Society may require direct contact with that institution.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories; district court civil and criminal cases; naturalization records
- **Where held:** Territorial court records for Oklahoma Territory (1890–1907) are at the National Archives at Fort Worth and the Oklahoma State Archives (per wiki_search result https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts)
- **Naturalization note:** Pre-1906 naturalizations can appear in any court of record — look in territorial district court files. After September 27, 1906, they were handled exclusively by federal courts.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Rectangular survey (federal public domain land state)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** General Land Office (GLO), U.S. Department of the Interior. Land offices were at Guthrie and Kingfisher for the original 1889 Land Run (per Wikipedia https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_Run_of_1889)
- **Types:** Homestead applications, final certificates/proofs, land patents, rejected applications; deed books at county recorders from 1890
- **FamilySearch:** Collection "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834-1907" (id: 1541872, 234,567 records, indexed + images, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872); also volume 005221388 (land-entry case files / homestead final proofs, 1889–1907, 402 images, 74% name-indexed — indexed + images)
- **BLM GLO website:** glorecords.blm.gov holds homestead patent records (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run)
- **NARA:** Homestead applications and final certificates at NARA, Record Group 49; rejected applications also survive and may contain family details (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run)

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Spanish-American War (1898); many Land Run settlers were Civil War veterans from other states
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, draft registrations at NARA; state militia records at Oklahoma State Archives
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/), Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/)

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/)
- **Physical records:** Individual county/township cemeteries; church burial registers in the Mission and Church Records collection (1654321)

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Territorial newspapers began in Guthrie and other towns established during the 1889 Land Run
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/); Oklahoma Historical Society digital archives
- **Content value:** Homestead legal notices (required published notice of intent to prove up a land claim, naming claimant, witnesses, and land description), marriage and death notices, land advertisements

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Context:** Most Land Run settlers migrated internally from Kansas, Texas, Missouri, and other states rather than directly from abroad (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts). Tracing origins requires searching departure-state records.
- **Naturalization:** Pre-1906 naturalizations are in territorial court records at NARA Fort Worth and Oklahoma State Archives. After 1906, federal courts exclusively.
- **Passenger lists:** For the European-origin generation, NARA holds passenger arrival manifests (https://www.archives.gov/). Passenger lists record every person aboard including infants and young children — examine the full manifest for all family members when researching a family.

### Tax records
- **Types:** County-level property tax rolls from the 1890s (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts)
- **Date range:** From 1890 (county organization)
- **Where held:** Oklahoma State Archives; county courthouses
- **Substitute value:** Tax rolls substitute for missing census years and confirm a settler's presence in a specific county

### Other record types
- **Dawes Commission enrollment jackets:** FamilySearch volume 005221389 (1898–1910, 176 images, 0% name-indexed — browse-only images, must be viewed image by image with no search capability). Essential for families with Native American heritage or who interacted with the enrollment process for the Five Civilized Tribes. Also covered by collection 1987432.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Early Land Records 1834–1907 (234,567 records); Indian Censuses and Rolls 1851–1959 (567,890 records); County Marriages 1890–1995 (456,789 records); Mission and Church Records 1820–1965 (123,456 records) | Free |
| BLM GLO Records (glorecords.blm.gov) | Land patents and homestead records | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Homestead files RG 49; territorial court records; naturalization records; military records | Free/in-person |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census and other collections | Subscription |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | Military records | Subscription |
| FindAGrave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 2 digitized volumes for 1889–1910 (totalResults: 2 — the complete result set). The volume_search response did not include a summary block, so aggregate counts by record-type group are not available. The 4 FamilySearch indexed collections are the full set returned for Oklahoma.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives at Fort Worth | Oklahoma Territory territorial court records, district court files, naturalization records, 1890–1907 | In-person; some records by mail request |
| National Archives (Washington, D.C.) | Homestead applications and patents (RG 49, GLO) | In-person; digitized portions online |
| Oklahoma State Archives (Oklahoma City) | Territorial records, early statehood records, tax rolls | In-person; some online |
| Oklahoma Historical Society (Oklahoma City) | 1890 special territorial census; territorial newspapers; local histories | In-person; some digital |
| County courthouses | Deed books, marriage licenses, probate files from 1890 | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- The 1890 special territorial census at the Oklahoma Historical Society (not confirmed as fully digitized by tool results)
- Rejected homestead applications at NARA (not confirmed as fully digitized)
- County-level tax rolls from the 1890s
- Territorial court minute books beyond what is in the indexed FamilySearch collections
- Original church registers not captured by FamilySearch collection 1654321

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey states that a specific Oklahoma record set was destroyed or lost. The standard 1890 federal census was destroyed nationally, but the Oklahoma Historical Society holds a special territorial census as a surviving substitute (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run).

## Research tips
- **Start with the homestead file, not the patent.** A homestead final proof file (FamilySearch volume 005221388 or NARA RG 49) typically includes the claimant's age, state of origin, length of settlement, and two witness statements — far richer than the patent alone. Rejected applications also survive (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run).
- **Search the departure state first.** Most Land Run settlers came from Kansas, Texas, or Missouri (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts). Without a home-state record giving birthplace and parents, Oklahoma territorial records alone will often leave origins unclear.
- **Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory are two separate record systems before 1907.** Know which side of the territorial line your ancestor was on — it determines which repositories and record types apply.
- **Use the 1890 territorial census at the Oklahoma Historical Society** as a substitute for the largely destroyed 1890 federal census. It is described as one of the few surviving 1890 census records in the nation (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run).
- **Check the Dawes Rolls even for non-Native families.** Neighbors, witnesses, and intermarried whites sometimes appear in related Dawes Commission documentation. FamilySearch volume 005221389 (browse-only) and collection 1987432 cover this material.
- **Newspaper legal notices are a hidden research source.** Homesteaders were required to publish notice of intent to prove up their claim; these notices name the claimant, witnesses, and land description. Newspapers.com and the Oklahoma Historical Society digital archives hold territorial newspapers.

| NARA (archives.gov) | Homestead files RG 49; territorial court records; naturalization records; military records | Free/in-person |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census and other collections | Subscription |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | Military records | Subscription |
| FindAGrave (findagrave.com) | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 2 digitized volumes for 1889–1910 (totalResults: 2 — the complete result set). The volume_search response did not include a summary block, so aggregate counts by record-type group are not available. The 4 FamilySearch indexed collections are the full set returned for Oklahoma.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives at Fort Worth | Oklahoma Territory territorial court records, district court files, naturalization records, 1890–1907 | In-person; some records by mail request |
| National Archives (Washington, D.C.) | Homestead applications and patents (RG 49, GLO) | In-person; digitized portions online |
| Oklahoma State Archives (Oklahoma City) | Territorial records, early statehood records, tax rolls | In-person; some online |
| Oklahoma Historical Society (Oklahoma City) | 1890 special territorial census; territorial newspapers; local histories | In-person; some digital |
| County courthouses | Deed books, marriage licenses, probate files from 1890 | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- The 1890 special territorial census at the Oklahoma Historical Society (not confirmed as fully digitized by tool results)
- Rejected homestead applications at NARA (not confirmed as fully digitized)
- County-level tax rolls from the 1890s
- Territorial court minute books beyond what is in the indexed FamilySearch collections
- Original church registers not captured by FamilySearch collection 1654321

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey states that a specific Oklahoma record set was destroyed or lost. The standard 1890 federal census was destroyed nationally, but the Oklahoma Historical Society holds a special territorial census as a surviving substitute (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run).

## Research tips
- **Start with the homestead file, not the patent.** A homestead final proof file (FamilySearch volume 005221388 or NARA RG 49) typically includes the claimant's age, state of origin, length of settlement, and two witness statements — far richer than the patent alone. Rejected applications also survive (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run).
- **Search the departure state first.** Most Land Run settlers came from Kansas, Texas, or Missouri (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts). Without a home-state record giving birthplace and parents, Oklahoma territorial records alone will often leave origins unclear.
- **Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory are two separate record systems before 1907.** Know which side of the territorial line your ancestor was on — it determines which repositories and record types apply.
- **Use the 1890 territorial census at the Oklahoma Historical Society** as a substitute for the largely destroyed 1890 federal census. It is described as one of the few surviving 1890 census records in the nation (per https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run).
- **Check the Dawes Rolls even for non-Native families.** Neighbors, witnesses, and intermarried whites sometimes appear in related Dawes Commission documentation. FamilySearch volume 005221389 (browse-only) and collection 1987432 cover this material.
- **Newspaper legal notices are a hidden research source.** Homesteaders were required to publish notice of intent to prove up their claim; these notices name the claimant, witnesses, and land description. Newspapers.com and the Oklahoma Historical Society digital archives hold territorial newspapers.

Here is the locality guide the agent produced:

---

## Alabama Region, circa 1800 (Pre-Statehood)

**Jurisdictional Context**

In 1800, what is now Alabama was part of the **Mississippi Territory**, organized by Congress in 1798. Alabama Territory wasn't separated out until 1817, and statehood came in 1819. The Mobile district (south Alabama) had additionally been under Spanish colonial control until 1813, so records for that area are split between Spanish and American jurisdictions.

---

## Digitized, Browsable Volumes

**FamilySearch returned zero digitized browsable image volumes for Alabama in the 1780–1820 period.** There is nothing to page through on FamilySearch for pre-statehood Alabama — no unindexed image browsing is available there for this era.

---

## What Does Exist

### Name-Indexed Collections on FamilySearch
- **Mississippi Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907** — covers the territorial period and overlaps your target years
- **County Court Records, 1799–1920** — earliest county-level records
- **Alabama Church Records, beginning 1803** — the earliest surviving church registers

### Territorial Census Substitutes (not on FamilySearch)
The best sources for 1800 are **census substitutes** held physically at the **Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH)** in Montgomery:
- Mississippi Territory censuses: **1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810**
- Territorial **tax lists** and **militia rolls**

None of these are digitized or name-indexed online.

### Spanish Colonial Records (Mobile Area)
For south Alabama before 1813, the Spanish colonial archives held in **Seville, Spain** contain church registers and land grants. Copies are at the **Library of Congress**.

---

## Priority Repositories

| Repository | What They Hold |
|---|---|
| Alabama Dept. of Archives & History (Montgomery) | Territorial censuses, tax lists, militia rolls |
| FamilySearch (online) | Land records, court records, church records (name-indexed) |
| Library of Congress | Spanish colonial records, Mobile area |
| Archivo General de Indias (Seville) | Original Spanish colonial records |

---

## Suggested Next Step

Build a research plan targeting specific ancestors, using the territorial census substitutes, tax lists, and land records as primary sources. For the Mobile area, factor in the Spanish colonial records track separately.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Alabama Region (1780–1820, Pre-Statehood)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Alabama Territory created 1817 from the eastern portion of Mississippi Territory (1798–1817); statehood 14 December 1819
- **County seat / administrative center:** Territorial government centered at Natchez (Mississippi Territory capital); Mobile was the principal settlement in the Alabama region
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Mississippi Territory (1798–1817), then Alabama Territory (1817–1819)
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the population tool for this pre-statehood period
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, fur trade, and expanding cotton cultivation; Mobile Bay commerce
- **Ethnic composition:** American settler families migrating from Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia (especially after the Creek War 1813–1814); French, Spanish, and creole populations around Mobile; Creek and Cherokee nations across much of the interior
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic in the Mobile area (French/Spanish colonial legacy); Baptist and Methodist among American settlers in the interior
- **Key historical events:** French founded Mobile 1702; British control 1763–1780; Spanish control 1780–1813; US acquired Mobile 1813; Creek War 1813–1814 opened the interior to American settlement; Alabama Territory organized 1817; statehood 1819

## Boundary changes
- France administered the Mobile area 1702–1763; Britain 1763–1780; Spain 1780–1813
- 1798: US organized the Mississippi Territory, encompassing most of present-day Alabama and Mississippi
- 1817: Congress split the territory — eastern portion became Alabama Territory; western portion became the state of Mississippi
- 1819: Alabama achieved statehood
- **Research consequence:** Records from ca. 1800 were created under the Mississippi Territory. After 1817 they were reorganized under Alabama Territory, then state authority. Search under both Mississippi Territory and Alabama headings for the territorial era. This is a temporal split, not a geographic one: before 1817, all Alabama-region records are Mississippi Territory records; after 1817, they are Alabama Territory or Alabama records.

## A direct answer on digitized browsable volumes
FamilySearch `volume_search` returned **0 digitized image volumes** for Alabama in the 1780–1820 period. There are no browse-by-image volumes in FamilySearch for pre-statehood Alabama — no image sets that can be browsed page by page, whether name-indexed or not. All FamilySearch records for this period are accessible only via name-indexed collections (record_search), not volume browsing.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil registration system existed in the Alabama region ca. 1800. The FamilySearch Wiki Alabama Vital Records page returned only generic content during this survey; no specific registration date can be stated from tool results.
- **What exists:** No civil births, marriages, or deaths were registered by territorial government ca. 1800
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records are the sole vital-record source for this period

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic (Mobile area); Baptist and Methodist (interior, primarily after ca. 1800)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials (Catholic); minutes, membership rolls (Baptist, Methodist)
- **FamilySearch collection:** Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950 — 156,789 indexed records, 78,394 images; starts 1803, covering only the tail end of the target period (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1986396). Also: Mississippi, Church Records, 1800–1950 — 87,654 records, 43,827 images (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2034891)
- **Colonial Catholic records:** Spanish-era church registers for Mobile are described in the FamilySearch Wiki as held at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress; French colonial records are at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer in Aix-en-Provence and on microfilm at the Mobile Municipal Archives (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)
- **Language:** Catholic records in this period are in Spanish and/or French
- **Digitization level:** Name-indexed + images (1803+) for the FamilySearch collection; colonial Catholic records physical or microfilm only

### Census records
- **Federal census:** First federal census covering the Alabama region was 1810 (as part of Mississippi Territory). Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890 — 287,634 indexed records, no images — starts 1810 (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2016756)
- **Territorial censuses:** Mississippi Territory conducted censuses in 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 enumerating settlers in present-day Alabama. These are held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History in Montgomery, not on FamilySearch (source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)
- **Census substitutes for Mississippi Territory:** Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792–1890 — 198,340 indexed records, no images — covers from 1792 (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1927171). May include territorial-era substitutes for the Alabama portion of the original territory.
- **Digitization level:** Name-index only (no images) for FamilySearch collections; original territorial censuses physical at ADAH

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, administrations, guardianships, court minutes
- **Alabama collection:** Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985 — 438,210 indexed records, 219,105 images; earliest records from county formation beginning 1809 (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1537764). Indexed + images.
- **Territorial-era court records:** Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920 — 245,670 indexed records, 122,835 images; covers territorial period from 1799 (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1855293). Note: scoped to Mississippi state — coverage of the Alabama portion of the original Mississippi Territory is uncertain from tool results.
- **Where held:** County courthouses and Alabama Department of Archives and History

### Land records

## Jurisdiction overview

- **County seat / administrative center:** Territorial government centered at Natchez (Mississippi Territory capital); Mobile was the principal settlement in the Alabama region
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Mississippi Territory (1798–1817), then Alabama Territory (1817–1819)
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the population tool for this pre-statehood period
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, fur trade, and expanding cotton cultivation; Mobile Bay commerce
- **Ethnic composition:** American settler families migrating from Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia (especially after the Creek War 1813–1814); French, Spanish, and creole populations around Mobile; Creek and Cherokee nations across much of the interior
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic in the Mobile area (French/Spanish colonial legacy); Baptist and Methodist among American settlers in the interior
- **Key historical events:** French founded Mobile 1702; British control 1763–1780; Spanish control 1780–1813; US acquired Mobile 1813; Creek War 1813–1814 opened the interior to American settlement; Alabama Territory organized 1817; statehood 1819

## Boundary changes
- France administered the Mobile area 1702–1763; Britain 1763–1780; Spain 1780–1813
- 1798: US organized the Mississippi Territory, encompassing most of present-day Alabama and Mississippi
- 1817: Congress split the territory — eastern portion became Alabama Territory; western portion became the state of Mississippi
- 1819: Alabama achieved statehood
- **Research consequence:** Records from ca. 1800 were created under the Mississippi Territory. After 1817 they were reorganized under Alabama Territory, then state authority. Search under both Mississippi Territory and Alabama headings for the territorial era. This is a temporal split, not a geographic one: before 1817, all Alabama-region records are Mississippi Territory records; after 1817, they are Alabama Territory or Alabama records.

FamilySearch `volume_search` returned **0 digitized image volumes** for Alabama in the 1780–1820 period. entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania — Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region (1860–1890)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties
- **County seat / administrative center:** Pottsville
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** 89,510 (1860); 116,428 (1870); 129,974 (1880); 172,927 (1900)
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining dominated; the county was central to the lower anthracite field
- **Ethnic composition:** Heavy Irish immigration beginning mid-1840s, alongside Welsh, English, German, and later Eastern European miners
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant for Irish immigrants), Methodist, Episcopal, Welsh Congregational / Welsh Calvinist Methodist
- **Key historical events:** Molly Maguires era (late 1860s–1870s), Great Railroad Strike of 1877, significant labor organization activity

## Boundary changes
- Schuylkill County boundaries were stable throughout 1860–1890.
- Formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 events may be in those parent jurisdictions.
- The neighboring anthracite county of Lackawanna was carved from Luzerne County during this period; records for the Lackawanna Valley before that formation are filed under Luzerne County.
- Neighboring counties were not listed in wiki results returned for this survey (the FamilySearch Wiki county page returned only generic content).

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Pennsylvania Vital Records was not available during this survey (the page redirected to generic content); no specific civil registration start dates can be stated from tool results for this county.
- **What exists:** 1 digitized volume of marriage records, 1870–1910 (DGS 007936753, 94 images) — browse-only, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; must be browsed image-by-image with no name search. No birth or death volumes appear in FamilySearch for this period.
- **Where held:** County courthouse, Pottsville; FamilySearch browse-only volume at familysearch.org.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic baptismal and burial registers; Pennsylvania triennial state tax assessments from 1853 (list occupation and sometimes nativity).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (dominant for Irish immigrants); Protestant denominations. Catholic parishes in the coal region were established between 1840 and 1870 to serve Irish and Eastern European immigrant communities. [Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records]
- **Diocesan jurisdiction (critical):** Before 1868 all five anthracite coal counties fell under the Diocese of Philadelphia. From 1868, Luzerne and Lackawanna belong to the Diocese of Scranton and Northumberland to the Diocese of Harrisburg; Schuylkill and Carbon remained with Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. [Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records]
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations.
- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** DGS 007936751, 1842–1895, 187 images, in both English and German — researchers must be able to read German for entries in that language. 0% name-indexed, browse-only.
- **FamilySearch indexed collection:** Collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, labeled "Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records (synthetic test fixture)," 1708–1985, 982,415 persons, 1,245,830 records — the "synthetic test fixture" label in the title suggests this may be test data; verify availability in the production FamilySearch catalog before relying on it.
- **Language:** English, German, and possibly Latin for Catholic sacramental registers.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** All federal censuses 1790–1940 cover Schuylkill County. The 1880 census is the first to record the relationship of each household member to the head of household — especially valuable for proving family connections. [Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania,_United_States_Genealogy#Census_Records]
- **1890 gap:** The 1890 federal census population schedules are mostly destroyed nationally; use the 1880 and 1900 censuses alongside Pennsylvania triennial tax assessments to bridge the gap. [Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania,_United_States_Genealogy#Census_Records]
- **State / other enumerations:** Pennsylvania state assessors enumerated coal-region residents triennially from 1853; assessment ledgers list householder, real estate value, occupation, and sometimes nativity. [Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records]
- **Access:** 1850 Schuylkill County federal census on Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1276/); 1860–1900 censuses indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, guardianship files, letters of administration.
- **Date range:** DGS 007936749 covers 1851–1930 (412 images); collection 1999196 (Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994) has 3.2 million images for the whole state.
- **Digitization level:** DGS 007936749 — browse-only (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable). Collection 1999196 — images-only, 0 person records indexed.
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County Courthouse, Pottsville; FamilySearch digitized volumes and statewide probate image collection (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196).

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania).
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, tax records.
- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** DGS 007936752 — Deed Records, 1815–1900, 543 images, 22% name-indexed. This is the best-digitized volume for Schuylkill County, with partial name search capability.
- **Tax records:** Pennsylvania Tax and Exoneration Lists, 1768–1801 available on Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/7667/) — predates the target period but useful for establishing family presence. Triennial state assessments from 1853 cover the target period.
- **Where held:** Recorder of Deeds, Schuylkill County Courthouse, Pottsville; Pennsylvania State Archives for state patent records.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Pennsylvania Land and Property did not return specific content during this survey. Contact the Pennsylvania State Archives for original patent records.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865); many Irish coal miners served in Pennsylvania volunteer regiments.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants (Civil War era), draft registrations.
- **Where held:** NARA; Pennsylvania State Archives holds state adjutant general records.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Catholic parishes maintained burial grounds; Protestant denominations had separate cemeteries in Pottsville and throughout the county.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave and BillionGraves provide some coverage; extent not confirmed by tool results during this survey.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers held by individual parishes and cemeteries; contact Diocese of Philadelphia (pre-1961) or Diocese of Allentown.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Pottsville's Miners' Journal is the most significant coal-region paper throughout 1860–1890.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, mine accident reports (naming individual workers), Molly Maguires trial coverage, labor dispute reports, and legal notices.
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Library and local historical societies hold microfilm; Newspapers.com and similar services may have digitized issues.

### Immigration / emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia and New York (Castle Garden pre-1892, Ellis Island from 1892) were the primary arrival ports for Irish immigrants destined for the anthracite region.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests, declarations of intention, naturalization petitions.
- **Naturalization:** Pre-1906 naturalizations scattered among Schuylkill County courts (Quarter Sessions, Common Pleas, Orphans' Court). DGS 007936750 — Naturalization Records, 1849–1915, 298 images — browse-only, 0% name-indexed. After September 1906, centralised at NARA Philadelphia (eastern Pennsylvania). [Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Naturalization_Records]
- **Content note:** Passenger arrival manifests list all persons aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest for all family members when researching a family.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Pennsylvania triennial state property assessments (from 1853); county-level property and personal property tax.
- **Date range:** State assessments from 1853 cover the entire 1860–1890 period.
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives; county tax records at Schuylkill County Courthouse.
- **Substitute value:** Triennial assessments are the best substitute for the destroyed 1890 census; entries sometimes record nativity, which is critical for Irish immigrant research. [Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records]

### Specialized coal-region indexes
- **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855–1898:** Names approximately 41,000 colliery workers across the lower anthracite field, drawn from company payroll books that survived a 1903 records consolidation. Entries include occupation (loader, breaker boy, mule driver), wage rate, and parish of origin where stated. [Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records]
- **Mine-inspection and accident reports:** Organized by colliery, not by person — less direct as a genealogical index but useful once the specific colliery is known.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records 1708–1985 (982K persons; verify as production data); Pennsylvania, Probate Records 1683–1994 (3.2M images, collection 1999196); 5 digitized volumes: deed records 22% indexed, probate / naturalization / church / marriage records browse-only | Free |
| Ancestry | Pennsylvania Tax and Exoneration Lists, 1768–1801 (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/7667/); 1850 Schuylkill County Federal Census (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1276/) | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned all 5 digitized volumes matching Schuylkill County for 1860–1900 — the result set is complete with no additional pages.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Schuylkill County Courthouse, Pottsville | Deeds, probate, court records, marriage records, naturalization records | In-person or mail request |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | State assessment ledgers (from 1853), state vital records (post-period), adjutant general military records | In-person or online finding aids |
| Diocese of Philadelphia Archives | Catholic parish registers for Schuylkill County (pre-1961 records) | Contact diocese |
| Diocese of Allentown Archives | Administrative successor for Schuylkill and Carbon County Catholic records from 1961 | Contact diocese |
| Schuylkill County Historical Society, Pottsville | Local histories, newspapers, finding aids | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- **Birth and death records for 1860–1890:** No indexed collection or digitized volume found during this survey. The FamilySearch Wiki page for Pennsylvania Vital Records did not return specific content; civil registration start dates cannot be confirmed from tool results. Contact the Schuylkill County Courthouse and Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Catholic parish registers (originals):** DGS 007936751 is a browse-only partial digitization; original registers are held by the Diocese of Philadelphia (pre-1961 records) and the Diocese of Allentown.
- **Pennsylvania triennial state tax assessments (1853 onward):** Not found in any online FamilySearch collection or digitized volume; held at the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Mine company payroll books:** Originals in company and historical archives; the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index is a derived finding aid, not the full payroll records.
- **Probate and naturalization records:** Browse-only digitized volumes exist on FamilySearch (0% name-indexed); original records at Schuylkill County Courthouse.

## Known record losses
No tool result during this survey stated that a specific Schuylkill County record set was destroyed or lost. The destruction of the 1890 federal census population schedules is a nationwide loss, not specific to this county. For potential courthouse fires or record deterioration, contact the Schuylkill County Courthouse and the Schuylkill County Historical Society.

## Research tips
1. **Search the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index first:** Before standard census or vital records, check this index of ~41,000 colliery workers (1855–1898). Entries may give parish of origin — the single most useful clue for Irish immigrant miners. [Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records]
2. **Diocese matters for church records:** Schuylkill County Catholic records are with the Diocese of Philadelphia (not Scranton) for all of 1860–1890. Requesting from the wrong diocese produces a false negative even when records survive. [Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records]
3. **Pennsylvania triennial tax assessments (from 1853) substitute for the missing 1890 census** and sometimes record nativity directly — a rare direct link to Ireland when other records are absent. [Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records]
4. **Naturalization records are the second-best source for Irish origin:** Pre-1906 declarations and petitions in county courts name country of origin and sometimes county or town in Ireland. DGS 007936750 (1849–1915) must be browsed image-by-image; after September 1906 check NARA Philadelphia. [Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Naturalization_Records]
5. **The 1880 federal census is the pivot year for family reconstruction:** First census to record each member's relationship to the head of household — use it to confirm whether a co-resident is a son, boarder, or unrelated. [Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania,_United_States_Genealogy#Census_Records]
6. **Search the Miners' Journal (Pottsville) for accident reports, obituaries, and labor trial coverage** — the coal industry generated extensive named-worker coverage throughout 1860–1890.

---
**Unsurveyed anthracite coal counties:** Luzerne, Lackawanna, Northumberland, and Carbon counties are part of the same anthracite coal region and each needs its own locality survey. Records for the Lackawanna Valley before Lackawanna County's formation from Luzerne County are filed under Luzerne County.
