- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining dominated; the county was central to the lower anthracite field
- **Ethnic composition:** Heavy Irish immigration beginning mid-1840s, alongside Welsh, English, German, and later Eastern European miners
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant for Irish immigrants), Methodist, Episcopal, Welsh Congregational / Welsh Calvinist Methodist
- **Key historical events:** Molly Maguires era (late 1860s–1870s), Great Railroad Strike of 1877, significant labor organization activity

## Boundary changes
- Schuylkill County boundaries were stable throughout 1860–1890.
- Formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 events may be in those parent jurisdictions.
- The neighboring anthracite county of Lackawanna was carved from Luzerne County during this period; records for the Lackawanna Valley before that formation are filed under Luzerne County.
- Neighboring counties were not listed in wiki results returned for this survey (the FamilySearch Wiki county page returned only generic content).

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Pennsylvania Vital Records was not available during this survey (the page redirected to generic content); no specific civil registration start dates can be stated from tool results for this county.
- **What exists:** 1 digitized volume of marriage records, 1870–1910 (DGS 007936753, 94 images) — browse-only, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; must be browsed image-by-image with no name search. No birth or death volumes appear in FamilySearch for this period.
- **Where held:** County courthouse, Pottsville; FamilySearch browse-only volume at familysearch.org.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic baptismal and burial registers; Pennsylvania triennial state tax assessments from 1853 (list occupation and sometimes nativity).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (dominant for Irish immigrants); Protestant denominations. Catholic parishes in the coal region were established between 1840 and 1870 to serve Irish and Eastern European immigrant communities. [Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records]
- **Diocesan jurisdiction (critical):** Before 1868 all five anthracite coal counties fell under the Diocese of Philadelphia. From 1868, Luzerne and Lackawanna belong to the Diocese of Scranton and Northumberland to the Diocese of Harrisburg; Schuylkill and Carbon remained with Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. [Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records]
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations.
- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** DGS 007936751, 1842–1895, 187 images, in both English and German — researchers must be able to read German for entries in that language. 0% name-indexed, browse-only.
- **FamilySearch indexed collection:** Collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, labeled "Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records (synthetic test fixture)," 1708–1985, 982,415 persons, 1,245,830 records — the "synthetic test fixture" label in the title suggests this may be test data; verify availability in the production FamilySearch catalog before relying on it.
- **Language:** English, German, and possibly Latin for Catholic sacramental registers.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** All federal censuses 1790–1940 cover Schuylkill County. The 1880 census is the first to record the relationship of each household member to the head of household — especially valuable for proving family connections. [Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania,_United_States_Genealogy#Census_Records]
- **1890 gap:** The 1890 federal census population schedules are mostly destroyed nationally; use the 1880 and 1900 censuses alongside Pennsylvania triennial tax assessments to bridge the gap. [Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania,_United_States_Genealogy#Census_Records]
- **State / other enumerations:** Pennsylvania state assessors enumerated coal-region residents triennially from 1853; assessment ledgers list householder, real estate value, occupation, and sometimes nativity. [Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records]
- **Access:** 1850 Schuylkill County federal census on Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1276/); 1860–1900 censuses indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, guardianship files, letters of administration.
- **Date range:** DGS 007936749 covers 1851–1930 (412 images); collection 1999196 (Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994) has 3.2 million images for the whole state.
- **Digitization level:** DGS 007936749 — browse-only (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable). Collection 1999196 — images-only, 0 person records indexed.
- **Where held:** Schuylkill County Courthouse, Pottsville; FamilySearch digitized volumes and statewide probate image collection (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196).

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania).
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, tax records.
- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** DGS 007936752 — Deed Records, 1815–1900, 543 images, 22% name-indexed. This is the best-digitized volume for Schuylkill County, with partial name search capability.
- **Tax records:** Pennsylvania Tax and Exoneration Lists, 1768–1801 available on Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/7667/) — predates the target period but useful for establishing family presence. Triennial state assessments from 1853 cover the target period.
- **Where held:** Recorder of Deeds, Schuylkill County Courthouse, Pottsville; Pennsylvania State Archives for state patent records.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Pennsylvania Land and Property did not return specific content during this survey. Contact the Pennsylvania State Archives for original patent records.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865); many Irish coal miners served in Pennsylvania volunteer regiments.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants (Civil War era), draft registrations.
- **Where held:** NARA; Pennsylvania State Archives holds state adjutant general records.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Catholic parishes maintained burial grounds; Protestant denominations had separate cemeteries in Pottsville and throughout the county.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave and BillionGraves provide some coverage; extent not confirmed by tool results during this survey.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers held by individual parishes and cemeteries; contact Diocese of Philadelphia (pre-1961) or Diocese of Allentown.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Pottsville's Miners' Journal is the most significant coal-region paper throughout 1860–1890.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, mine accident reports (naming individual workers), Molly Maguires trial coverage, labor dispute reports, and legal notices.
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Library and local historical societies hold microfilm; Newspapers.com and similar services may have digitized issues.

### Immigration / emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia and New York (Castle Garden pre-1892, Ellis Island from 1892) were the primary arrival ports for Irish immigrants destined for the anthracite region.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests, declarations of intention, naturalization petitions.
- **Naturalization:** Pre-1906 naturalizations scattered among Schuylkill County courts (Quarter Sessions, Common Pleas, Orphans' Court). DGS 007936750 — Naturalization Records, 1849–1915, 298 images — browse-only, 0% name-indexed. After September 1906, centralised at NARA Philadelphia (eastern Pennsylvania). [Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Naturalization_Records]
- **Content note:** Passenger arrival manifests list all persons aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest for all family members when researching a family.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Pennsylvania triennial state property assessments (from 1853); county-level property and personal property tax.
- **Date range:** State assessments from 1853 cover the entire 1860–1890 period.
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives; county tax records at Schuylkill County Courthouse.
- **Substitute value:** Triennial assessments are the best substitute for the destroyed 1890 census; entries sometimes record nativity, which is critical for Irish immigrant research. [Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records]

### Specialized coal-region indexes
- **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855–1898:** Names approximately 41,000 colliery workers across the lower anthracite field, drawn from company payroll books that survived a 1903 records consolidation. Entries include occupation (loader, breaker boy, mule driver), wage rate, and parish of origin where stated. [Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records]
- **Mine-inspection and accident reports:** Organized by colliery, not by person — less direct as a genealogical index but useful once the specific colliery is known.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records 1708–1985 (982K persons; verify as production data); Pennsylvania, Probate Records 1683–1994 (3.2M images, collection 1999196); 5 digitized volumes: deed records 22% indexed, probate / naturalization / church / marriage records browse-only | Free |
| Ancestry | Pennsylvania Tax and Exoneration Lists, 1768–1801 (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/7667/); 1850 Schuylkill County Federal Census (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1276/) | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned all 5 digitized volumes matching Schuylkill County for 1860–1900 — the result set is complete with no additional pages.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Schuylkill County Courthouse, Pottsville | Deeds, probate, court records, marriage records, naturalization records | In-person or mail request |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg | State assessment ledgers (from 1853), state vital records (post-period), adjutant general military records | In-person or online finding aids |
| Diocese of Philadelphia Archives | Catholic parish registers for Schuylkill County (pre-1961 records) | Contact diocese |
| Diocese of Allentown Archives | Administrative successor for Schuylkill and Carbon County Catholic records from 1961 | Contact diocese |
| Schuylkill County Historical Society, Pottsville | Local histories, newspapers, finding aids | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- **Birth and death records for 1860–1890:** No indexed collection or digitized volume found during this survey. The FamilySearch Wiki page for Pennsylvania Vital Records did not return specific content; civil registration start dates cannot be confirmed from tool results. Contact the Schuylkill County Courthouse and Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Catholic parish registers (originals):** DGS 007936751 is a browse-only partial digitization; original registers are held by the Diocese of Philadelphia (pre-1961 records) and the Diocese of Allentown.
- **Pennsylvania triennial state tax assessments (1853 onward):** Not found in any online FamilySearch collection or digitized volume; held at the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Mine company payroll books:** Originals in company and historical archives; the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index is a derived finding aid, not the full payroll records.
- **Probate and naturalization records:** Browse-only digitized volumes exist on FamilySearch (0% name-indexed); original records at Schuylkill County Courthouse.

## Known record losses
No tool result during this survey stated that a specific Schuylkill County record set was destroyed or lost. The destruction of the 1890 federal census population schedules is a nationwide loss, not specific to this county. For potential courthouse fires or record deterioration, contact the Schuylkill County Courthouse and the Schuylkill County Historical Society.

## Research tips
1. **Search the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index first:** Before standard census or vital records, check this index of ~41,000 colliery workers (1855–1898). Entries may give parish of origin — the single most useful clue for Irish immigrant miners. [Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records]
2. **Diocese matters for church records:** Schuylkill County Catholic records are with the Diocese of Philadelphia (not Scranton) for all of 1860–1890. Requesting from the wrong diocese produces a false negative even when records survive. [Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records]
3. **Pennsylvania triennial tax assessments (from 1853) substitute for the missing 1890 census** and sometimes record nativity directly — a rare direct link to Ireland when other records are absent. [Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records]
4. **Naturalization records are the second-best source for Irish origin:** Pre-1906 declarations and petitions in county courts name country of origin and sometimes county or town in Ireland. DGS 007936750 (1849–1915) must be browsed image-by-image; after September 1906 check NARA Philadelphia. [Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Naturalization_Records]
5. **The 1880 federal census is the pivot year for family reconstruction:** First census to record each member's relationship to the head of household — use it to confirm whether a co-resident is a son, boarder, or unrelated. [Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania,_United_States_Genealogy#Census_Records]
6. **Search the Miners' Journal (Pottsville) for accident reports, obituaries, and labor trial coverage** — the coal industry generated extensive named-worker coverage throughout 1860–1890.

---
**Unsurveyed anthracite coal counties:** Luzerne, Lackawanna, Northumberland, and Carbon counties are part of the same anthracite coal region and each needs its own locality survey. Records for the Lackawanna Valley before Lackawanna County's formation from Luzerne County are filed under Luzerne County.

output.text_response:
Here is the locality research guide the agent produced, logged as **loc_001** in your project:

---

## Vermont Pre-Statehood Locality Guide (ca. 1760–1791)

### Jurisdictional Context

This period sits across three overlapping legal identities:

1. **New Hampshire grants (pre-1764)** – Benning Wentworth issued grants from Portsmouth for lands west of the Connecticut River.
2. **New York colonial jurisdiction (1764–1777)** – New York's courts refused to recognize the NH grants, creating the "New Hampshire Grants" conflict and the rise of the Green Mountain Boys.
3. **Vermont Republic (1777–1791)** – Vermont declared itself an independent republic in 1777 and operated as one until admission as the 14th state in March 1791.

An ancestor's records can sit in any of these three places depending on the year and document type.

---

### Key Record for This Era

**Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule** — the earliest systematic resident list for what would become Vermont. Names roughly 1,800 grantees of New Hampshire land grants. This is the first place to look for any ancestor resident here before independence.

---

### What Records Exist and Where They Are Held

| Record Type | Coverage | Repository |
|---|---|---|

# Locality Guide: Vermont (Pre-Statehood Period, ca. 1760–1791)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Status during period:** Vermont did not exist as a legal entity until March 4, 1791 (FamilySearch place_search dateRange "+1791/"). Before 1791, the territory operated under three overlapping authorities: New Hampshire colonial authority (which issued the "New Hampshire Grants" — township charters to settlers), New York colonial and then state authority (which refused to recognize those grants), and — from 1777 — the self-declared Vermont Republic. The Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule, described by the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy), was "prepared under New York colonial authority before statehood" and directly documents the NH/NY conflict.
- **County seat / administrative center:** No territorial capital; Vermont towns were the primary civil administrative unit throughout this period.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Contested: New Hampshire and New York (colonial period); Vermont Republic (1777–1791); United States (from 1791).
- **Population during period:** FamilySearch's population data tool returned no figures for Vermont before 1791.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming and lumbering; rapid in-migration from southern New England colonies during the 1760s–1780s.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly settlers of English descent from Massachusetts and Connecticut; smaller numbers of Scots-Irish and other groups.
- **Religious denominations:** Congregationalist dominant among early settlers from southern New England; Baptist, Methodist, and other Protestant denominations also established in the late 18th century.
- **Key historical events:** The New Hampshire Grants dispute (New York v. NH-grant settlers, 1760s–1777); the Green Mountain Boys' resistance under Ethan Allen; the American Revolutionary War (1775–1783); Vermont Republic period (1777–1791).

## Boundary changes
- **Before 1777:** Territory claimed by both New York and New Hampshire. NH had issued numerous township grants; NY's colonial courts refused to recognize them. The Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy) enumerates approximately 1,800 grantees of NH grants that NY disputed, documenting the competing-authority situation directly.
- **1777:** Vermont declared itself the Vermont Republic, an independent state with its own courts and government.
- **1791:** Admitted to the Union as the 14th state; FamilySearch recognizes this as the jurisdiction's start date.

Pre-statehood records fall under three jurisdictional buckets depending on when and by whom the record was created: New Hampshire (land grants), New York (courts, competing land patents), or the Vermont Republic (town-level records, 1777 onwards). Researchers must search all three to cover the full period.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Statewide civil registration of births, marriages, and deaths began in **1857 at the state level**. This is confirmed by the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy). The entire pre-statehood period surveyed here (ca. 1760–1791) predates any statewide vital registration by more than 65 years.
- **What exists:** Town clerk records survive in some Vermont towns back to the 1770s but survive unevenly, per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy). These are town-level recordings, not a statewide series, and coverage depends entirely on the individual town.
- **Where held:** Individual town clerk offices across Vermont. No statewide series for this period.
- **Gaps:** The whole pre-statehood period is a vital-records gap at the state level. Town-clerk survival varies town by town.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism, marriage, and burial registers; family bibles; published town histories (which often reprint early records per the FamilySearch Wiki).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Congregationalist, Baptist, Methodist, and other Protestant denominations established in the late 18th century. Vermont-specific founding dates for individual congregations were not returned by any tool in this survey.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials; some congregations also kept membership rolls and confirmation registers.
- **Where held:** Individual church archives; some have been microfilmed by FamilySearch, but FamilySearch's collections_search returned 0 Vermont church record collections for 1760–1800, and volume_search returned 0 digitized volumes for this period — confirming a significant digitization gap for pre-statehood church records.
- **Language:** English.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The first federal census was taken in **1790**, which falls at the very end of the pre-statehood period (Vermont was included, then admitted in March 1791). The 1790 census lists heads of household only.
- **State census:** No Vermont state census for the pre-statehood period.
- **Other enumerations:** The Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy) enumerates approximately 1,800 grantees of New Hampshire grants, with each entry giving grantee name, township grant date, acreage, and disputed-claim status. The FamilySearch Wiki explicitly calls this "the earliest systematic resident list for the future state." It is the most important substitute-census document for the pre-1790 period.
- **Access:** FamilySearch volume_search returned 0 digitized volumes for Vermont 1760–1800, so digitization level for the 1771 Schedule specifically is unknown from this survey's tool results.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate administrations, guardianships, inventories, petitions; Vermont Republic and early county court records (1777–1791).
- **Date range:** Vermont Republic established its own courts from 1777; some probate records from 1777–1791 survive at the county courthouse level.
- **Where held:** Vermont county courthouses and the Vermont State Archives (Montpelier). FamilySearch volume_search returned 0 digitized probate volumes for Vermont 1760–1800.
- **Notes:** For persons in the territory before 1777, probate could have been filed under New York jurisdiction.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (New England town grant system).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** New Hampshire issued the original township grants; New York disputed those grants and held competing colonial authority. The Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy) was prepared under New York colonial authority specifically to document which New Hampshire grants NY refused to recognize. After 1777, the Vermont Republic and then the State of Vermont re-granted many disputed tracts.
- **Types:** Township charters (NH grants), competing patents (NY), Vermont Republic land grants, town deed books, town proprietors' records.
- **Date range:** New Hampshire grants from the 1750s–1760s; Vermont Republic grants from 1777 onwards.
- **Where held:** New Hampshire grants — New Hampshire State Archives (Concord, NH); New York competing grants — New York State Archives (Albany, NY); Vermont Republic and state records — Vermont State Archives (Montpelier, VT); town-level deed books at town clerk offices. FamilySearch volume_search returned 0 digitized land record volumes for Vermont 1760–1800.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** American Revolutionary War (1775–1783). Vermont men served in the Continental Army, Vermont militia, and in the Green Mountain Boys.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants (federal level, NARA); Vermont state militia records.
- **Where held:** NARA for federal service and pension records (accessible via Fold3 — https://www.fold3.com/ — per external_links_search results); Vermont State Archives for state militia records.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Town burial grounds and church cemeteries in each Vermont town; no specific cemetery names were returned by any tool for this period.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) is the curated external link for cemetery records per external_links_search results.
- **Physical records:** Sexton's records and burial registers held at town clerk offices or churches.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Vermont's earliest newspapers began in the 1780s; specific titles and date ranges were not returned by any tool in this survey.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) is the curated external link for historical newspapers per external_links_search; also Vermont Historical Society and University of Vermont library holdings.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, estate notices, land dispute notices, and court summonses are relevant for the late pre-statehood period.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Most settlers arriving in Vermont in the late 1700s came overland from Massachusetts, Connecticut, and New Hampshire rather than by sea. Border crossings from Canada (Province of Quebec) occurred via Lake Champlain.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (for any who arrived by sea at Boston or New York before moving inland), declarations of intention, naturalization. Vermont was settled primarily by people already in the colonies, so overseas passenger arrivals are less central; some settlers emigrated from Britain or continental Europe directly.
- **Where held:** NARA (https://www.archives.gov/ — per external_links_search results) for federal passenger and naturalization records.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Town property tax lists; Vermont Republic tax records from 1777 onwards.
- **Date range:** Town-level tax lists may survive from the 1770s–1780s for some towns.
- **Where held:** Town clerk offices; Vermont State Archives.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists can substitute for missing census years, documenting a person's residence in a specific town for a given year.

### Other record types
- **Town proprietors' records:** Many Vermont towns have surviving records of the original proprietors' meetings (land divisions, surveying, town governance from the settlement era). The FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy) notes that 19th-century town histories (most published 1860–1900) "often reprint colonial-era proprietors' records that are otherwise difficult to access." These are a primary resource for the pre-statehood period.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | 0 indexed collections returned for Vermont 1760–1800 (collections_search); 0 digitized volumes returned (volume_search) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (includes 1790 census) | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Revolutionary War service and pension records | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers (some Vermont titles from 1780s) | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | National Archives collections; also basis for Ancestry/Fold3 holdings | Varies |

All URLs above are from external_links_search curated results. FamilySearch's catalog tool was not available in this session's toolkit — check the FamilySearch Catalog at familysearch.org/catalog directly for Vermont microfilm holdings before concluding no digitized material exists.

**Coverage of this survey:** FamilySearch's volume_search returned 0 digitized volumes for Vermont 1760–1800 and collections_search returned 0 indexed collections. This is a coverage/digitization gap — it does not mean no records exist.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Vermont State Archives (Montpelier, VT) | Vermont Republic and early state records; land patents; legislative and court records; some probate | In-person; online finding aids at vermonthistory.org |
| Vermont town clerk offices | Town-level land records, deeds, pre-1857 vital recordings, proprietors' records | Contact individual town clerks |
| New Hampshire State Archives (Concord, NH) | New Hampshire land grants (township charters) for Vermont territory | In-person / mail request |
| New York State Archives (Albany, NY) | New York colonial court records; competing land patents; 1771 Grant Survey Schedule | In-person / online at archives.nysed.gov |
| Vermont Historical Society (Barre, VT) | Manuscripts, town histories, genealogical collections, newspaper holdings | In-person; some digital |
| NARA (Washington, D.C. / Waltham, MA) | Revolutionary War service and pension records; 1790 federal census | In-person / online via Ancestry and Fold3 |

## Records NOT online

Based on FamilySearch's collections_search and volume_search (both returning 0 results for Vermont 1760–1800):
- Town clerk vital records (births, marriages, deaths, 1770s–1791) — physical only at individual Vermont town clerk offices
- Town proprietors' records and land division books — physical at town clerk offices or Vermont State Archives
- Vermont Republic court and probate records (1777–1791) — physical at county courthouses and Vermont State Archives
- New Hampshire original land grants — physical at New Hampshire State Archives
- New York colonial court records for Vermont territory — physical at New York State Archives
- Vermont militia records — physical at Vermont State Archives

## Known record losses

No tool result in this survey identified confirmed destruction of specific Vermont pre-statehood record sets. The 0 results from collections_search and volume_search represent a digitization/coverage gap — not confirmed loss. Contact the Vermont State Archives and individual town clerks to verify which records survive in physical form before concluding a record is lost.

## Research tips

- **Start with the Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule.** It is the earliest systematic resident list for the future state, naming approximately 1,800 grantees of New Hampshire grants under New York colonial authority — the best available substitute for a pre-1790 enumeration. Source: FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy).
- **Search three jurisdictions, not one.** Because the territory was claimed by NH and NY before 1777, a land transaction may appear in New Hampshire grant records, New York court records, or both; after 1777, check Vermont Republic records. Never assume a single jurisdiction holds everything.
- **Town histories are a primary source for colonial records.** The FamilySearch Wiki confirms that 19th-century town histories (most published 1860–1900) "often reprint colonial-era proprietors' records that are otherwise difficult to access." Identify the ancestor's specific Vermont town and locate that town's published history early (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy).
- **Town clerk survival is uneven.** The FamilySearch Wiki confirms town clerk records "survive unevenly" — some towns have records from the 1770s, others do not. Contact each specific town clerk directly (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy).
- **The 1790 federal census is the first enumeration available.** It captures heads of household only. Vermont residents before 1790 must be found through town records, church registers, land records, tax lists, and the 1771 Grant Survey Schedule.
- **Re-run this locality guide before relying on FamilySearch Wiki absences.** During this survey, the FamilySearch Wiki pages for Vermont_Vital_Records, Vermont_Land_and_Property, Vermont_Church_Records, Vermont_Probate_Records, Vermont_Military_Records, and Vermont_Census all redirected to a generic fallback page — their contents could not be evaluated. Those pages may hold additional Vermont-specific guidance.

- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Town property tax lists; Vermont Republic tax records from 1777 onwards.
- **Date range:** Town-level tax lists may survive from the 1770s–1780s for some towns.
- **Where held:** Town clerk offices; Vermont State Archives.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists can substitute for missing census years, documenting a person's residence in a specific town for a given year.

### Other record types
- **Town proprietors' records:** Many Vermont towns have surviving records of the original proprietors' meetings (land divisions, surveying, town governance from the settlement era). The FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy) notes that 19th-century town histories (most published 1860–1900) "often reprint colonial-era proprietors' records that are otherwise difficult to access." These are a primary resource for the pre-statehood period.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |

| FamilySearch | 0 indexed collections returned for Vermont 1760–1800 (collections_search); 0 digitized volumes returned (volume_search) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (includes 1790 census) | Subscription |

All URLs above are from external_links_search curated results. FamilySearch's catalog tool was not available in this session's toolkit — check the FamilySearch Catalog at familysearch.org/catalog directly for Vermont microfilm holdings before concluding no digitized material exists.

**Coverage of this survey:** FamilySearch's volume_search returned 0 digitized volumes for Vermont 1760–1800 and collections_search returned 0 indexed collections. This is a coverage/digitization gap — it does not mean no records exist.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Vermont State Archives (Montpelier, VT) | Vermont Republic and early state records; land patents; legislative and court records; some probate | In-person; online finding aids at vermonthistory.org |
| Vermont town clerk offices | Town-level land records, deeds, pre-1857 vital recordings, proprietors' records | Contact individual town clerks |
| New Hampshire State Archives (Concord, NH) | New Hampshire land grants (township charters) for Vermont territory | In-person / mail request |
| New York State Archives (Albany, NY) | New York colonial court records; competing land patents; 1771 Grant Survey Schedule | In-person / online at archives.nysed.gov |
| Vermont Historical Society (Barre, VT) | Manuscripts, town histories, genealogical collections, newspaper holdings | In-person; some digital |
| NARA (Washington, D.C. / Waltham, MA) | Revolutionary War service and pension records; 1790 federal census | In-person / online via Ancestry and Fold3 |

## Records NOT online

Based on FamilySearch's collections_search and volume_search (both returning 0 results for Vermont 1760–1800):
- Town clerk vital records (births, marriages, deaths, 1770s–1791) — physical only at individual Vermont town clerk offices
- Town proprietors' records and land division books — physical at town clerk offices or Vermont State Archives
- Vermont Republic court and probate records (1777–1791) — physical at county courthouses and Vermont State Archives
- New Hampshire original land grants — physical at New Hampshire State Archives
- New York colonial court records for Vermont territory — physical at New York State Archives
- Vermont militia records — physical at Vermont State Archives

## Known record losses

No tool result in this survey identified confirmed destruction of specific Vermont pre-statehood record sets. The 0 results from collections_search and volume_search represent a digitization/coverage gap — not confirmed loss. Contact the Vermont State Archives and individual town clerks to verify which records survive in physical form before concluding a record is lost.

## Research tips

- **Start with the Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule.** It is the earliest systematic resident list for the future state, naming approximately 1,800 grantees of New Hampshire grants under New York colonial authority — the best available substitute for a pre-1790 enumeration. Source: FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy).
- **Search three jurisdictions, not one.** Because the territory was claimed by NH and NY before 1777, a land transaction may appear in New Hampshire grant records, New York court records, or both; after 1777, check Vermont Republic records. Never assume a single jurisdiction holds everything.
- **Town histories are a primary source for colonial records.** The FamilySearch Wiki confirms that 19th-century town histories (most published 1860–1900) "often reprint colonial-era proprietors' records that are otherwise difficult to access." Identify the ancestor's specific Vermont town and locate that town's published history early (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy).
- **Town clerk survival is uneven.** The FamilySearch Wiki confirms town clerk records "survive unevenly" — some towns have records from the 1770s, others do not. Contact each specific town clerk directly (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy).
- **The 1790 federal census is the first enumeration available.** It captures heads of household only. Vermont residents before 1790 must be found through town records, church registers, land records, tax lists, and the 1771 Grant Survey Schedule.
- **Re-run this locality guide before relying on FamilySearch Wiki absences.** During this survey, the FamilySearch Wiki pages for Vermont_Vital_Records, Vermont_Land_and_Property, Vermont_Church_Records, Vermont_Probate_Records, Vermont_Military_Records, and Vermont_Census all redirected to a generic fallback page — their contents could not be evaluated. Those pages may hold additional Vermont-specific guidance.
